speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to communicate to the House the substance of a letter which I received this morning from Colonel Farquhar, of whose death in action we heard last evening. It is with deep and unfeigned sorrow that we have heard the news of his untimely death. He was one of the finest characters I ever knew; and of all the able men who have filled the position of Military Secretary to the Governors General of Canada, I do not know of any one who performed the duties of that responsible position more efficiently, or who more thoroughly endeared himself to the Canadian people, than did Colonel Farquhar. I know that all the hon. members of the House will join with me in an expression of our deep sorrow for the loss which the Empire has sustained in his death, and in a message of sympathy to those whom he has left behind. A few days ago I had a letter from him in the trenches, in which he spoke with very great pride of the bearing of his regiment in the field, and of the fine work which they had done. At that time he said to me that the work had already received the strong commendation of the General Commanding the Division. This morning I received a further letter from him, and, if the House will permit me, I will read a few short extracts from 81 i
this letter and the telegrams which accompany it. The letter is dated March 4:
You may like to have a copy of these telegrams. The episode which called them forth was the rushing of a German trench and its subsequent destruction. The enemy had been very active in front of us, and a night reconnaissance made it clear to me that we had an opening. For various reasons, it was inadvisable to occupy the trench, so J got leave to rush it and pull down the parapet. Crabbe and Papineau led the party, the latter being our bomb thrower. They both showed very great
dash and ran the Teutons off their legs	
Nothing could have been more spirited than the way the men went in.
The messages wrhich Colonel Farquhar enclosed were as follows:
From the Irish Fusiliers:	"Well done
P.P.C.Li.1.''
From the Second Army through the Brigade Major of the Fifth Corps: The following message from the Fifth Corps: The corps commander has great pleasure in transmitting to you following message from Second Army: "The army commander wishes you to express to the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry his appreciation of the grand piece of work performed by them this morning.''
From General Plumer:	" Please give my
heartiest congratulations to the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry on their gallant and useful exploit."
From the officer commanding the 3rd King's Royal Rifles: "Best congratulations on splendid achievement last night. Please tell us how you do it."
From 1st Canadian Division:	" Heartiest
congratulations on success last night."
From Sir John French, Commander in Chief: " To Colonel Farquhar, commanding Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry: I heartily congratulate you and your gallant men on your successful operation this morning. Please express to Lieutenant Crabbe and the party he led my great appreciation of their services."
From General Snow:	" Well done P.P.C.
Congratulations on your splendid work."
From the Twenty-eighth Division through the Brigade Major: "Twenty-eighth Division wire hearty congratulations."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The intelligence which has just been conveyed to the House by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister arouses our sorrow and also our pride and gratification that we have this testimony to the good work done by our boys at the front. May I be permitted to say, I was touched to hear the name of Papineau mentioned as among those who have done so well. And the House will be gratified to know that the gentleman who is the bearer of this name is a great-grandson, of one who did good work in his day, and in his own way, for freedom in Canada. The words of praise of Gol. Farquhar, I am sure, are a deserved tribute. It has been my personal privilege to know a good many

of those who have held the office that he held, and it is due to him to say that in his tact, kindness and good judgment, as well as in his constant desire to do his duty, he was the equal of any of his colleagues.

speechtext: -MEMBERS IN ACTIVE SERVICE.

I desire to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to a matter of some importance. I refer to the failure to pay the members of the Northwest Mounted Police who have volunteered for active service. They are not being treated on the same basis as other officials of the Government. Tt has been represented to me, and I am in sympathy with the representation, that they should receive their full pay while on service with the forces at the front. I bring the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister with a view to ascertaining the possibility of something being done in the direction I have indicated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will look into the matter to which the hon. gentleman refers. At present I am not aware of any member of the Mounted Police being engaged in active service. Several members of the force made application to get their discharge in order that they might serve at the front. That is the only aspect of the matter that has been brought to my attention.

There are members of the Mounted Police now in the fighting line in France who are British army reservists, and who have gone to the front in that capacity. It is felt that they ought to be treated the same as other officials of the Canadian Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The matter has not been brought to my attention so far as I recollect. I will make inquiry with regard to it.

Bill No. 4, respecting certain patents of the Lohimann Company-sMr. Fripp-in Committee.
On section 1-order of commissioner:

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
As the hon. member
in whose name this Bill appears is not present, I may explain that this is an

application for the renewal of two patents, one of which was taken out in 1911 and the other in 1912. In each case the fees were paid for six years. Section 38 of the Patent Act provides that the patentee must manufacture within two years. Upon application, however, within six months after the granting of the patent, an order may be issued providing that the patent shall come under the provisions of section 44, which is commonly known as the licensing provision. Under this provision the owner of the patent may be required to grant a license to another person or persons to manufacture and sell the patented invention, and if this is not done within a certain period of time the patent may be cancelled. In this case the owner of the patent, Mr. Lohmann, died before the expiration of the time within which application would have to he made to have the patent come under the provisions of section 44; therefore that privilege was lost. The object of this Bill, therefore, is to place those who are now in possession of the patent in the same position as they would have been had the application for the licensing privilege been made within the specified time. The patent in question is a patent for the prevention of the corroding or rusting of metal. It is a process patent, and I understand that it is one in respect of which the Department of Agriculture would be willing to grant a license. It is not in every case that the owners of patents are allowed to come under the licensing provision, but when this application came before the Private Bills Committee it was thought that the privilege should be extended in this case. I myself felt, as a member of the committee, that, considering the whole circumstances, the application for renewal should be granted.
Mr. MACDONALD; Is the Commissioner of Patents satisfied?
Mr. REID; Yes; before the Bill was considered by the Private Bills Committee I took the matter up with the deputy minister and Commissioner of Patents, and they thought that it was fair and right that we should grant this renewal.

Steam Service between Canadian Atlantic ports and Australia and New Zealand, $140,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This is the same subsidy as last year, and a similar service has been carried on. There are some points in connection with it which it might be well to mention. The distance covered by this line of steamers is 15,656 miles, and it is in distance the longest service which we subsidize. It is a service which is subsidized one way. It takes exports from Canada to New Zealand and Australia. The vessels are free to get their freights as they choose back to the Old Country, and from the Old Country here, and then they pick up the service on this side. That arises from the fact that we cannot get a line, without expending a very large amount of money, which would keep to the one track, inasmuch as from Australia there is a comparatively small amount of freight offered for this side of the Atlantic, as Australia and New Zealand do the bulk of their trade exchange business with Canada by the Pacific Coast.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What will be the effect of the Panama canal on this route?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We cannot tell yet until it is tried by actual experiment, but the Panama canal might very well have the effect of carrying that traffic through it. The amount of freight that was carried last year was about equivalent to what was carried the year before, which had a value of $4,621,000 from Canada and $960,000 from the United States. The line is bound to fill all Canadian requirements before taking any freight from the United States. The articles that are principally exported are lumber, automobiles, vehicles, calcium carbide, paper, sole-leather, agricultural implements, rubbers, iron pipe, hardware, seed, fruit, cereal foods, wire, steel rails and organs. .

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What line of steamers is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The New Zealand Shipping Company.
May we expect to have a formal announcement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to the conclusion of negotiations on trade arrangements with New Zealand and Australia?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There is no conclusion and, therefore, there is no formal announcement to make yet.

It is four years since
you commenced.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There are two
parties to the bargain, and the Legislature in Australia has been subject to a good deal of political excitement and some political changes within the last year and 4 p.m. a half. They were in the throes of an election contest shortly after I reached Australia, and when that contest was decided the odd juncture was brought about of the dominant party, if you [DOT] can call it such, having a majority of one in the House and a majority of four to one against it in the Senate. Under those circumstances, not much progress was possible in any kind of legislation, and really nothing was done with the exception of passing estimates in which both sides agreed. There came another election contest by which the party that had been defeated the year before was successful in the House of Representatives, and retained the largest part of its majority in the Senate. That legislature had but a short meeting in the autumn, and then adjourned to meet again in the middle of April. They passed a resolution embodying tariff changes, and that resolution, of course, as with us, has the effect of law, but the tariff Bill itself remains for action when Parliament meets again. In that, tariff preference was arranged for the United Kingdom, the Mother Country, and for her alone.

What was the
nature of that preference? Do I understand the minister to say there was a change made in the British preference applicable alone to the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The tariff resolution which was brought down in the first part of the session raised the duty on almost all articles that were imported into Australia, and instituted a preference of ten per cent on articles coming from the United Kingdom, and giving that preference to no

other country. The matter stands for consideration, and whether or not anything will be done before they pass their tariff legislation cannot be said.
Then the minister is not likely to conclude any treaty with Australia in the near future; is that what the minister states.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The minister
states what he has stated; that no conclusions have yet been reached and consequently there cannot be any conclusions announced.
Is this subsidy meant for the promotion of foreign commerce?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, foreign commerce in this case with exclusive relation to the exports from Canada and without reference to imports.
Does the minister not expect anything to come back to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; frankly I did not expect anything to come back on these steamers, because under the arrangements which are necessary with the subsidy that is given, these steamers would have to load up in Australia and go may be to Africa, thence to Europe, and then come back here, and of course nothing could be taken by that roundabout route. I am saying nothing as to what stimulus in the way of exports back again has been given, but they would find their way through the Pacific ports.

Under usual circumstances I should think if was a very unprofitable line to subsidize; but perhaps I ought to congratulate this Government that they are not bringing anything back, because that might interfere to a certain extent with things being made in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This is, I think, the sole instance in which we have given way to the prejudices of my hon. friend.
Ocean and mail service between Canada and Great Britain, $1,000,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How is that -applied ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This service has been almost completely broken up, although if we compare it with the mail service from New York, we are not much worse of comparatively than the people are in the United States. Taking in two new steamers, the Calgarian and the Alsatian,
we commenced with a very good selection of steamers running from seventeen up to nineteen knots in speed. As soon as the war broke out, there commenced a system of requisition by the British Government for the purposes of the war. Owing to vessels being taken off from time to time, the service has declined until (now the whole fleet of the Canadian Pacific running between Canada and the old country is reduced to three cargo vessels and one passenger vessel. The best vessels of the Allan line have been requisitioned and are now in transport service. The Canadian Northern vessels have gone entirely off the route, having also been taken by the British Government for transport purposes. The White Star line may have one not very large vessel still running; all the others have been taken. The Allan line have still quite a number of vessels, but they are less important and of smaller cargo capacity and less speed. Therefore at the present time not only is this service crippled to a very large extent, but we are up against a somewhat grave condition of affairs in connection with the transportation of products from this side of the Atlantic to the other. The arrangements mentioned in the House the other day, that had been made by the Admiralty for the putting on of 18 vessels to carry supplies, unfortunately does not directly provide any carriage for general produce. It is meant entirely and solely for the carriage of British Government supplies, and incidentally of supplies going to our own troops, if there is space therefor. It is calculated, however, if we take into account what has been ordered in.this country and what has to go, that if those 18 vessels are secured,	all	the	space
that they can afford	will be taken
up with Government supplies, and that they will not afford any outlet either for general freights from this side or for freights which originate in contracts of companies or private individuals for war nur-poses on the other side. It of course relieves what may be possible of a chartered vessel-fleet from having to carry those supplies, and incidentally it is a help to the general transport of the country in that respect. There is a very great scarcity of vessel-space throughout the world, and we experience it in Canada to a verv laree extent. A list has been made of the vessels on the Great Lakes which are more or less able to carry ocean freight, and I believe that a considerable portion of the tonnase of the lakes will be chartered for the carrv-

ing of freight across the Atlantic. In fact, some of the lake vessels have been chartered already. These vessels, however, are small in carrying capacity, and therefore will not take the place of the immense freighters which have disappeared from our lines. At the present time an effort is beine made- and I hope it will be successful-bv which a number of the vessels that have been taken from our main lines may be released by the British Government, that Government chartering vessels from other than our regular lines to fill their places. All that can be done is 'ait this moment being done to bring that about, so that bv the first of May, if possible, we miay have a portion of the old carrying fleet back again at work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Have vou a special contract with any company?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The contract runs until the last of this month: but the vessels have been so disorganized that we have not had the service that we exnected to have; nor have we paid the subsidies that we expected to pay. Although the contract runs up to the end of this month, a system of readjustment will have to be followed whereby we shall pay as subsidies what is reasonable considering the less speed and less capacity of the vessels.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suppose you have no exclusive contract with any company; but you subsidize four companies, namely, the Canadian Pacific, the Allan Line, the Canadian Northern and the White Star, and you pay according to the amount of mail matter which they carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. They are paid on a basis of the speed and the capacity that they give us as compared with the speed and the capacity of the vessels which were contracted for.
Steam service between Canada and- Cuba, $25,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The appropriation was expended during the past years, although not during the year that has just passed. This service was carried on by the Elder-Dempster line. Mexican affairs became, as my hon. friend knows, very troubled and very mixed, and Elder, Dempster & Company gave up their service to

There has been no subsidized service between Canada and Cuba during the last year; but this item was kept in and is still kept in, so that if it happens that an advantageous arrangement can be made, we shall have this sum with which to carry it out.

Has the minister made any effort to negotiate some preferential tariff arrangements on behalf of Canada with Cuba? I do not know whether that is a practical question, but I have often heard it suggested in the maritime provinces, particularly in my own province, which at one time had a very considerable trade with the island of Cuba. Under favourable conditions a large trade might be built up between Cuba and Canada, particularly through Eastern Canada. I have heard the opinion expressed by business men in Halifax that if some modifications of the Cuban tariff on Canadian products could be secured it would facilitate trade very much. I imagine this matter has been brought to the attention of the minister at some time or other, and 1 should be glad to hear a statement from him with regard to it.
feir GEORGE FOSTER:	The attention
of the department has been constantly directed to that matter. But as mv friend knows, the United States and Cuba up to the present time have a trade arrange ment by which each gives the other a preference

affair, a portion of the Constitution of Cuba?

speechtext: I do not think so. But changes in the sugar tariff, which was the great incentive to Cuba to make the arrangement, will soon come into operation in the United States, and sugar from Cuba will no longer be in a favoured position in the United States market. When that takes place it may be possible to make some arrangement with Cuba. But at present, while that preference continues, there is not much that can be done. Cuba offers a market for quite a number of our products. The returns under the old service show that in 1912 the value of products exported was $62,969, consisting chiefly of fish, potatoes, paper, lumber, oats and hay.

If the minister has the information at hand, I should like to know what the imports and export figures are for the eleven months of the present fiscal year ending February. I am particularly anxious to know the effect of the West India Treaty upon trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I have not the figures referred to, but I will make a note of the point, and before we are through with these Estimates I will give an answer. I can give the figures of the carrying by this route. I think there was a sailing or two with these new vessels in the latter part of 1913, but the service really began in 1914. There was an unfortunate shipwreck, and one of the vessels went down on the Nova Scotia coast, and that somewhat disarranged the service. I can say generally, from inquiries made the other day, that the freight offerings are very satisfactory, in fact, the agent of the company
told me that they were not able to take all the freight that offered from sailing to sailing, and a quantity remains over. The movement of flour has been particularly good. The passengers carried in 1914 in twenty-six trips were 3,287, and the freight 142,718 tons, value $2,618,000. In this there was nothing of United States origin, all being of Canadian origin.

Can the minister inform me whether there are any differences between the Canadian Government and the West Indian Islands, who were parties to the treaty with respect to the interpretation of that treaty? My recollection is that since the close of Parliament last June, there was some difference of opinion in regard to sugar, some change in regard to the Dutch standard. I may not be right as to that, but my recollection is that there was a good deal of correspondence on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The correspondence that took place had reference not to the matter that the hon. gentleman has just mentioned, but to the extension of the preference to outside dependencies. An Order in Council was passed two years ago under which we extended the British preference to all the British dependencies that had not previously enjoyed it, with one or two unimportant exceptions. The question then arose as to what effect that would have on the sugar market, having particular regard to Mauritius sugar. It was felt in the West Indies that this extension of the preference might affect the Canadian market for the West India Island product. As a matter of fact, not a pound of sugar came into this country from Mauritius last year; I understand that Mauritius sugar goes chiefly in other directions. After a good deal of correspondence, it was decided that upon the expiration of the preference given to the other West Indian Islands and British dependencies, the question with regard to Mauritius will be taken up with the consideration of what further general action will be taken in this respect.
There was some question as to the Dutch standard, was there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Dutch standard is made up every year in Amsterdam, chiefly from a collection of Java sugars. This standard is made up by traders, and has no official significance in Holland, not being used as a basis of tariff. There wa3 some little difference in colour between the

standard of this year and that of last year, hut the new standards are now made up and will be here in the course of a few weeks. There may be no difference between the new standard and standards of the past.

What is the nature of the Order in Council-perhaps I am not describing the instrument properly-under which the British Government, shortly after the declaration of war last year, prohibited the export of sugar from the West India Islands? Did that prohibition apply to exports to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
The West India exporters, under that Order in Council, could export only to the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Is that Order in Council still in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. Great
Britain's idea was to make it possible for her to buy all these sugars in the West Indies and other places, to sell them to the British refiners at a certain rate and then to fix the price at which the refiners should sell to the consuming public; this she did. As soon, however, as Canada directed the attention of the British Government to the manner in which this might affect our trade, the prohibition was entirely taken away so far as Canada was concerned.
How long was it in existence? Under its provisions, were large quantities of sugar actually purchased by the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not think
it operated to prevent any sugar from coming to Canada that would otherwise have come. The prohibition lasted about three weeks; perhaps less.
Do the freight rates between Canada and the West Indies meet with public favour, or is there adverse criticism of them? Are the rates revised each year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The contract is so drawn that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has the power to approve the tariff of rates. No tariff of rates can be put into effect until it receives the assent of the minister. The tariff rates that were instituted when this service was inaugurated were about the same as those which existed under the Pickford and Black

arrangement; at the same time the vessels engaged in the service were more commodious and better in every respect. If there were any changes at all in the rates, there were but few; in some cases I think they were a little lower. When the war broke out, bringing with it additional risks and additional transport difficulties, the rates then in force were considered too low. My hon. friend knows that the service between Canada and the West Indies is a very difficult one. Although outward freights have been very good, the very occurrence to which my hon. friend referred, practically took away the major amount of return freight, and shipments' coming back were so small, the war risks so great, the rate of wages paid so much higher, that for these and other reasons the company asked for an increase in their rates. To a certain extent I acquiesced in that respect; I did not give them all they asked for, but I did give a fair increase in rates. I would not be able to say there is no criticism, but so far as I can judge, I think the rates are reasonable, and I think that that is the general view. This company have always treated very sympathetically any suggestions I have made with a view to the betterment of the service, and in most instances have done what I thought was reasonable that they should do.
Have these rates been increased ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The rates have been increased, by permission of the department.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Simply for the reasons which I have been trying to state. It may be argued that if you subsidize a steamship service, no longer should the general influences which go to make freight rates higher or lower have their force; that the subsidy itself is a guarantee against any increase of freight rates. While that argument has some force, I do not think that under all circumstances it is applicable. After considering the matter carefully, and having regard to the best advice which I was in a position to obtain, I gave this increase in the rates of freight, deeming it to be not unreasonable under the circumstances.

Upon what principle did they ask for that increase ? Was it because of a loss in freight, which would have to be met by an increase in rates, or

was it because they wanted to participate in the world-wide increase in freight rates ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think I stated, but perhaps not clearly enough, the grounds upon which they claimed the increase. First, owing to the prevailing abnormal conditions, the freight from the West Indies practically fell to nothing.
When you take away the sugar business you take away the greater part of return cargo to fill the transport from the West Indies. They were therefore in the Dosition of having a contribution one way of freight that was large, and another contribution the other way that was abnormally small; and that arose from a condition over which neither they nor we had any control. There has also been an increase in wages, and in the price of provisions and coal; so that in view of all these conditions and the war risk I think their ground for an increase a reasonable one.
Will this freight rate tariff remain in force for a year, or does the department reserve the right to amend it in the event of a return to normal conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, certainly, we have that right. This is iust a temporary increase. When these abnormal conditions pass away or begin to pass away the increase in rates will diminish or pass away along with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, they have a very good interinsular service. Their services fit in with each other very well; in fact,
I think the best possible arrangement has been made in that respect.
