stagedirection
speechtext: which they take some timber, box boards, and the like. From St. John they take deal and lumber. These steamers carry a great variety of freight. Last year they carried goods of Canadian origin * to the value of $9,000,000 odd, nearly $1,000,000 more than the preceding year; and of United States origin, $1,705,000, as against $3,000,000 the preceding year, so that Canadian exports show an increase for the year of a little over a million dollars, and United States exports a decrease of a little over a million. The ships take from Montreal chiefly oats, wheat, cereals, oil cakes, hay, lumber, cotton waste, jewellers' sweepings and so on.

It is a very useful service. Have any steps been taken to regulate the freight rates, particularly since the outbreak of war ? I notice by the newspapers, and I have heard from shippers of lumber, that vthe freight rate on lumber has almost trebled since the war broke out. Now, if the Government were to see that reasonable and fair rates were charged- and I think that under the subsidy contracts they have power to control the freight rates-it might do a great deal towards making general freights reasonable. If the subsidized lines would carry at reasonable rates, other steamship companies not subsidized would be obliged to follow suit, I think, to a certain extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, to a certain extent, provided the call was not so immeasurably greater than could be filled by the subsidized steamers. I do not recollect a single complaint as to rates having been made to the department with reference to this line, and as regards the freight rates of the Manchester line I think I should have heard if there had been any complaints, for such matters very quickly find their way to the department. With reference to our regular lines, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Allan line, and others, I know from personal knowledge that they have kept their own freight rates down, and not only as regards the transport of British Government supplies and our own supplies, but as regards what other freights they have been able to carry in addition. They have kept their rates down to a reasonable level, and I am very glad to know they have not taken advantage of the general rise in charters and freights to exact extortionate rates. As my hon. friend knows, the minister has the power of revising the rates, but it is a very difficult task in these times to decide what a reasonable freight rate is.

Winter steam service between St. John, Dublin and Belfast, $7,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the usual vote.
Was the service performed this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, in a way.
Who were the contractors ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The same contractors as before, the Ulster Steamship Company Limited,	of Belfast,
but instead of the usual eight or nine sailings, only four were given. Some of their vessels were taken and the service was disturbed. Of course, we have only paid the subsidy in proportion to the trips they made.

Why is it necessary in
these various services between Canada and British ports in the winter season to compel the vessels to make the two ports of St. John and Halifax? Why could not there be some arrangement under which some lines would go to St. John and some to Halifax, so that there would be a direct service to and from each port? There is an added danger and delay in compelling the steamers to make both ports. I do not know whether it is feasible, I do not know whether the people of the two ports would be satisfied or not, but I have always thought that it was a very great mistake, both in connection with the mail and freight service, to compel the companies to make both ports. I believe the people whom I have the honour -to represent would not be selfish or unreasonable in the matter, but would be quite willing to have these services fairly divided between the two ports. It seems to me that during the winter season the services between Canada and Great Britain, and between Canada and the West Indies, could be divided between the two ports. The present arrangement adds to the inconvenience, delay and expense of the vessels, and it must add very greatly to the inconvenience of shippers.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
A good deal of what my hon. friend says may be true, but he and I have lived some considerable time and we have both been acquainted with St. John and Halifax during all that long time. My hon. friend knows that there are some difficulties that stand in the way of an adjustment on this brotherly and economical

basis that he is proposing. As far as this service, and what I may call the smaller services, are concerned, there has been no agitation in the last two years as between St. John and Halifax. They seem to have settled into the way of carrying on the transportation system and-
I suppose they have got tired agitating.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It would be courting the fates, I am afraid, if I were to be adventurous enough to propose a change So long as things are going on in peace and quietness, I would rather let them go on.

I am sorry to hear that from my hon. friend. It seems to me that he would be just the one to take hold of this matter, ignore what has taken place in the past and strike out upon the new path which he would consider to be right. It is a great mistake to be satisfied with what has been in the past. We are apt to get into a rut and continue a state of affairs which it is not advantageous to continue. My hon. friend says that there has been no complaint during the last two or three years. He can understand that the people of St. John have got tired of complaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
They will be
pretty well tired out if they do not complain.
I do not see why a satisfactory arrangement could not be made that would be more convenient to both sides.

Does my hon.
friend refer to passenger, freight and mail services?

Yes, all services. If we could not give a weekly service at each port then I would give a fortnightly service, one week to Halifax and the next week to St. John. In regard to freight steamers, I would pick out the different subsidized lines and arrange for some to go to St. John and some to go to Halifax, so that each port would have a direct service. I am sure it would be an infinitely better service if you had one direct mail steamer running from St. John and one from Halifax. Even if there could only be a fortnightly service from each port you would have a direct service. There is waste of money, there is added danger and inconvenience and neither port gets the opportunity for development which might take place if there were a direct service.
m

I have no doubt that in so far as the freight service is concerned, there must be a divided service as between St. John and Halifax. St. John is a very important port for export and import trade, and doubtless it will be a port which will in the future handle a great deal of our import and export traffic. I would not care to admit, however, that the same division in steamship services could be as fairly applied to the ordinary passenger and mail steamships. I would prefer to take the position that the steamships should be left to select their own ports and that the Government should make a contract with the companies for the port which they desire. I think they would be the better judges as to the ports which would afford them the best of facilities and which, generally speaking, would be most acceptable to the travelling public. The Government, more than a year ago, adopted as its policy the suggestion I am now making, but under political pressure I fear they were led to abandon it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce could tell us exactly what was the cause of the abandonment of that programme. I do not say he should tell us, but I only mean to say that if he cared to he might and could. There is a distinction between the freight service and the ordinary passenger and mail service. I would like to ask the Minister if there was a contract entered into recently for the Atlantic mail service with the Canadian Pacific Railway, White Star and Canadian Northern lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For next year?
For next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is absolutely impossible to make any contracts; there are no vessels for you to contract with.
I understand that, but I thought a contract might be tentatively made hoping that normal conditions would shortly be resumed and that the service could again be started up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The trouble
about that is that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for instance, which contributed most of the vessels, and some very excellent ones, have not a single vessel of that description, and they do not know whether these vessels will come back to them in two months or a year or whether they will ever come back. We have taken the vote so that if matters do arrange themselves we can make a contract, but the

contract will only be made on the basis of the vessels offered.
Winter service between St. John and Glasgow, $7,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This service is performed by the Donaldson line. They have been interrupted as well, and they made but eleven voyages last year instead of fifteen or sixteen.
Winter service between St. John, Halifax, and London, $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The same remark applies to this; they have made a lesser number of voyages than in preceding years, but they have carried a large amount of freight in the meantime.
Steam service between Canada and Australia or New Zealand, or both, on Pacific ocean, $180,509.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What company has this contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Union
Steamship Company of New Zealand.
Was this service interrupted?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
These vessels have not been requisitioned, and they are carrying on the service.
Steam service between Canada, China and Japan, $253,333.34.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That service has been interrupted, and, in fact, dismantled. The Empresses have all gone, one after another, and the Monteagle is at present the only vessel left.
Steam service between Prince Rupert, B.C., and Queen Charlotte Islands, $16,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What company conducts this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it a weekly service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There are two round trips each month from November to March, and four round trips each month during the remaining seven months of the year.
Steam service between Victoria and San Francisco, $3,000.
What traffic is there to justify this?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This is not justified by traffic, although it has traffic. This is to keep the covenant which was made at

Confederation with British Columbia, under which a service was to be kept up between Victoria and Vancouver and San Francisco.
Is it at all utilized?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. The subsidy at that time was in the vicinity of $20,000. I remember when I was in the Government before, the uselessness of the service, compared with the amount of money
5 p.m. expended on it, did not commend itself to the department, and we cut it down to this sum, which is the smallest with which we could keep the traffic alive.
Is it a passenger and freight service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes; 3,630 passengers were carried; 3,534 tons weight, and 4,386 tons measurement. The traffic last year was a little less than in the preceding year.
In which direction is the greater portion of the traffic?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The out traffic in passengers is 200 more than the in traffic. The in traffic in freight is the larger, which will be exactly to the liking of my hon. friend from Red Deer.

But it makes out a very strong case against the views of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to maintain a steamship company to carry into Canada so much of American products. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the member for Red Deer had better get together on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am afraid we are as near together as we will ever get on this point.
Is there any desire on the part of the people of British Columbia to continue this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. I made them the offer that I would take this sum of money and put it on any other service, if they would agree to it, but they would not. So long as objection is made the articles of faith must be adhered to.
What are the chief products inward?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The articles exported are liquors, automobiles, household goods and salmon; the income is bottle caps, cement caps and empty cylinders.
Steam service between Victoria, Vancouver, way ports and Skagway, $12,500.

speakerposition: subtopic
Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The total distance run on this service is 447 knots; the number of passengers carried was 7,500, and the freight 8,000 tons.
Steam service between Vancouver and northern ports of British Columbia, $16,800.
I suppose this service is to ports in northern British Columbia which are not served by a railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Who are the contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Union Steamship Company of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does that include the service between Vancouver and Prince Rupert?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The regular
sailings are from Vancouver to Granby Bay, which is on Osbervatory Inlet.
The service takes in the northern British Columbia ports from Vancouver Island.
Steam service, from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1915, between GaspS Basin and Dalhousie or Campbellton, $20,000.
Will the minister explain that item?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend knows that item as well as I do, and the section of country which is served. I will explain the situation of the matter as it is. This service was performed between Gaspe Basin and Dalhousie and Campbellton. The old service was carried on by the Gaspe and Baie des Chaleurs Steamship Company. Last year the proprietor of that line died, and the estate was not able to carry on the service. An arrangement was made for two years by which the service, which was then semi-weekly, should be made a weekly service, and the amount paid was half of the old subsidy. This service was undertaken by the present company, which put on two boats, the Gaspesia and the old Canada. The boats ran all the way through to Montreal, thus making the .weekly service. No subsidy was given either theoretically or practically for the service between Gaspe and Montreal, because there are other subsidized services on that line; but it was considered by this company that it would be profitable to it if it extended the service to Montreal. The company therefore ran its two boats to Montreal and did a better business for itself. I cannot say that the service in that way was at all satisfactory to the people between Gasp6
and Campbellton. It certainly was not satisfactory, because what the people asked for was the old semi-weekly service. I had some negotiations with the company, and it was willing to take up the semi-weekly service be.tween Gaspe and Campbellton with the steamship Gaspesia, but it asked the sum of $20,000 to do it. The company is under contract to carry on the service as last year until the end of the present year.
I made the company an offer of $15,000 for this service, if it would put on the Gaspesia between Campbellton and GaspA At present I do not see my way clear to give $20,000 for that service, and the company does not see its way altogether clear to perform it for any less. The company can stand upon its contract and run the service until the end of 1915 as it was run last year. Unless either the company or I come to a better frame of mind on the subject, that is the way in which the matter will have to stand.

I understand that the
merchants on the coast are quite willing that the service to Montreal should be kept up, because the minister will understand that it is a great economy to carry by water all the goods that are required in our district. As regards the service between Campbellton and Dalhousie and Gaspe, especially during the months of May, June and July, during the fishing season, it is very important that there should be a semiweekly service between those points. The minister should stretch a point and see that that service is put on, if not for the whole season, at least for half of the season. I know that the minister has had representations from Campbellton and Dalhousie. I hope that he will give the matter full consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I certainly will
do so.
Steam service between Halifax and Canso, $5,000.
What steamer is performing that service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Scotia.
Steam service between Halifax and Newfoundland via Cape Breton ports, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That service is
being carried on by the Seal, an excellent vessel, which gives a good service.

Can the minister tell
me at what ports in Cape Breton the Seal proposes to call?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Halifax to St.
Peter's, St. Peter's to Grand Narrows, Grand Narrows to Baddeck, Baddeck to North Sydney, North Sydney to Sydney, Sydney to Ingonish, Ingonish to Neil's harbour, Neil's harbour to Aspy bay, Aspy bay to St. Paul's island, St. Paul's island to Channel, Channel to Codroy, Codroy to Bay St. George, Bay St. George to Bay of Islands, Bay of Islands to Bonne Bay. If there is any other hay or island there than those, the Seal would probably call at them. She seems to cover most of them.

What will happen
when the St. Peter's canal is closed? Some of those ports are available only by reason of the fact that the Seal goes through that canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It was closed
last year.
It is not closed yet.

I understood that the Department of Railways and Canals had determined to close the canal and complete the improvements.
Steam service between Halifax, Spry Bay and ports in Cape Bretori, $4,000.

This is the only steamship line that gives an all-year-round service in eastern Nova Scotia. I am particularly interested in this because it is the only means of communication we have by water [DOT]between Halifax and the constituency I have the honour to represent. The contract expires, I think, about the 21st of March. Will a new contract be made in due course?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If not already made it will be made.
Steam service between Halifax, South Cape Breton and Bras d'Or Lake ports, $4,000.
Is this vessel, the Scots-burn, assigned to call at any particular ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The same ports as last year.

I am anxious that she should call at the northern ports in Victoria county. When steamers are subsidized it is desirable that they should make calls at ports not otherwise reached. They are only too anxious to slip these calls if they are allowed to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The ports called at are Halifax, St. Peter's, Grand Narrows, Iona, Baddeck, Sydney, North Sydney, Glace Bay, Port Morien, Main-a-dieu, Louis-
burg, Gabarus, East Bay, Johnston's Harbour, Irish Cove, Big Pond and Castle Bay.
It does not go north at all. It is highly desirable that these ports should be called at.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This is the same list as last year.

The northern part of Victoria is a great fishing centre, and it is sometimes very difficult for the fishermen to get their catch to Halifax. As this is a subsidized service, it would be of great advantage to have a vessel call at these ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps some other service goes there.

At these places along the Bras d'Or lakes, where the railroad runs and where the boats are almost knocking against one another, it is not so important to have a subsidized service as at places along the coast where there are no railroads.
Steam service from the opening to the close of navigation in 1915 between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands, $18,000.
Has the minister ever had a request from Mr: Leslie for a subsidy for a service between some Nova Scotia point and the Magdalen islands?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: On several occasions, but not this year.
The minister must have discouraged him very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There was no very great encouragement given last vear. though he wias listened to and we discussed the matter. But it does not seem possible to run a double service to the Magdalen islands, and the service now under discussion is the old-established line, and far the quickest route for mail.

Mr. Leslie's application has strong support from the Halifax Board of Trade and those interested in fisheries, and I believe the service would be of great advantage to the people of the Magdalen islands. I hope that if the matter is again presented the minister will look at it more favourably, at least that the minister will not discourage the applicant.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I shall be glad to see him.
Has the minister had an application for a subsidy for a service between the Magdalen islands and the mainland of Gaspe to which the islands belong?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not that I remember.
The present service is from Pictou?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. a verv eood vessel and a very good service.
Steam service between Petit de Grat and Intercolonial railway terminus at Mulgrave, $7,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Leslie is the contractor for this service.

Has the minister received
word as to inefficiency of the service in the winter time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Representations were made last autumn and winter. But at a certain season, as the hon. member knows, it is very difficult to make some of these ports, and you do not want to impair the ship. I think the company has done its best under the circumstances.

The complaint that I have in mind is that he is obliged to lay the steamer up for inspection and repair at certain seasons of the year, and that he does not carry on the service with another boat during that time. The company which performed that service previously had several boats, and when the regular boat was laid up for repairs, the service was not interrupted. I suppose the contractor could hardly be expected to keep two boats on hand for the purpose of performing this service.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There is a provision in the contract whereby he is permitted to lay off for two weeks in winter and two weeks in summer. These are comparatively short periods.
Schooner service between Pictou, New Glasgow, Antigonisb and Mulgrave, $1,000.
Has an application for increased subsidy in connection with this service been received this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Some correspondence has been had with regard to an increased subsidy, or, more properly, with regard to the placing of a different kind of vessel on the route, which would involve a larger subsidy. It is not possible during war time to accede to these requests.

I think this is the only schooner service along the coast. Until a few years ago, we had a steam service. The service performed by the schooner is very satisfactory, all things considered, but the
trouble is that the harbours have been neglected and steamboats are not able to reach the wharves. During the years 1912, 1913 and 1914 money was provided for the necessary improvements, but the work has not been done, and as a result we now have a schooner service instead of a steam service.
If the minister has any influence with the Minister of Public Works, I would ask him to do something in the way of having repairs made to the wharves and breakwaters, and to have dredging done at these ports which will ensure it as satisfactory a service as we have had in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is true that because of the shallow water it is difficult for large boats to get into these ports. As to how much influence I may have with the Minister of Public Works, I do not quite know; I will try him and see.
Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1915 between Pictou, Mulgrave and Cheticamp, $7,500.
Is it the intention of the department to subsidize a schooner to operate along a portion of this route?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, it is not.

That is unfortunate. The port of Margaree is in pretty had condition and a steamboat would be of no use, because it would not be able to get to the wharf. If a schooner were subsidized to run say from Margaree to Mulgrave, it would be a great help to the people living round that port. There was a time when a steamer could get into that harbour, but unfortunately, like other ports along the coast of Antigonish county, this port has been neglected. $10,000 was provided in 1910-11 to effect an improvement in the condition of the harbour, hut the amount has not been spent. I am sorry that the minister does not see his way clear to provide a small subsidy for a schooner along with route.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As my hon.
friend will see, I am not adding any increases by way of subsidies. I am afraid that if I once departed from the rule, the whole fence would come down.
Steam service between Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton and Newfoundland, $16,500.

What are the ports of
call?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The service is carried ou by the Dominion Coal Company, Limited, between Montreal and Newfoundland, with calls at Prince Edward Island

and Cape Breton ports. It is practically applicable to Prince Edward Island in that it gives the island the advantages of regular calls for the traffic which during certain months of the year it carries on to a considerable extent with Newfoundland. The ports of call are: in Prince Edward Island, Summerside and Charlottetown; in Nova Scotia, North Sydney and Sydney; on westbound trips, Sydney.
The terms of last year were similar to these?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

I understand that the steamer, although it made regular trips into Sydney harbour, did not call at the port of North Sydney, which is named as one of the ports of call. I hope the minister will see to it that the company carry out their contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The calls at Summerside and North Sydney are conditional upon there being a sufficient depth ot water and a reasonable amount of freight offering at those ports. I have not received any complaints with reference to either of these ports, but I shall be glad to consider any representations which may be made.

The complaint may
not have reached the minister last year, but it is said that a considerable amount of freight for North Sydney was taken by the steamer to Sydney, and that the consignees had to get it over on the ferry or the best way they could. The boats of the Reid Newfoundland Company call at the terminus of the Intercolonial railway at North Sydney; there is quite a depth of water there, and I do not see why the boats of this company should not call there also.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know that they have said that there is not a sufficient depth of water there, but I will look into the matter.
Steam service between Rivitre du Loup, Tadoussac, and other north shore ports, $6,000.
Sir WIlFRID LAURIER:	Is that a
summer service alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes.
Steam service between St. John and Bridgetown, $2,500.
Does this steamer call at Digby and intermediate ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Thirty-two
round trips are made between St. John and Bridgetown, calling at Ray's Creek, Tupper-ville, and Round Hill; and on and after

June 1, 1914, calling fortnightly at Clements-port and Deep Brook.
Steam service between St. John, Digby Annapolis and Granville, viz., along the west coast of the Ananpolis basin, $2,000.
Is this not a duplicate of the service mentioned in item 210?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is not a duplicate, with the exception of that part of the way from St. John *across. It is not a duplicate at the ports.

Would the minister
consider restoring the subsidy that was paid to the other steamship line between St. John and Bear river? It is a very important service, but the subsidy was withdrawn two or three years ago, and for reasons which never appeared to me very sound. Has the minister been asked to restore that subsidy?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think there
has been some correspondence about it.
There always has been some correspondence about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will look it up and give my hon. friend tne facts.
I would rather see the people who were giving that steamship service before get the subsidy, and the minister can keep his facts. I do not think the company was treated quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I shall be willing to discuss it with my hon. friend when I get the facts, or be very glad to have him talk it over with me at any time. There was no politics in tue withdrawal of the subsidy; it was a question of economy, and advantage to the public service.
Steam service or services between St. John, Westport, and Yarmouth and other way ports' $8,500.	'

What boats are performing that
service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Westport III of the Insular Steamship Company, and the John L. Cann, of Cann & Sons, Limited.
Does the minister propose to take $800 off the contract with Hugh Cann & Sons and hand it over to the Insular Company? I understand they were notified to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The question is up with reference to the Insular Company and the Hugh Cann Company. During the latter part of the fall the Westport III intermitted her trips on the ground that she

was losing money. The subject was brought to my attention, and we now have a vote of $8,500 for this service. I am trying to arrange for a reasonable and equitable division of the subsidy between the Insular Company and the Hugh Cann Company, so as to keep both these services going.
What are the amounts paid to each?''

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Insular Company received $2,271.63, and the Hugh Cann Company $5,871.18. The Westport III has a trackage of 132 miles, and the other vessel a trackage of 96 miles. The contention of the Insular Steamship Company is that they receive a smaller portion than is their due, and I am trying to make an equitable division between the two companies, either on the basis of the same number of trips, or, if the pay is not sufficient, by cancelling a few of the trips. - Both of these are important services, and I wish to come to a conclusion which will be agreeable to the two companies.
The Westport III serves a portion which has no other service, and the intermission of this for a few weeks last fall was very bad for the fishing industry.

I am sorry that a difficulty has arisen between these two companies. The services performed by both are very important indeed, and I am confident that at the present subsidy there is no money in it for either. Messrs. Hugh Cann & Company have informed me that if the minister carries out his notice to them, that their subsidy will be reduced by $800, tney will have to take their boat off. Their service was carried on with great regularity during the year, not a single trip being missed; and by the 31st March next, they will have made 12 more trips than the contract calls for. This is a most important service to the south of Yarmouth; goods are transferred at Yarmouth and go to the ports in Shelburne county. If that boat is taken off it is going to be a great inconvenience to the merchants of Yarmouth and the merchants on the shore to the south of us. I trust the minister can see his way clear to keeping the amount paid to Hugh Cann and Sons the same as it was last year, and also that he may be able to supplement by a few hundred dollars-say $800-the amount paid to the Westport Steamship Company. They have an excellent service and they are doing a lot of good to the different ports at which they call. It would be a great inconvenience to the merchants of Yarmouth if these services were interfered with. We have the Canadian Pacific railway; the goods heretofore have had to come to Digby, they have had to be reshipped there and they come to Yarmouth, but not in the order in which they are loaded at St. John and brought direct to Yarmouth. I do hope the minister will consent to the increase of $800, which I think the Westport Company are entitled to. I know that they have not made a dollar and that if the amount of the subsidy is not increased they will have to take their boat off. It is the only case in which I would advocate any increase in the expenditure this year, and I do it because they should certainly have this small amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I quite agree with what my hon. friend says as to both of these services. If I can keep them both on I will be glad to do so.
Steam service during the season of 1915 between Sydney and Bay St. Lawrence, calling at way ports. $6,000.
Is there any change in the service there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The same as last year.
Expenses in connection with the supervision of subsidized steamship services, $3,000.
Was this amount expended last year, or is there an official attached to the department who performs this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have a regular official of the department who gives his whole time to the work of supervision during the season of navigation. He goes over all the routes, calls at all the ports and makes inquiries as to the convenience of the transfers. He supervises the sanitary and other arrangements of the steamships, and I must say he is a good officer and that his work has had an excellent effect upon the service.
What is his name?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Tupper-a good name.
It was once.
How often is he supposed to go?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He goes over the route once each year at least, and if there is any special necessity to make an examination he is sent to make it.
This pays for his travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This pays for his salary and travelling expenses.
May I ask the minister whether the statutory votes immediately under the items we have been considering will be expended this year, or are they for interrupted services?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The first one, the Canada, China and Japan service, is wholly interrupted, and the other, the Canada-France service, is partially interrupted.

I see that the total amount voted, and including the statutory votes, is $2,962,000. Will the minister inform the committee what proportion of the amount he expects will be expended during the next fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I cannot tell exactly, but I should say that of the Atlantic ocean services, outside of the large vote of $1,000,000, we shall expend the whole. With reference to the Pacific ocean services, with the exception of the Canada, China and Japan service, we will probably expend the whole, unless something occurs that has not occurred this year in the way of disturbance. In the local services I think every one of them will eat the whole amount that is appropriated to it, because the services are constant. They are going on, they are not interrupted, and the contract generally is pretty well lived up to. While there may be the omission of a few passages, it will not amount to a great deal. There will probably be an expenditure of between $2,250,000 and $2,500,000.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Indians-Ontario ; relief, medical attendance and medicine, $11,000.

How is that money
spent?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Superintendent general of Indian Affairs):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Indians in the northerly section of Ontario, north of Lake Superior and in James bay district, depend largely on the chase for their living. In consequence of the war the Hudson Bay Company and other fur-traders are this year limiting their purchase of furs, and it is expected that the Government will have to outfit the Indians this year instead of the fur-traders, as formerly. It is contemplated that we will have to distribute more

relief to destitute Indians and consequently there is an increase of $4,000 in this vote.
How many Indians reserves are there in Ontario?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are over thirty.
I presume there will be no extra relief required for the Indians on reserves in the older portions of the province; this is for the Indians who depend mostly on the fur trade?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Indians-Quebec ; relief, medical attendance and medicine, $17,000.
How many Indian reserves are there in Quebec?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: About sixteen.
What are they?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Becancour, Bersimis, Cacouna, Caughnawaga, Lorette, Micmacs, Maniwaki, Maria, Mingan, North Timiska-ming, Oka, Restigouche, Seven Islands, St. Regis, St. Francis.
What is the total Indian population of Quebec?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Nearly 13,000.
Is it growing?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It remains about stationary.
Are the Quebec Indians affected by the war as are the Ontario Indians?	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Northern Quebec Indians will be. The Indians in Quebec have very little funds of tneir own from which they can draw, and we have to maintain a great many of them especially in the outlying reserves.

What is the population
of the Restigouche Reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: 523; it is about stationary.

How many Indians are
there at Maria?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: Is there a physician appointed permanently for these Indians or do you employ a medical man as he is required?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: At some of them, Restigouche for example, we employ a physician as he is required.
Is that found to be more costly than if you had a permanent physician?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It depends on the proximity of tne medical man to the reserve and the number of patients. In some cases we would not be warranted in paying a medical man a salary and in other cases the salary works out to better advantage perhaps.
Is a medical man employed at the request of the Indian agent or of the Indians themselves?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The agent employs him.
Has the agent to employ a man named by the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Where the Indians do not themselves contribute towards the expense, they are not permitted to take their own physician. The department I think generally employs tne physician recommended by the Indian agent. Sometimes the department cannot recommend a man because it does not know whom to recommend.

What was spent for
medical service on the Restigouche reserve last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Dr. Frenette, $73.05; Dr.
A. Martin, $388; Dr. L. G. Pinault, $18.25.
What is the residence of Dr. Frenette?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not know.

Dr. Martin and Dr.
Pinault reside in Campbellton. Dr. Frenette is a stranger to me. The hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) recommended a doctor who resided about fortv miles awav from the reserve. Whether this Dr. Frenette resides at Campbellton or not, I do not know. The minister would be at a disadvantage employing for political purposes people living at a distance from a reserve. The agent began to do some road makine last year and the year before on the Maria reserve. I had a letter asking that more work be done on that road. What has been done?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: $500 was spent on that reserve last year.
Does that complete the work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There will very likelv be
spent a similar amount during the present
season.

How is that work done?
By day labour by the Indians?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: By day labour. Indians being employed as far as possible.
I suppose the work is under thS control of the agent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Was there any trouble on the Restigouche reserve in connection with the saw-mill there?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec; general legal expenses, $5,500.

I understand the department has some legal men attached to it? It is difficult to understand what work should be done by lawyers not connected with the department that could not verv well be done by those officials of the department who are legal men.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have a law clerk in the inside service, but those expenses are in connection with outside work. The case of the Oka Indian reserve had to be carried to the Privy Council, and it involved a considerable expenditure. We had to engage some Montreal lawyers. In the last few years there have been a large number of cases in Canada which have been paid out of this appropriation.
Does the department undertake the defence of Indians who are charged with crimes in different parts of Canada ? In such cases, does the department pay counsel to conduct their defence ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not unless the offence is a capital one.
This item is for legal expenses in Ontario and Quebec. How are the expenses divided between Ontario and Quebec ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The appropriations are
grouped under Ontario and Quebec legal expenditures. I have .a list of the cases that have been tried, some of which are in Quebec and some of which are in Ontario. I have not any tabulated statement -as to how many of them are in Ontario and how many in Quebec.
Has the minister the names of the Ontario legal men who were engaged ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is the ease of Booth vs. the King, on which were engaged Chrysler and Bethune. J. C. Judd was engaged in connection with the Cayuga Indians. A. B. Thompson was engaged re

the Rama, Indians. Macdonald, Shepley, Donald and Mason were also engaged. Those are the names of the lawyers from the province of Ontario.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to a special case in my own riding. At the present time we have a few members of a tribe called the Malecites who are scattered over the country. Only one family lives in the town in which the reserve is. The man's name is Baptiste Launiere, and he is very poor. On the reserve there are two lots with pulp wood on them. I would advise the minister to take note of the matter, and see if he can find his way clear to sell those two lots and give the money to the Indians, as the department used to do before. The reserve is located in the township of Whitworth in the county of Temiscouata. During last fall I was obliged to write to the department asking it to permit that poor Indian to cut some pulp wood, because the agent down there was very hard to deal with and wanted to keep the pulp wood. After writing the department twice, I succeeded in having permission given to that poor Indian, who was nearly starving, to cut some pulp wood on those two lots.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that some relief was given in that particular case.

Yes, but after I wrote twice to the department. I had to tell the department to put its agent right and to make him take a little more care of the Indians under his charge.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: Will the minister say whether it is permissible to cut pit-props on Indian reserves, and to sell them to any person that chooses to buy ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: On some reserves thev cut pit-props quite extensively.
Is it permissible in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think so.

Is there any nenaltv
for purchasing pit-props cut by the Indians on the reserves there?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If the props are cut in trespass or if they are not cut according to our regulations, there is a penalty.

I have a case in mind which arose a year or two ago. The Indians on a reserve in Antigonish, being industrious, cut pit-props and sold them to a dealer who had been in the habit of buying year after year and who paid the regular market 
price. Soon after he was waited on bv a so-called officer of the department-I do not know whether that officer had authority or not. Then a man was put in charge of the props and the props were loaded with others on a car. The purchaser was subjected to a penalty of $15 and also expenses of something like $25 or $30. So, not only had he to pay for the props; but he also had to pay a penalty exacted by the department, and on top of that something like $1.50 a day for a fortnight or more that the man was in charge.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The props were cut in trespass.
The purchaser was not a trespasser. The Indians brought in the props in the usual way and were paid in the usual way. But somebody got busy and the purchaser was penalized.

Have the fur operations
in northern Quebec been profitable? Are they self-sustaining?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They had a fairly good year, but they are not self-sustaining: the department has to assist them.
Are the furs taken in northern Quebec sold to one or two companies?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Indians dispose of them where they please.
What about the liauor business there, is it extensive or is it well controlled by the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have not had many complaints, and very few serious ones. We have officials for the express purpose of keeping down the illegal traffic in liquor and keeping liquor away from the Indians. We recognize that it is very injurious to the Indians in Quebec or any other province, and we have had comparatively little trouble with it in the past year.
The general tone among the Indians as to morality and temperance is improving, is it not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

I think it would be interesting if the minister would give a statement to the country of the Indian population at the present time. Is it increasing or decreasing? And could he tell us, also, the difference, if there is any, between the relations with the Government of Indians on a reserve like that of the bay of Quinte and Indians in the Northwest.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have here the report of the Department of Indian Affairs, which will give the information in as direct a form as possible. It says:
the Indians of Ontario are more prosperous than those of other parts of Canada. Though they number over 26,000, the expense of looking after them is comparatively small.
There has always been a good deal of interest manifested in the question of Indian population, and I am glad to say that, while some bands show a considerable increase and others a slight decrease, the total population remains approximately 100,000. The table immediately following shows a net decrease of 2,716. This, however, does not mark an actual decrease in numbers by death or emigration. It is difficult to secure accurate statistics for the interior of the far North, and it was thought advisable to eliminate from the census returns that were merely conjectural. Gradually, as this part of the country opens up and becomes more accessible, it will be possible to secure reliable statistics.	-
Examination of the table referred to will disclose decreases in Manitoba, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, besides that already mentioned in the Northwest territories. In Manitoba there is a decrease of 532, in New Brunswick 14, and in Prince Edward Island 4. Increases will be found in the other provinces; Ontario heading the list with 342, while British Columbia shows an increase of 198, Yukon 139, Quebec 93, Saskatchewan 80, Alberta 52, and Nova Scotia 32.
It is impossible to secure an accurate yearly census of the Eskimos, and their population is shown as 3,447, the same as last year.
