Is Ungava included with Quebec?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They are more largely selfsupporting.

That brings me to my other question-the difference, if any, in relations with the Government as between the Indians of a reserve like the bay of Quinte Reserve, and the Indians of the reserves in the West.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Indians of the Bay
of Quinte reserve are entirely self-supporting, so that they cannot very well be compared with the Indians of the reserves in the Northwest, to whose relief we have to come each year.

Self-supporting Indians
are the wards of the Government, are they not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes. Of course, the Bay of Quinte Indians have trust funds of their own.

If I may be pardoned for interrupting the consideration of the Estimates, I wish to announce to the Minister of the Naval Service that I have just received a wire containing the information that the village of Port Colborne in the county of Welland, which has a population of less than two thousand, collected for the patriotic fund $13,000 in two days, or over $6 per head of the population.

I think the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) deserves to be congratulated. I met the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) a couple of nights ago, and he told me that Quebec is still ahead of Ontario.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec; general expenses, $51,075.

What do these general
expenses consist of?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Can the minister give us * the figures for Ungava separately?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not that before me.
Are there reserves in Ungava under the control of the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
A fair inference from the figures that the minister has given is that

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: General expenses of management at the different agencies, including salaries, office expenses, clerical expenses, travelling expenses. There is a reduction of over $700 under that head.

When the item respecting Indian schools is reached, I would like the minister to give a statement as to the number of schools, the number of pupils, and what advancement the Indians are making along the line of education.

Indians-Nova Scotia, salaries, $6,200.

Will the minister
explain the increase?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is an apparent, not a real increase. The salaries of two Nova Scotia superintendents, which were voted under the heading of general expenses, have been put under the heading of salaries; this accounts for the difference.
Was a new superintendent appointed within the last year or two?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Superintendent Foster was appointed, I think, within the last year.
Whom did he succeed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It was a new appointment.
What rendered the new appointment necessary?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are two superintendents in Nova Scotia, Mr. Boyd and Mr. Foster. I cannot of my own personal knowledge say very much about Mr. Foster, because his appointment was made during my absence. I presume, however, that it was made on the recommendation of the inspector, the agents, and the deputy superintendent general.

I think this is a case in which my hon. friend should economize. It takes $6,200 to pay salaried officials to look after 2,000 Indians in Nova Scotia, an increase of $3,600 over last year. It is simply putting the fifth wheel on the coach to appoint another superintendent in Nova Scotia, and I think my hon. friend the minister will have very great difficulty in justifying the appointment on any other ground than that Mr. Foster, who is a very estimable gentleman, was a good political servant. In this year of special taxation upon the people, I think the minister ought to consider whether or not he can get along with one superintendent down there.

Has the number of Indian
agents in the province of Nova Scotia been increased within the last couple of years?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
During the last two or
three years I think but one additional appointment has been made.

Where was that appointment
made?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: At Windsor, Hants county.
How many agents are there in Hants county at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Two.
How many Indians are there in Hants county?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Eighty.
What salary is paid the agents in Hants county?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The laTge amount of $100.
It is quite large for the work they have to do. Is that the usual salary paid to agents in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The highest salary is $200.
Who receives the highest salary?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Chisholm, at Halifax, Mr. Freeman, at Lunenburg; Mr. Macdonald, at Richmond.
The salary paid the former Indian agent at St. Peter's was $100. Upon whose request was the salary of the, present agent increased to $200?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I presume in the
first place at the agent's own	request, and then on the recommendation of the heads of the department, who considered that the agent was doing sufficient work to warrant the increase.' $100 is a very small salary.
Has the department any official record to show that the present agent is doing more work than his predecessor?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If they have not, they certainly have something to show that it costs a good deal more to live to-day than it did two or three years ago.
Is the present agent dependent on his salary as Indian agent for his living?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I presume not, but every little counts.
Has the Indian population increased to any extent?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, it is about stationary.
What is the salary of the agent at Antigonish?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: What does the agent in Yarmouth get?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: The agent at Yarmouth gets $50, and the agent at Hants $200. I do not think that is justice.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is the salary he has been getting for a number of years.

I am surprised at the amount of money that is being spent in paying officials who have practically nothing to do. I see that $8,000 is being given for the relief of the Indians all over Nova Scotia. Why is this money not divided amongst the Indians, who certainly need it more than some of the agents who get this money? I think the minister might very well increase the salary of the agent at Yarmouth from $50 to $100.
Do I understand that the only cause for increasing the salary of the agent in Richmond was the increased cost of living.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say that.
That is the only reason the minister gave.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I said there was nothing on file to show whether there had been an increase in the work.
Has there been any increase in the number of Indians under his authority?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Very little.
Has there been any increase at all?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not think 60.
As a matter of fact, there has not been. Does this item include the salaries of teachers in the Indian schools?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
What are the particular duties of Mr. Foster, and what counties are under his supervision?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The western counties. He inspects the reserves and reports upon each one.
How many counties?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Halifax, and all west of Halifax.
Including Colchester county and Cumberland county?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not the list here, but I could get it for the hon. gentleman if he desires.
Are his duties confined to certain counties, or has he general jurisdiction over the province?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The province is divided
between Mt. Boyd and Mr. Foster.
Who made representation as to the necessity of this additional superintendent?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman moved for a return.
There was nothing in it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: As I said at the opening of my remarks, personally I know nothing about this appointment. It was made in my absence. I presume that some person has been in the city of Ottawa and recommended the appointment of another Indian agent in that province.
A very easy way.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The appointment was considered necessary. Personally I know nothing whatever about it.

I am bound to say that if the minister had been here he would never have made the appointment. I submit that the reason he has given for the appointment-that some person went to the Indian Department at Ottawa and said: We should like to have another superintendent down in Nova Scotia, and you had better appoint Mr. Foster-is not a good and sufficient reason why we should appoint another salaried official for the purpose of looking after the Indians who in the past have been perfectly well looked after by one superintendent. I ask the minister to look into this question and save this money, especially in this year of taxation and hard times. This -money would buy postage on 54,000 letters. I can quite see why the minister does not feel inclined to justify the appointment of this additional superintendent, and I am sorry he cannot give us any better justification of it than he has. I understand from my hon. friend from Halifax that the return which was brought down gave no information whatever except as to salary.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is notning on the
file.

Who was acting
minister when the hon. gentleman was away?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I was away so long, I
regret to say, that two or three ministers acted duing my absence-on one occasion

the Minister of Justice; on another the general utility man, the Minister of Customs; and on another the Minister of Public Works. I cannot say under whose regime the appointment was made.
Has the minister discovered whether there is any work for this new appointee to do?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Certainly. He forwards
his reports to the department.

I know that, but has
the department discovered whether beyond the sending in of a report, there has been any work for him to do since the date of his appointment?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
He visits and inspects
the reserves, and makes his reports.

I do not
think the minister should be allowed to disclaim responsibility in that matter. Mr. Boyd had jurisdiction over New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and I never heard that he was overburdened with work, or that he could not get over the whole country and still have lots of time to spare after doing his duties. The idea of appointing an extra superintendent at a salary of $1,800 and travelling expenses and $500 for an office is absurd in these hard times, when you are putting a tax on everything the poor man has to consume. Imagine this large amount of money being spent for salaries, when only $8,000 is being given for the relief of the Indians ! The only qualifications required, I suppose, were that the appointee should have been a good party man; and he was appointed, I suppose, solely because a job had to be found for him. There might be some justification for this sort of thing if the treasury was overflowing and the whole country was revelling in prosperity, but in these times I do not think the minister will find anybody in the maritime provinces, where the Indians are so badly used, to justify this appointment.
When was the salary of the agent at St. Peter's increased to $200?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: About two years ago.
When was he appointed to that office?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
He was paid $100 in the
year 1913-14, so it must have been about the 1st of April, 1914, or before, that his salary was raised to $200.
Has the minister found any Teason since for increasing the gentleman's *salary other than what he has stated ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are some agents who are paid less than this agent was receiving, but most of the -agents were drawing $100. There had been complaints, I am informed, from the province of Nova Scotia, that salaries generally were too low.
Complaints from the agents ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Including the agents, certainly; you cannot blame them for that.
Not from the Indians ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No. The opinion of the officers of the department was that the salaries of most of these agents in Nova Scotia were too low for present day conditions. While there are more Indians in some of these counties than in others for the agents to look after, the more deserving cases were considered, and in these cases it was found necessary to increase salaries.
Why was not an increase made all round ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Some cases were more deserving than others, and if we had done it all at once the hon. gentleman would have been the first to have criticised us for it. We must do it little by little, and probably next year, if we have more funds, we will look after the others.

The other evening, when we were discussing the salaries of fishery inspectors, we found that salaries were increased all round except in the case of a fishery inspector who had run an election against my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), and that was the Teason why his salary had not been increased. Who are the Indian agents in Nova Scotia whose salaries have been increased since this Government came into power ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is rather a difficult matter to tell at the present moment. I can provide the hon. gentleman with a statement if he so desires.
This is the time to have the statement. We are here considering the item of salaries of Indian agents in Nova Scotia, and one would have thought that this was the time to have this information.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We cannot anticipate all the questions that will be asked.

These are questions that should appear obvious to the mind of the minister inasmuch as we are discussing salaries. The superintendent of Indian agencies, Mr. Boyd, lives within ten miles

of the Indian reserve of St. Peter's. I know as a matter of fact that a laTge portion of the duties that fall to the Indian agents in other parts of Nova Scotia are performed by the superintendent, and I think there is no justification whatever for having an Indian agent at St. Peter's in view of the fact that the superintendent is living so close to the reserve, and that his duties take him very frequently to the reserve for the purpose of looking after the interests of the Indians. Whatever excuse there might be for increasing the salaries of Indian agents in otheT parts of the province of Nova Scotia, there is no justification for increasing the salary of the agent at St. Peter's, for the- reason that a large proportion of the duties that would otherwise fall to him are discharged by the superintendent.
Mr, LAW: Would the minister give the committee a memorandum of the agents in the maritime provinces who receive ithe magnificent salary of $50 a year ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is only one other
agent in Nova Scotia who gets $50 a year.
Is it the intention of the minister to level up the $50 man to $100? Will the minister say where he is stationed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Indian agent in Shelburne county has $50, and there are only forty Indians there. In Yarmouth there are 54 Indians, and that is the reason why the salary is so low.
In Shelburne there are 40 Indians, and the agent gets $50 a year, while in Hants there are 80 Indians, and there are two agents getting $100 a year.
What are the names of the two agents in Hants?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Wallace and Mr. Stephens.
Where do they live?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: One at Windsor and the other at Shubenacadie.
I suppose the minister knows that these are purely political appointments?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, I do not know that.

Then the minister does not need to inquire very far before he finds out. Throughout eastern Nova Scotia, where there are quite a number of Indians *-some 2,000-in a great many oases the Indian agent is the Roman Catholic clergy-83
man who lives in the vicinity of where the Indians are. He has always been the agent because, being spiritual adviser to these children of the forest, he is their natural guardian. That being so, it is an additional reason why there was no necessity of having a new superintendent. I know the agent in my county, who is a very worthy clergyman of the Roman Catholic church, and he has always been in charge of the Indians there. I know he does not need two superintendents over him to see that his treatment of the Indians is proper. It is absolutely and totally unnecessary. The minister says to the committee that personally he is not responsible. Of course, he has to assume the responsibility of what the roving minister may have done or what the Minister of Public Works may have done in his absence. There is a limit to this kind of thing. It becomes an absolute farce when we find the Government, within the last year and a half, hunting up excuses to find new offices. When you take into consideration the fact that in a great many cases the local agents are the clergy of whom I have
9 p.m. just spoken, the absurdity of the appointment of two men to supervise these agents becomes apparent. The minister ought to look into this matter with the view of seeing whether, if there is going to be any attempt at economy anywhere, he can get along with one inspector. The minister should look into this matter and see if this additional superintendent is necessary in view of the fact that there is nothing in the department to justify it and in view of the fact that the chief officer of the department is not quoted as favouring it.

This is clearly a case where the necessities of the poor Indians are being exploited by politicians supporting the present Government in Nova Scotia, just as the necessities of the poor soldiers at the front are being exploited by dishonest contractors. That is all that can be said about it. That is the plain English of the whole story. I know a case in which an Indian on one of the reserves in Nova Scotia has haa a contract from the department to look after the fires in the Indian schools. He was getting thirty dollars a year for four or five years. A year ago he said to the superintendent: "In addition to making the fires I am supplying the wood which is burned in the school, and all I am getting is thirty dollars a year." The superintendent said: "You will have to speak to the agent"

13'4

and he did speak to the agent. The agent said: "The department has no money, and cannot afford to pay you more than thirty dollars for making the fires and supplying the wood; money is scarce now; the Indians are costing the country a great deal." Then he turned around and said: "Where do you spend the thirty dollars?" "The man mentioned the name of the merchant who supplied him with such necessaries as he was able to buy, and the agent said: "Why, that man is a Grit; do you think I would recommend you to get more money to spend at his store? You will have to be contented with thirty dollars."

I presume there are quite a number of the Indians who are comfortably well off, and would not accept assistance from the department; is there available, information in the department to show how many of the Indians in Nova Scotia are indigent and require assistance?
' Mr. ROCHE: We can compile such a statement from the records of the department.
Are these 2,000 the entire number of Indians, or only those who are wards of the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is the total Indian .population of the province.
Do I understand the minister to decline to look into the question as to the necessity for this official?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not at all; I do not wish to leave that impression. I have no personal knowledge of the appointment of this gentleman, and if the facts are as stated by the hon. member for Pictou to-night, I have learned more than I have known before. I have no information supplied me as to who recommended the appointment or as to why the official was appointed. 1 naturally took it for granted he was appointed because there was necessity for such an official. I have no objection whatever to tell the hon. gentleman that I will make inquiries into the question of what duties he is discharging, and as to whether his appointment was necessary.
Indians, Nova Scotia; relief, $8,000.
How is this relief distributed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Relief was distributed in the counties of Annapolis, Guysborough, Antigonish, Cape Breton and Colchester, and for such articles as clothing, provisions, fertilizers, bags, lumber, seed grain, potatoes, shingles, window-frames, and so on.
[Mr. Kyte.J
The application for relief and seed grain has to come through the agent?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Indians, Nova Scotia; medical attendance and medicine, $5,000.
How are the doctors paid for their attendance on the Indians?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Some are paid by salary and others according to accounts rendered for medical service.
Has there been any increase in this expenditure since the present Government came into power?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Very little. In 1914-15 it was $5,000 and in 1915-16 it is $5,000.
What was it in 1912-13?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not the particulars for the expenditure of 1912-13, but in 1913-14 the expenditure was $6,000.
The Indian agent at Sydney is also the medical attendant?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
What salary does he get?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: That does not include medicine?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, it includes medicine.
Suppose an Indian calls in a doctor outside of their regular medical attendant, and that doctor sends a bill to the department, will the department pay the bill? .

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Only in an unusual case
or in an emergency. As a rule, the doctor who is appointed is supposed to be called in by the Indians and he is paid by the department.

Cases of emergency might arise where the Indians would suffer greatly if they were not allowed to call in a physician outside of the regular medical attendant. Dr. A. 3. Deveau, of Meteghan, Digby county, had an account for $228.07 against the department for services rendered while he was in Halifax county and the department has declined to pay it. The minister being a physician, has, I suppose, faith enough in his profession to know that a medical man does not usually send a bill unless he has rendered services for it. I am satisfied>
in this case that Dr. Deveau has rendered services to the Indians for the amount of his account. I commend the

matter to the earnest attention of the minister, because I think there might be cases in which the Indians would suffer if the physicians called in by them are not paid for their services. I know Dr. Deveau personally, and I know he would not send in an account unless it was perfectly correct, and under the circumstances it is only fair that the department should pay it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will have the case looked into. I understand that this gentleman was not the regular medical attendant and that he acted without the assent or direction of the agent or the department. If we allowed that policy to. prevail as a rule, I am afraid we would be landed in a good deal larger expenditure than at present. I shall look into the case.

Suppose
the regular medical man cannot attend to a case and he calls in another physician, would the department pay the substitute or would the regular physician have to pay him?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The doctor must pay out of his own salary.
In every case?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

That seems rather
hard.

I moved for a
copy of the papers in regard to the doctor employed to attend the Indians in my county. The correspondence disclosed that from somewhere unseen and unknown came the suggestion that Dr. J. McKenzie should not be any longer employed as doctor, and that some doctor from elsewhere should be employed, because it was said that Dr. McKenzie lived at Pictou and that Pictou was not the proper place for a doctor to reside at who was to wait upon the Indians. From time immemorial the different doctors who have attended those Indians have lived in the town of Pictou, the Indian settlement in the county being at Pictou landing where the white people as well as the Indians do all their business with the town, and a new settlement having grown up at a place called Sylvester, which is in close proximity to the town. There was therefore no reason for making the change on the ground of the necessity of the Indians being better treated. The Indians did not make any complaint; there does not appear to have been any request from 83*
the agent that the change should be made, and I do not think the idea came into the mind of the gentleman in charge of the Department of the Interior, without a suggestion from somewhere, that Dr. McKenzie's services should be dispensed with and another appointment made. By whom was the suggestion made to the minister?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The suggestion came to me from the officials of my department that Dr. McKenzie, who, I believe, was a resident of Pictou, was not as conveniently situated to the major portion of the Indians as a doctor would be who resided at New Glasgow.
The reports did not show that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It was stated that most
of the Indians are on the New Glasgow side of the waterway, and that a doctor from Pictou would have to cross over-I do not know how far it is-10 miles?
No. It is less than a mile by the ferry.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand that the
ferry is not in operation during the nighttime, when frequently a doctor's services are required. The ferry would also be out of operation during a portion of the winter season. All that was pointed out to me, and that was the reason why a doctor at New Glasgow was appointed.
Who suggested this to the officials of the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I cannot answer that question. I am not personally aware who made such a suggestion; nor do I think the question as to who made the suggestion is at all germane to the subject, as long as the facts warranted the appointment of a doctor at New Glasgow. The hon. member will admit that it is more convenient.
Absolutely not at all.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That was the case submitted to me, and it seemed a pretty good ' one.

I do not know who made out the case. All I can say is that some person who wanted to get Dr. Keith appointed wrrote a letter, which has not been brought down in the file, to the officials of the Department of uve Interior suggesting that a change should be made. Ever since Confederation the different doctors who have been in charge of these Indians have lived in the town of Pictou. I do not be-

lieve that any one interested in the lands *suggested that change. The Indians did not suggest it, arid there was no reason in the world why the officials of the department should bother their heads about this question unless somebody wanted Dr. McKenzie put out and Dr. Keith put in his place. The correspondence shows that Mr. Boyd made two reports, and that in the second one, which was full and complete and was made after the department had made the change of doctors, it was shown that the r more convenient place for the doctor to be in was the town of Pictou. All the people, both white and Indians, who live at Pictou landing, receive their medical attention at Pictou. I do not believe there is a doctor from New Glasgow who goes to Pictou Landing once a year. When paper's are moved for in this House, the minister should bring down the full information. I do not see why he should start off a return with the statement that the gentleman in charge of Interior affairs has suddenly received an inborn inspiration on a question, and why on that inspiration he should proceed to slide a doctor out. Such a procedure is neither reasonable nor proper. Such inspirations do not come without some mundane suggestion.
They do not work from t'he inside.

Dr. McKenzie succeeded his father, who succeeded another medical man who died. They all lived in the town of Pictou and they all attended the Indians perfectly satisfactorily. Who was it who put the little idea into the head of the gentleman in charge of Indian Affairs that the Indians were not being properly looked after? Before the department gets the second Teport from Mr. Boyd the necessity is so great that it dismisses Dr. McKenzie, without any allegation as to his qualifications or his politics. There was a certain gentleman named Dr. Keith who was greedy for the job, and certain friends of his, if they did not write a public letter, wrote a private letter suggesting that Dr. McKenzie should be dismissed. I think the rhinister should bring down that letter.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: The papers do not show any recommendation from the agent or from the inspector. Was not this done when you were away?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not think so.

I think this case
must have slipped through in your absence.
Indians, Nova Scotia; miscellaneous and unforeseen, $4,300.
There is a very considerable increase in this item over last year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is a transfer from one
account to another. It is in exactly the same position as the item of salaries for the Nova Scotia superintendents. This account was formerly charged up to another item. This year we are putting it in its proper place. It is only an apparent increase.
Indians, Nova Scotia; repairs to roads and diking, $600.
Where was this money spent last year?

Whycocomagh reserve, $300; Chapel Island, $220; Heatherton, $31; total, $551.
Indians, Nova Scotia; rebuilding Indian Council House, Chapel Island, $2,500.
What is this for?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The mission house where the Indians are in the habit of congregating once a year was burned, and this is for the purpose of rebuilding it, the Indians not having sufficient funds of their own.
Was the building which was destroyed built by the Government originally?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It was built many years ago, and if not entirely built by the Government, the Government gave some assistance towards it.

I commend the Government for this vote. I endeavoured, when the late

Government was in power, to get assistance for the Indians in building their new church, but that Government refused to make an appropriation. But while I commend the vote, I rather object to it being put through under false pretences. This is called a vote for an Indian council house. There is no such thing there as a council house and never has been. There is a very beautiful chapel on the island, built by the Indians with contributions obtained from the white people. There was also a residence for the priest who attends upon the Indians for about two weeks when they have their mission. This glebe house, as it is locally called, was destroyed by fire, and this vote, I understand, is to rebuild it. I am glad the vote is here; I think it a very commendable one as the Indians are not in good circumstances and the building of a new glebe house without assistance would involve very considerable sacrifices for them. -
What is the building to cost?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is estimated at $2,500. There is a special room for a council room according to the plan. I think I remember that last session, when the Indian Department estimates were under consideration, some hon. gentlemen strongly urged that this vote should be made or commended one that was proposed.

The money was not
spent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, there was difficulty about the plans and the work has been delayed.
Has an agreement been reached as to the character of the building?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The building is a story and a half high, and on the ground floor are council room, dining room, kitchen and bedroom.	.
Has the work been commenced?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
Is it intended to call for tenders?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That has not been decided upon. As is frequently the case in such buildings, the Indians have promised to do a good deal of work themselves and to supply a certain amount of material. Sometimes, by employing the Indians and paying them for their services and purchasing from them what material they can supply, we
find the work can be more economically done.
What advantage is it to employ the Indians if you pay them as you pay anybody else?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It would be an advantage to the Indians.

But not to the Government. I tell the minister now, in good time, that if he wants to avoid difficulty, he will call for tenders for this building. There is no reason why he should not do so. As he has stated, any assistance received from the Indians will be paid for, and there will be no advantage gained by the department in having the building put up by day's work. But he will be opening the door to very considerable trouble in that way. I think $2,500 is a very reasonable amount for such a structure as intended. It is a residence for the priest during the two weeks he is there giving a mission to the Indians. That is all it will be used for. I am glad it is being constructed, but I want it to be constructed in a manner that will not open the door for charges hereafter. There seems to be a certain laxity in the affairs in the minister's department in that region. In order to avoid that, and so that we may not come back at him next year with complaints as to the way this money was spent, I suggest to him, and earnestly advise him, to call for tenders.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The department has no objection to calling for tenders. It has not yet been decided.
So frequently they are not called for. I am asking the minister to make a special note of this case.

How many council houses are there now in Nova Scotia? How often do the councils meet? And would the minister give us some idea of the manner of opening a council and of the deliberations that take place?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have no information on that subject.
Indians, New Brunswick; salaries, $1,984.
Is there any authority by which right can be given by the department or by the Indians to run a road across an Indian reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That is quite often done. The department is prepared to allow road allowances across a reserve. In some cases

we have to secure a surrender from the Indians before the road can be run. The municipality or whoever is promoting the road can appeal to the Government on the subject either direct or through the Indian agent.
The proceedings are the same when municipalities or private individuals wish to run a road across a reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No; private individuals are not allowed the privilege of expropriating.
Is it only in a case of expropriation that a road may be run across a reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, but a private individual cannot ask to have a road constructed across an Indian reserve and have his wish acceded to.
Provided the assent of the Indians was obtained, would the department be willing to permit individuals to run a road across their reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It would largely depend upon the nature of the case. If the Indians had no objection, and a strong case were made out in favour of it, the department might be inclined to view the request favourably.
How many agents are there in New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Three.
The province is divided into three districts, I presume?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are three districts, the south western division, the northern division, and Big Cove division, Kent county.
How does the Indian population of New Brunswick compare with that of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Indian population of New Brunswick is 1,920. There is a difference of about 100 between the Indian population of New Brunswick and that of Nova Scotia.

There is a striking difference between the salaries paid to agents in the respective provinces. In Nova Scotia the salaries of agents amount to $6,200, while in New Brunswick they amount to only $1,984.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are more agents in Nova Scotia.

Why?
IMr. Roche.]

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are more reserves and the reserves are more widely scattered.
Who has been appointed in the place of the late Mr. Irving?
No appointment has been made.
There are two agents in New Brunswick, then, and one vacancy?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. A. Ii. MACLEAN: Would the minister allow this item to stand until the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., returns?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I will have some Supplementary Estimates; he may discuss it when they are brought up.
Indians, New Brunswick; relief, $8,000.
Who was the inspector in connection with the construction of a school-house at the Edmunston Indian reserve, and how much was he paid for his services?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Auditor General's report does not give the name, but it states that he was paid $5 a week for fifteen weeks.
Was he inspector for the whole of the construction?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
The man who was appointed inspector knows absolutely nothing about cement work or about the construction of a building?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Was he not worth $5 a
week?

No, not even that,
because he does not know anything about the construction of a building. If the building is properly constructed, it is on account of the honesty of the contractor, not the efficiency of the inspector, because he did not know anything about his work.
Is the distribution of this relief left entirely to the agent ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Indian himself makes application to the agent. The agent investigates the case and issues his order on the merchant for the relief.
Indians, New Brunswick; miscellaneous and. unforeseen, $850.
I believe that during the last two or three years a certain person has not only bought lumber from the Tobique reserve, but has obtained also the title to three or four lots on the reserve.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is the case in respect of which the ho-n. member for Garleton -moved for a return a couple of weeks -ago. The information -has been brought down.
Are the Indian agents supposed to look -after the Indians all over the province, or only those -in the special reserves over which they have authority ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Indian agent has jurisdiction over all Indians, whether located on the reserve or otherwise.

On many occasions it has come to -my attention that there are isolated camps or families of Indians located here and there who are sometimes in destitution. I think -the -agents -should look after these people.
Indians, New Brunswick; repairs to roads, $458.

I do not understand
why so much money is voted for roads for reserves in the province of Ontario and so little for those in New Brunswick. Is this amount voted on the basis of population or of mileage?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is voted by reason of
the necessity for the expenditure.

I think the amount
for New Brunswick is rather small. The roads through the Indian reserves down there are very bad. I know that last year the department spent a little money on them, but we should like more money spent this year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There have been very few applications.
Indians, New Brunswick; to provide for encouragement of agriculture, $1,000.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is to provide seed
grain and implements for Indians who may be in need of them. It has been found that the Indians require from time to time to have their implements implemented. This is not a very large amount.

I wonder whether this
amount is sufficient for the purpose. Has the Government ever taken into consideration the question of educating the Indians along agricultural lines so that they might learn to maintain themselves? In my county there are many Indians who are getting no assistance at all, but who are able to maintain themselves on little farms and, to a certain extent, educate their families. Instead of voting a small amount like this each year, should not something on broader lines be done, which would be
of lasting benefit to the Indians throughout the country.

It has given me great pleasure to see the Indian agent at Tobique giving a great deal of his time to educating the Indians in the science of agriculture. He has taught them how to sow and reap, how to keep their barns, how to whitewash their houses, and so on. Altogether this gentleman has done a great deal for the department, and I have received letters of congratulation in regard to him. Unfortunately he lost his job because he sided with the Liberals on reciprocity, and since then the Indians have gone back a great deal in agriculture. I think with my hon. friend from Westmorland that not sufficient money has been spent on the Indians in the last few years. 1 believe that if they were approached in a proper manner they could be taught to maintain themselves on the products of the reserves.
Indians, Prince Edward Island; salaries, $600.

How many agents
have we in Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This item is to pay the
salary of the Indian Superintendent, the Rev. J. A. Macdonald, and of the Assistant Superintendent, Mr. J. O. Arsenault, whose salaries are respectively $400 and $200.
Indians, Prince Edward Island; medical attendance and medicines, $850.
How many doctors have we in Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Two, Dr. J. A. Stewart and Dr. E. G. Gillis.
Indians, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories; implements, tools, etc., $11,893.

Could the minister give us a statement respecting the existing condition of affairs in regard to the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve? The minister will remember that discussions on this subject have taken place in the House on several occasions.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
All the information that I can give is that after tilts question came up last session I handed the case over to my colleague the Minister of Justice. I understand that he has instituted proceedings, but how far they have gone I am not sure. I understand that some negotiations have been going on between the purchasers of this land and the Department of Justice with a view to settling the matter outside

of court, but matters have gone so far now that witnesses have been subpoenaed, and it looks as if everything was ready for the case to be prosecuted . The case is at such a stage now that there need be little delay.

Can the minister
tell us what were the grounds for the commencement of court proceedings?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A commission of certain
judges was appointed in Manitoba to inquire into the validity of the surrender of this reserve, and the majority of that commission reported that the surrender was illegal. That, in essence, is the basis of the court proceedings.
Was the Commission appointed by the Dominion Government.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, by the Provincial
Government. In view of that commission's report that the surrender was illegal, and in view of the case that was made out in this House a few years ago by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and other members, the Minister of Justice considered that we should not allow the case to stand at its present stage.

I have not seen very much about these court proceedings, but I presume the action would be brought in the Exchequer Court and would be for the cancellation of the patents if they had been issued by the Indian Department-and I think in a number of cases they had been issued-to men who had bought the land, not from the Indians, hut from the speculators in the Indian lands. How many actions have been brought by the Justice Department? Do I understand that an action has been brought, against a large number of the speculators?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not being a lawyer, I am not very conversant with the legal aspect of the case, but I understand the court proceedings were to set aside the surrender. If the court decided that the surrender was illegal, that would make null and void all subsequent purchases under the surrender.
When did the Manitoba Commission report to the Manitoba Government?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not know the exact date, hut it may have been a year and a half ago.
[Mr. Roche. 1

So far as the present Dominion Government is concerned, then, I am correct in saying that apart from the action, whatever it may be, taken by the Justice Department, nothing has been done in the period of three and a half years since this Government came into office in regard to the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve, a proceeding which was alleged by some members of this House some five or six years ago to have been outrageous. I think that is the correct assumption, is it not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not know that it is quite correct; but if, during this time, we have not made a great deal of progress, it may be because the other party to the suit has wished to arrive at some settlement in order to prevent the case going into court. I think delay has been occasioned because of that fact.
Who is the other party to the suit?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are many parties to the suit.

The position, Mr. Chairman, appears to be this, as far as the Dominion Government is concerned, nothing has been done in regard to the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve, and nothing would have been done by this Government, judging from the conduct of the Government, had it not been that some action was taken by the Government of Manitoba. Just what this action was I am not in a position to say. I can only say, from rumours I have heard and from statements I have seen in the newspapers, that I understand that after this Government came into power the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and other members who were interested in the matter, having lost hope of getting the present Government to do anything in regard to the surrender of this reserve, resorted to the Government of Manitoba, and that Government directed their registrar, in the proper registration district, to issue no titles on the patents that had been issued by the Department of the Interior, or upon any assignments of those patents. That is a subject for reasonable and fair criticism. We in the House of Commons, and in the committee of the House, had listened to the discussion of this subject, not by the hour, but by the day. I remember very well hearing speeches made by the hon. member for Selkirk in the session of 1909-10, and for two or three years afterwards, on this subject, which, in so far as length is concerned, excelled anything

that was ever heard in Parliament. All kinds of charges were made by the hon. member for Selkirk and other hon. members sitting on the Opposition benches at that time. If I remember correctly, the House was divided on a motion of want of confidence in the late Government in regard to the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve. The former Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Mr. Frank Pedley, was charged with all sorts of maladministration in regard to the obtaining of that surrender. All these statements were contradicted by an affidavit made by Mr. Frank Pedley, and I predict that any legal proceedings in connection with the matter will result in leaving it exactly where it is. Delay on the part of this Government, and intervention on the part of the Government of Manitoba, at the instigation of the hon. member for Selkirk and perhaps others, have resulted in preventing the settlement of the land adjoining the town of Selkirk for a number of years, and, if I am correctly informed, there is very grave dissatisfaction existing in and around Selkirk in regard to the action of this Government and of the Provincial Government with respect to the holding up of the patents or the titles for these particular pieces of land, thereby preventing the land in and around Selkirk from being occupied by farmers and properly cultivated. During two or three years, almost every week, certainly at very short intervals, the matter of the surrender of the St. Peter's reserve was discussed, and discussed at length, on the floor of this House. For the last three or four years the hon. member for Selkirk, and the other hon. gentlemen who formerly discussed that question, have remained silent. Nothing has been said. I submit to the
10 p.m. Minister of the Interior that, considering the situation with respect to this land in and around Selkirk, action should be taken by the Government in order to hurry the settlement of this very vexed question, and action should be taken without delay.
My hon. friend (Mr. W. M. Martin) is not apparently very well informed. He stated that a commission had been appointed by the Manitoba Government after this Government had come into power.

The minister said that.
Mr. BRADBURY. You will remember that it was appointed before this Government came into power and it was appointed to deal with the question of title.
I was taking the word of the minister. -

That was simply done because the registrar general refused to accepted the patents and to issue titles on them. Then it was up to the Manitoba Government, in defence of its guarantee fund, to demonstrate whether that title was a good title or not, and the only way the Government could decide it was by appointing a commission. The Government appointed a commission of its own volition simply to protect the province. My hon. friend, who is a lawyer, knows that the - Torrens title carries with it the guarantee of title. When the outrageous manner in which this surrender had been made and the manner in which the Indians had been fleeced out of their holdings was pointed out to this House, the registrar of the province took -warning and refused to issue title on these patents. The consequence was that the Manitoba Government, in its own defence, appointed a commission of three of the most eminent judges in Manitoba. This commission sat and took evidence. There was a majority report and a minority report. The majority report declared that the surrender was illegal and that there was nothing to justify the issue of titles on this surrender. The consequence was that when my hon. friends were in power we asked the Government to remedy the evil that had taken place.

My hon. friend
does not mean to say that the commission reported before the late Government went out of office. The commission only reported eighteen months ago, according to the statement of the Minister of the Interior.

I think they reported before the Government went out of power, In 1911 the surrender took place and I pointed out in the House in 1908 and 1909 the character of the surrender and called the attention of the Government to it. It was in 1912 that the commission was appointed, I think.
The commission of judges.

The commission of
judges. However, I admit frankly that there has been an unnecessary delay in bringing matters to a settlement. The late Government were seriously to blame. The change

took place under the late Government and they ought to have rectified it. This question was handed down to this Government to deal with.
What has this Government done to deal with it?

I will tell you what
this Government has done. This Government has instituted a case in the Exchequer Court of the Dominion for the purpose of setting aside the surrender. I think there are 400 or 500 Indians involved, together with others who are purchasers, numbering 500 to 600 all told. The Exchequer Court has issued an order naming a certain number of gentlemen to accept service for certain groups, and the case is now ready for trial.

I understood from the minister that subpoenas had been issued for witnesses, but, according to the statement of the hon. gentleman, the position of the case is that some men have been appointed to accept service for certain groups. .1 presume that means to accept service of Ithe original process in the Exchequer Court, and, therefore, the ease has only commenced.
Every one of these men has been served.
Then what is the use of having the groups?

The men have been appointed to accept service and they have been served. The reason the case has not been proceeded with is that there have been some negotiations going on. The gentlemen who secured this land have been negotiating to have some settlement without going to court, and I confess frankly that in my own estimation I have done something I ought not to have done in the interests of justice to the Indians; I have asked the Government to accept a settlement from these men so that the case may not be dragged out in the courts for years. I believe to-day as firmly as I did when I made my statement on the floor of this House, that there was perpetrated on the St. Peter's Indians one of the greatest outrages that ever has been perpetrated on any body of men in Canada. There is no question about that. I have not made one statement on the floor of this House that I want to retract. My hon. friend refers to the charges I have made against the former Deputy Superintendent
!Mr. Bradbury. ]
General of Indian Affairs. My statement stands to-day just as strongly as it stood the night I made it on the floor of this House, and it is absolutely true. The charge was that he took with him into the meeting at which the surrender was to take place, 15,000, and he said to these Indians: If you vote for this surrender I will divide this $5,000 among you, and if you do not I will take it home and you will not get a cent. That is my statement, and that statement is absolutely true.
Is it not a fact that whatever was paid to the Indians on the day of the surrender was paid on account of the purchase price of the Indians' interest in the land?
This is what the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs has said since.
Was not that a fact?

I believe it was a
fact. But, Mr. Chairman, the Indians did not understand it that way, and it was not explained to the Indians that way. The Indians understood he was giving that money for voting for the surrender. However, there is no use going into that discussion now. As I understand it, the Department of Justice has the case in hand, and at the very next sitting of the Exchequer Court we may expect it shall go to trial. The surrender is being attacked, and I understand that if the surrender is successfully attacked that that practically ends the case. But, Mr. Chairman, I enter my protest here that, that ought not to end this case. The men who are responsible for the outrage perpetrated on the St. Peter's Indians should be criminally prosecuted. There is no question in my mind about that. However, I will not press that part of it. As far as the town of Selkirk is concerned, the agitation that has been raised in that town through the press of the country has been paid for by the men who have been trying to get away with these Indian lands. There is no question about that. The quicker the case can go to trial the quicker it will satisfy me.
What settlement has been recommended to the Department of Justice?

I do not think there should be any secret about this thing and I do not intend to make a secret of it. There have been a good many offers made by these people. I have been approached my-

self more than once, but I was not approachable, and as it stands to-day I understand that the Government has agreed that if these people make a fair settlement, that the money to he paid into the Indian Department is to be distributed among the Indians pro rata. Just "what the amount is going to he, I am not in a position to say. Whatever the amount, it is to be arranged with the Indians and to be paid into the Indian Department to be put to the credit of the minister, I suppose, and distributed among the Indians. I understand there has been a very reasonable offer made to these men.

What portion of the Blood Indian reserve is open for lease to individual farmers in the district adjacent to that reserve? A year or so ago a lease held by private concerns expired. In answer to a question that I asked, the minister stated that the lease had not been renewed, and that leases were being made to individuals at certain rates per year for stock. The idea amongst the farmers of the district is very strongly in favour of their being given an opportunity to graze their cattle and other stock on this reserve, if an arrangement can be made with the Indians. At first the Indians were favourable to it, but afterwards they expressed opposition to the idea. It has been stated that an official of the department, who was inclined to be friendly to the company who wanted a renewal of the lease, encouraged the Indians to oppose the idea of individuals in the district having an opportunity to secure leases on the reserve for grazing purposes, and favour the private company.
I believe it would be beneficial to the mixed farming movement in Southern Alberta if some arrangement could be made to lease this land to individual farmers on a permanent basis. Temporary leases have been granted, but a permanent policy should be adopted of leasing the reserve for grazing purposes to farmers in the immediate vicinity who at the present time do not possess sufficient land for grazing purposes and who can utilize the reserve in that way. The minister has had the matter before him in the past, and I would like to know if there is any possibility of a permanent policy in this direction being adopted and carried out.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When I was out West about a year and a half ago, a deputation of gentlemen waited upon me from the neighbourhood of that reserve and made representations such as my hon. friend has made here to-night, namely, to allow a number of settlers adjacent to the reserve to have free access to it and not to tie it up in any one lease. The deputation which appeared before me and advocated that policy, repre-

sented in the main, Mormons. Subsequent to that visit, I asked the chief inspector of Indian agencies to visit the reserve and to find out the will of the Indians. As far as my information goes, I do not think he attempted to stampede the Indians into any particular line of policy; hut he called a meeting of the Indians and put the whole question before them, 'and they expressed strong disinclination to allow the adjacent farmers access to their reserve. There was a lease in the name of a man named Mc-Ewan from Brandon, and Gordon and Ironsides had made an arrangement with him for the stocking of the reserve. That lease terminated about a year ago, and it has not been renewed. We are charging them $3 per head and are getting by that more than the Indians have been in the habit of getting under their own lease. We have not finally decided as to our permanent policy. There are many things to commend this policy suggested by my hon. friend, although it has been claimed by a great many who have made representations to the department, including the Indians, that there would be a good many practical difficulties in working out such a policy by reason of the mixture of the stock. Herdsmen would be required to keep the stock 'separate, and a good deal of trouble would arise between the different owners. The question has been surrounded by a good deal of difficulty and trouble; and inasmuch as the Indians are getting quite a revenue under -the existing temporary arrangement, we have not seen fit to disturb it. We are quite open, however, to take into consideration the suggestion of the hon. member. We have consulted the Indian inspectors; and they have consulted the Indians, and I understand that the great preponderance of the Indians present at the meeting were against that policy. I do not know whether that was their view at the outset or not, but I am sure the chief inspector would not be guilty of attempting to stampede the Indians into an opinion that they had not held in the first place.

Indians, general: to provide for expenses in connection with epidemic of smallpox and other diseases, $10,000.
On what basis do you estimate the expenditure for the coming year to be $10,000? Is that based on the experience of the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, we spent over $13,000 last year.
The expenditure Is accounted for by doctor's accounts?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is under a number of
different headings. Quarantine, for instance, is one item, and to enforce a strict quarantine on the Indians is a somewhat difficult matter, and very expensive.
Do those medical attendants receive a yearly stipend?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They are the regular medical attendants, and have often to call in the provincial health authorities.

What expenses under
that item were made in Nova Scotia last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: None at all; there was no smallpox there.
It need not necessarily be smallpox.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Oh, no; scarlet fever or any disease of an epidemic or contagious character; but you were remarkably healthy down there last year.
Amongst what Indians is this money spent?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Among the Caughnawaga,
the Chippewas and the Lorette Indians. Then, we had to spend a large amount last year in connection with the smallpox on Manitoulin island.
Indians, surveys: Ontario, Quebec and Maritime provinces, $3,000.
What is the explanation of that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This item is intended to ' provide for the subdivision of the Pays Plat Indian reserve in Ontario, the re-survey of the disputed limits of the Big Hole tract in New Brunswick, and of the Whycocomagh reserve in Nova Scotia. The vote also provides for any unforeseen and necessary surveys in re-marking the boundaries of Indian reserves in the older provinces.
How long have these surveys been going on?.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: For some years.
In this particular case or in otheT cases?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, these are new and will be completed this year.
Who disputes, these boundaries?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The resident settlers on the borders of the various reserves.
Are you having any litigation about them?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not know that we have had any litigation, but it frequently happens that lines are overgrown and obliterated and

it is necessary to remark them. Those on the adjacent territory are the persons who make the requests.
Do you not think that might stand for a year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is not a very large item.

Every little makes a muckle, and there are a lot of little ones.
Progress reported.
