speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister of the Interior), the House went into Committee, Mr. Sevigny in the chair, to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Governor in Council shall have power to provide for the purchase, sale and distribution, during the year 1915, among such farmers and settlers in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan as apply for the same, of seed grain, fodder for animals, and other goods, by way of relief, in such quantities and upon such terms as to the taking of security for the repayment of the cost of seed grain, fodder and other goods by way of relief so supplied, as shall appear necessary or proper, and that the agreement dated the eighteenth day of February, 1915, between the Minister of the Interior, on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, and the Hon. George A. Bell the Provincial Treasurer on behalf of the Government of Saskatchewan and the agreement dated the thirteenth day of February 1915, between the Minister of the Interior on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, and the Hon. Arthur L. Sifton, on behalf of the Government of Alberta, relating to the means by which such seed grain, fodder for animals, and other goods by way of relief may be furnished, and that any action heretofore taken by the Governor in Council or by any department of the Government of Canada during the years 1914 and 1915 to provide the said farmers and settlers with seed grain, fodder for animals or other goods by way of relief, be approved, ratified and confirmed.
Will the minister please state the main terms oi the agreement referred to as having been entered into between this Government and the provincial governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The terms are the same in each case. The agreement provides t/hat liens to be taken against the land for the advance of seed grain shall be given priority over existing liens, the provincial governments to introduce legislation to that effect. That has already been done by the legislature of Alberta, and we have the agreement of the Saskatchewan government that a similar Act will be passed in that legislature. We are to be given a prior lien also for the relief of other than seed grain. That is the agreement in essence. Of course, in the Bill to be introduced based on this resolution there is a schedule containing the agreement.

I understood that there was some difference in the agreements entered into with the two provinces, that the province of Alberta had gone a little farther with respect to agreeing to pass legislation giving this Government a first lien upon lands for the supply of seed grains. My idea of it was that in Alberta they had agreed to pass legislation giving a first lien not only for seed but for certain classes of feed.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That was included in both agreements.

Then, are we to understand that before it would agree to advance any seed grain outside the restricted area spoken of, and even inside that restricted area, the Dominion Government insisted on the provinces passing legislation giving this Government a first charge upon land to the extent of the value of the seed grain advanced?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not know that this is the term to apply-that this Government " insisted." Of course, the Dominion Government wished to have sufficient security, because we are dealing with a vast amount of the funds of the people of' Canada. As the hon. gentleman knowis, in 1908 the late Dominion Government would not go even this far. The arrangement made on that occasion was that they would only advance seed grain to holders of unpatented land, inasmuch as this Parliament had not jurisdiction over the patented lands. The provincial Governments borrowed the money from the Dominion at five per cent and 84	.
themselves took the first lien against the land. We are taking the same 'Security that they took in 1908, and we are dealing with both patented and unpatented lands, because both provincial governments consider that the extent of the crop failure last year was beyond their coping with. We therefore ask the provincial governments to place us in -a similar position to that which they occupied as to security in 1908.

Do I understand that it is a condition of the agreement to advance money to buy 'seed grain that the charge of the Dominion Government shall be a first lien upon the patented lands, ahead of the mortgages ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, the same as the provincial governments had.
And without the consent of the mortgagees ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
I do not think that was done in 1908. The Government then was only dealing with unpatented lands.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The provincial governments dealt with patented lands.

With all deference, I think this is 'an entirely improper thing to do. It does 'seem to me that if a man or a company has lent money upon patented lands and taken 'Security upon those lands, it is a most extraordinary step to pass legislation which will wipe away that first lien and place another lien ahead of it. It may be said that it is for the advantage of the property and the improvement of the security which the mortgagee holds upon the land, but it seems to me contrary to every precedent of justice for the Legislature to intervene and put a lien ahead of an existing mortgage. Now, it does seem to me that where the conditions in the West are such as to require this Government to step in and grant relief, the Government might very well expect that on unpatented lands the loans should be made a first Charge upon the property; Because until the land is patented the homesteader cannot properly execute any encumbrance upon the property. That would be all right in respect of unpatented lands, but it seems to me that the Government ought simply to take a lien upon the interest that the owner of the property has in patented lands, unless the mortgagee or other person holding the encumbrance became a party to the agreement. Another objection arises out of that: it will tend to dis-



courage the lending of money to farmers in the West if the money-lender realizes that in case there is a bad harvest, a failure of crops, the legislature, by agreement with this Government, will step in and interfere with the first mortgage or lien that the mortgagee may have upon the property. He would be very doubtful as to the value of his security, and very reluctant to lend money in a country where the legislature, with the consent and approval of this Government, will so interfere with rights which have already been acquired, with mortgages already registered, and which give first liens upon the property. While disposed to favour to every possible extent the granting of the aid which is proposed, believing as I do that it is a step in the right direction entirely justified from every standpoint, I myself think it most unwise legislation to interfere with such rights without the consent of those in whom they are vested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John apparently does not fully realize the conditions under which this proposal is put forward, nor is he familiar with the practice which has prevailed in such matters in the past. As I understand, his remarks are addressed altogether to the question of the patented lands. The provision of seed grain for occupants of such lands has Ihitherto been dealt with by the provincial governments, and, presumably, those governments, being acquainted with local conditions, the requirements of the people and everything that makes for the best interests of all concerned, would be in at least as good a position to estimate the desirability of a measure of this kind as my hon. friend or any other hon. gentleman in this House. They are pursuing precisely the same course and adopting the same methods that they did under similar circumstances in the past. The Government would be very glad if the companies already holding first liens upon the lands would advance these amounts themselves; and, if any one of them desired to do so and to add the amount so advanced to its security and relieve the Government to that extent, I am sure there would be no possible objection to that course being pursued; but we have not observed any desire on the part of the companies to take that course, and the measure which is being proposed by the Minister of the Interior is one which it seems to me is in the interest not only of those who own the lands, but also of those who hold liens upon them. If these lands are left without provision for seed every one will

realize that the natural result will be a serious and unnecessary loss, not only to the owners of the lands, but also to the companies or other persons who hold liens upon them. This is a measure designed to make the land productive where otherwise it would not be productive. It is very likely that the crops for the coming year will be so ample as to justify most amply the aid which the Government proposes to give. My hon. friend proposes that the Government should make its security subsequent to that which already exists upon the land. I see no reason why that course should he taken, because this is eminently not only in the interest of the land owner, but of the lien holder as well. My hon. friend desires that we should take into account the interest of the lien holder; he should also remember that we are bound to take into consideration the interest of the land owner, the settler, and it is in the interest of the settler that this money, provided for a specific purpose, in order to make the land productive, should be a first lien upon the land itself; as, if this money were not advanced, the land, for this year at all events, would probably be useless, and a foreclosure of the mortgage would be forced, which would result in a loss to the owner of all his interest in the land. No one desires to interfere more than is absolutely necessary with vested rights, hut my hon. friend knows that under certain conditions of the law, the law relating to shipping, for example, the man who makes the last advance for the purpose of saving property and preserving it to the owner has the first lien, and this is very much on the same principle. We think that the Government ought to have the first lien because the money that the Government advances not only preserves the property for the land owner himself, but makes the lien of the mortgage holder secure as it otherwise would not be secure. Under the circumstances, it is easy to see that it is not only reasonable but absolutely desirable that the money advanced for this purpose should be the first lien on the land, because it is not only to preserve his interest in the land to the land owner, but to maintain the security of the lie'n holder and to make that land productive for the present year when otherwise it would not be productive.

It seems to me that the illustration given by my right hon. friend of the case of the party who salves a vessel or cargo having a first lien is not applicable.

Sir ROBERT BORDENI was not referring to salvage.

My right hon. friend
was referring to instances where the law which is invoked has been the law of the land for years, and therefore persons who may lend money upon vessels or upon cargoes lend it with the knowledge of the existing law and all rights that may intervene. That would be like this case if there were a law upon the statute book, not made retroactive in its character, but existing, which provided that in case at any time the Government should lend aid to settlers that would be a first lien upon the property. If that were the law, then any person taking a mortgage or security of any kind upon the property would take it with a knowledge that that was the law, and that his rights might be cut down to that extent in the future. However, that is an entirely different case. People who have lent money to settlers-and we know that there are vast sums loaned by companies in Eastern Canada more especially-have done it under the existing law, knowing that when they did it they would receive by means of their conveyance a first mortgage upon the patented lands of the mortgagor. Now it is proposed to change the law. It is practically proposed to lend money to the settler, and for that loan to take a lien ahead of the mortgage which the money lender has taken in good faith; and this mortgage of the money lender may represent the security of widows and orphans in the East, who are very largely interested in trust and mortgage companies. But the Government's lien is to come ahead of all existing encumbrances. When my hon. friend the Minister of Finance spoke early in the session of what he proposed to do for the farmers of the West, I thought this Government was going to do something for which they would deserve the credit of the people of this country, and more especially of the people in the West. But to-day I find that they are exacting the pound of flesh. They are going to charge the settler five per cent upon the money they advance for the purpose of- securing seed grain, and they are going to say to him and everybody interested in his land: In addition to that, we are going to take a first mortgage upon your property irrespective of what other claims there may be against it. Now that is not doing very much for the settler. It does not recognize to a very great extent the extraordinary condition of affairs which exist in the West, and which calls for this 84J
relief. My right hon. friend says that this is a benefit to the western country. I grant that, but is it not also a benefit to the whole of Canada that as large a crop as possible should be raised during the coming year in our western country? Is not that in the interests of the whole people of this country, and especially at this time when the Mother Country looks to Canada to supply bread stuffs for the Empire during this war? And yet the Government is approaching this question just as a money lender or almost a Shylock would, and is demanding the last dollar of security, and the very highest security which can possibly be given by the settlers in our western country. They are taking a step which is going to destroy credit, and which is going to prevent eastern loan and trust companies from investing in the West. This Government may say that they are helpless because of the action of the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan; but that action was taken _ because this Government insisted on it as a condition of granting this relief. I say this is going to unsettle conditions in the West so far as credit is concerned, and it is something which this Government ought not to insist upon. My right hon. friend says I am not familiar with the method of dealing with these things in the past. I grant that, but I know that when this party was in power previously to 1896, the Government of that day, when there was distress in the West and need for seed grain, did not insist on taking a first lien upon the property. I know that the Government advanced seed grain to the settlers, took as security a bond, with one or two sureties which were satisfactory to them. That is the course that was pursued along in the eighties to my own personal knowledge; at that time no such extraordinary demand was made as this Government is now making.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Were those loans to
farmers on patented lands?

I do not know, but I
presume not, because in the early days of settlement there was very little land that was patented. But I should think that, if a Government was prepared to lend seed grain to homesteaders on unpatented land, they would be more willing to lend to the owners of patented land because the security would be so much better. That was the course adopted along in the eighties, but I submit that the doctrine of this Government of trampling upon vested rights, of

setting aside first securities, and doing that without so much as asking the mortgagee for his consent, and of taking away the first lien which he has upon the property, I submit that that is entirely unjustifiable. I do not think this Government can shelter itself behind the fact that the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan are willing to pass this legislation. If they are willing to pass it, I am sure they are doing it simply because of the condition of affairs in the West, and because they have found that this Government would not grant relief unless such legislation were passed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The only two classes concerned in the subject of this discussion are the mortgagees and the Government representing the people of Canada. It would be impossible for any hon. member to pretend that, in asking the Government to take less security, he represents in any way the desire or interest of the farming community. The farmers of the West would be no better off if they gave a second or a third or a fourth encumbrance on their land instead of a first. To them it makes no difference whatever. Their interest is to get the seed grain, and-to protect themselves and their creditors. There are two classes: The Government of Canada, and the mortgagees, the moneyed interest; and the House will note with very considerable interest that when the interests of these two classes apparently clash the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is the champion of the moneyed interests. It is not long since he was on the other side of the fence, when he found very serious fault with this Government for being so closely allied to the interests of big finance. . Aside from that, I am not one who would argue that we should by reason of any contingency whatever do an injustice to mortgagees, any more -than to any other class; but I take the ground that this is doing them justice in every sense of the word, and that it is of great benefit to the farmers, and at t'he same time no more than justice to the *Government representing all the people of this country. We insist on a first lien on the land. We are charged with sheltering ourselves behind the actions of the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta, in that they agreed to giving us a first lien, and we are designated Shylocks because we ask for it. The hon. member for St. John forgets that in 1908, when we loaned these governments money, they themselves passed legislation operating over their own

respective provinces and taking to themselves this first lien ahead of all other mort-.gages; so that if we are in the Shylock class we have at least a precedent in the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1908. More than that; in 1908 the government of Saskatchewan made loans to the farmers on the security of a first lien. They also took security on the crop. They stated that their loan was to be ahead not only of .all mortgages but of all taxes, ahead of any charge that any one could place against the land. But the government of Alberta-and I do not know whether my hon. friend is aware of this-went farther than that. They made their loan a first charge against the land in every respect as to present and future encumbrances, and also took to themselves the power of collecting this money by taxation, and of enforcing the collection of this money over and above any other debt that the farmer might have Charged against his land or otherwise. That is how they collected the money. Year by year taxation was the enforced method of payment, and operated by that government against the farmers of the province; and I do not know that any fault was found with that, even by mortgagees. But what I am trying to impress on the hon. member for St. John is this: we do not in any way seek shelter behind the action of the governments of Saskatchewan or Alberta, or behind the action of any government or any party. We have, though, the precedent of the action of these governments when there was no compulsion whatever-whether there be compulsion now or not-when they acted of their own free will, and in their wisdom were governed by the conditions of their own provinces and by no other conditions.
It is argued that because we take a first lien on the land we interfere with outside rights-the rights of mortgagees. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister pointed out very clearly that the principle is analogous in every way to the principle which gives priority to the one who comes in as the last insurer of a cargo and thus takes the last and greatest risk. The hon. member for St. Jolhn argued that inasmuch .as we have not had legislation on the statute book enabling us to get this first lien the mortgagees did not contemplate such an Act and consequently that we should not pass it. 1 may be wrong in my common law, as I have not read the point for some time, but I have a recollection that it was the common law before there was any statute that the

party Who came in as the last insurer got the first lien.
On what class of property?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: On property insured on the sea.
We are not dealing with property on the sea.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It was recognized hy the courts, aside from the statute, as a matter of common justice and it is the same to-day. How can the mortgagee complain?
If my hon. friend says that it Is the common law or that the Government has a first lien to secure the advance of seed grain I am with him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I am arguing that the courts of justice decided that it was a matter of common justice to give the last insurer priority and, if it was common justice then, common justice is eternal. It does not vary with the years.
The mortgagee has a Tight to obviate this lien if he wishes.	He has the
right to come in and do what we are doing. We will only he too glad to let him do it. What is his complaint? Would it be better for him that we should let the land, the farmer and the country go? No, he is better off by what we are doing. I admit that it would be better still for him if we took a second, third or fourth mortgage and came in on top of a great many encumbrances but it would be an injustice to the whole people of Canada, because the whole people of Canada have no right to be called upon to lend money on such security as that.
I want to draw attention to another feature of the Bill. The Bill takes other security, which also was taken by the provincial governments in 1908; that is security on the crop. I do not know that this is thoroughly understood, but I can very briefly state the position. We get security as to the land, for all we advance, but we get priority only as to seed grain and fodder for animals. We get no priority as to other relief. As to other relief we simply come on top; that is a matter as to which we get no priority at all. As to advances for seed grain and fodder for animals we get priority entirely.
But on the crops we have priority, a first lien as to all advances. The Government would, therefore, be in a position if the circumstances warranted it, to
relieve the mortgagees at as early a date as possible, by realizing, where-ever possible. I believe it will be the desire of the farmers to be released from these obligations, wherever possible, and thus restore the conditions which by necessity are somewhat dislocated by the legislation.
Did the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta ask this Government to loan them money, and offer to deal directly with the farmers?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They voluntarily offered
the legislation, but they did not apply to borrow money in the way they did in 1908. As a matter of fact, they refused to do as they did in 1908. They did not wish to have anything to do with the collection, but they volunteered the legislation that is now being enacted.

I am in favour of this legislation. I believe it will be welcomed by the mortgagees. Many of the mortgagors have not even paid their interest, and if these farmers are not assisted this year the mortgagees would have to take a great deal of land that they do not want. I do not quite understand the hon. the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) in what he says with respect to liens on fodder and other supplies. Does the Government say that it will have a first lien for money advanced for provisions?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, not on the land. We get a first lien for money advanced for seed grain and fodder for animals on the land; but we get no first lien on the land for relief.
Do you get a first lien on the crop ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As to the crop, we get a first lien for everything.

The only objection I see is that it will interfere with any advantage the settlers might otherwise get from the amendment to the Bank Act, which was introduced by the hon. the Minister of Finance a few days ago.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.

The settler who has received fodder for his animals and provisions and who has been too late in applying for seed grain, cannot then apply to the bank because the bank will not advance him money for seed grain unless ia first lien is given to the bank on the crop. There are a great many settlers who did not apply in time. I am getting letters every day from settlers who did not file their application

and who have been refused on the ground that they were too late in applying.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The point of the hon. gentleman i<s that in many cases in the drouth-stricken districts, where a farmer has been compelled to ask for relief and that relief has been given, the Government lien is a first charge, and consequently, if he applies to the, hank, he cannot get an advance because the bank cannot get a first lien. That may be 'correct, but I do not think that when a settler is in the position that he has been compelled to get relief from the Government, he will not be able to get a loan from the bank anyway, even for seed grain. It may be that the effect that the hon. gentleman described would actually take place, but it is a very remote contingency that it may take place, because such a man could not get relief from the bank. He would get relief here.

Some settlers did not get their lands ready for seed, and their applications were rejected on that ground. Others did not apply in time. Under the amendment to the Bank Act, these men cannot get an advance from the bank, owing to the fact that the Government's lien has priority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to say a few words in reference to the observations made by the hon. member for St. John * (Mr. Pugsley). The object of this legislation is to secure advances made for the purpose of furnishing seed grain to the farmers of the West. It has been pointed out by the . right hon. the Prime Minister and by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) that the effect of the action of the Government will be to preserve the security of the mortgagees. It is in the interest of the mortgagees that these advances should be made by the Dominion Government. My hon. friend must know, in the course of his legal experience, that it is the common practice of the courts to give a charge in priority to a first mortgage for Salvage money advanced to preserve property upon which the first mortgage has been taken. In the course of my experience I have known that to be done a number of times. Let us take the case of a receivership, we will say, of a mining company, and let us assume that there are first mortgage bonds outstanding secured according to the laws of a province by a first mortgage charge. The mines have to be pumped out and preserved, and the same principle applies to railways and undertakings of all kinds.
[Mr. 'W'arnock.J
My hon. friend must know in the course of his legal experience, that when such an application, setting out all the facts, is made to a court, some one has to advance the money for the purpose of preserving the property in which not only the receiver representing the creditors and the company but the bondholders themselves are vitally interested; and the court, acting within its equitable jurisdiction, at once makes an order giving a charge in priority to the charge created in favour of the first mortgage or other bondholders.
Has the hon. gentleman ever known that to be done except in proceedings which are instituted by the bondholders themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have known it to be
done at the instance of the receiver representing all parties, and I have never known bondholders to object where the object of the charge was to preserve the property, unless they themselves were prepared to come forward and put up the money. There is no departure from legal precedent in what we are proposing to do.
What is the situation? We were confronted with something in the nature of a national calamity in the West; a great district was visited by drouth. There was no crop for miles and for hundreds of miles. In these circumstances there was great destitution and at a time of the greatest financial stringency- in this country the Government was, asked to provide funds, in the first place, to relieve those who were in distress and in some ca^es were starving, and in the second place, to provide seed grain for them, in order that they might put in next year's crop. Tfie Government provided, and gladly provided, and it was a great pleasure to us to so provide, a sum of money, amounting to between eight and nine million dollars for that purpose. The question arises as to how we are going to secure that money of the people of Canada, advanced under extraordinary circumstances, because it would not be advanced under ordinary circumstances. If my hon. friend will look at the correspondence in 1908 between the Minister of the Interior and provincial governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta, he will find that it was laid down by the Minister of the Interior, in the Administration of which he was a member, that once lands are patented any relief to be given must be given by the provincial governments. In 1908 the then Dominion Government made a loan- because the province could not obtain the

money readily on account of financial stringency-to the provinces, which in turn made loans to owners of patented lands, and took from them precisely the same security as we are taking to-day, and no untoward consequence resulted. I was in the mortgage business at the time, and I think I am reasonably well acquainted with loan conditions in the Northwest, and I never heard a single complaint from the mortgagees with regard to the action of the Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta. On the contrary, I have had managers of loan companies say to me that the Government should make these advances to provide for seed grain. It is true that within the last three or four weeks I have had communications passed on to me from mortgage companies, protesting against the Government taking a lien in priority of their mortgages. I pointed out to them precisely what I have pointed out to this House: that the situation was exceptional and abnormal, that a vast district in the West had been visited by unprecedented drouth, and that if we did not come ito the relief of those settlers, not only would they suffer, but the security upon which their _ first mortgages was held would be greatly depreciated. I pointed out, further, that the result that might be apprehended would be this: that if the farmers failed to secure seed grain which would enable them to raise a crop next year, not only would their security be depreciated, not only would the farmers' crop of next year he not available to pay their interest, but it might well happen that a whole district would be depopulated, because of an exodus, and if that should occur the value of the security held by the mortgagees would disappear.
In these circumstances, I have no hesitation in saying, and I have been a financial man for many years, that it is distinctly in the interests of the mortgagees themselves, just as it was to their interest in 1908, that the Government should make these advances, and that it is no hardship on the mortgagees that the advances so made from the money of the people of Canada should be secured by a lien-the lien bought for a comparatively small amount-in priority to the security of those mortgagees whose interests will be protected by the action of the Government.
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) says we are acting like Shylocks. I desire to say this to him: that from all over the West we have had requests, and repeated requests, that the Government should advance this
money, and we have met these requests as fairly as we could. I may say further to my hon. friend, that I have, in the many letters, to say nothing of personal interviews, impressed upon the bankers of this country the desirability of extending credit, in so far as they can safely do so without departing from the principles of sound banking, to the farmers of the West at this critical period in their history and in the history of Canada, in order that this year they may be able to secure seed grain and raise a crop which is so essential to them, and to Canada, and for that matter to the Empire. Everything that the Government could be reasonably expected to do has been done, and I am surprised at my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) rising in his seat in the interests of the mortgagees whose securities are advantaged, and putting forward views which, if the Government had held, would have prevented them from doing what they have decided to do and which they believe will be of great advantage to the farmers of the West.
There has been absolutely no protest from any of the farmers of the West against our action. On the contrary, there have been requests from all parts of the West for the Government to do precisely what it has done, and in addition to that my hon. friend knows that in 1908 the provincial government took precisely the security which this Government is taking to-day. In fact, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) says, they went farther in the taking of security than we have gone, and no untoward results have come from it. It gave advantage to the farmer, advantage to the mortgagee, and so far as I know no loss to any one concerned has resulted. Under these circumstances I say that the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) were ill-advised, and that, his criticism lacks foundation. I do not believe there is a manager of a loan company doing business in the West who, if it came to a question whether the Government would not make advances at all, or would make advances and take security, would not say that he is in favour of making advances and taking security.
That is what I complain of; you will not lend the money on fair terms.

speechtext:
Fair terms? We are lending salvage money to protect not only the farmers but the interests of the mortgagees as I have shown, and shown conclusively, in accordance with the practice of the
1.336

courts, and what we ask is the security which has been deemed essential and which has been taken by the provincial governments who are on the spot, and who, as the Prime Munster has said, know the local situations and are best fitted to judge as to what legislation will prove beneficial for the interests of all concerned. They have done that, and no question raised by my hon. friend in the House; hut when we do it, my hon. friend protests. Of course, he would protest. I have often thought that, if there were no ten commandments and if a member of this Government brought them down as they left the hand of Moses and as mey appear in Holy Writ, my hon. friend or some other hon. gentleman opposite would protest that they were class legislation of the most objectionable character.

I had no idea that J was going to stir up such a hornet's nest. My hon.- friend says-in effect-that my criticism is ill-advised and senseless; that it 'does not strike any one as amounting to anything. It is strange that it has taken my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, my distinguished friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), and my very able and eloquent friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), to attempt to answer the criticism which I have made. The reason is that they know that this condition upon which they insist is wholly indefensible. They know that they cannot justify the taking away of vested rights in this way. My right hon. friend, however, says: Oh, the land companies will consent, because, if it is put to them as a question of either insisting upon this condition or not getting the seed grain at all, they will say that it is in the interest of the West and therefore in their interest. That is what I complain of, namely, that this Government ought not to have put the people of the provinces of the West or the mortgagees or the loan companies in the position in which it has placed them. I am entirely in favour of the legislation authorizing the advancing of seed grain. I agree with my hon. friend the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) that it is the right thing to do; but what 1 am opposed to is the insisting upon those conditions and the violation of every principle of justice and fair-play with regard to those who have encumbrances upon western property.
What would you suggest?

I would suggest that under the present condition of affairs the 
Government ought to he willing to lend seed grain to the people of the West, taking a bond with one or two sureties in the case of persons whose security the Government does not think is satisfactory, and also taking a lien upon the grain which is raised from the seed so advanced to the farmers. That would be a reasonable proposition and something that the Government could justify. What I complain of is that the Government says: Although this is a national calamity, and we feel that it is in the interest of the whole people of Canada that good crops should. be raised during the present year; yet we are not going to advance a bushel of seed grain unless it is treated as a loan, unless we get 5 per cent interest, unless we have a first lien upon the property, putting us ahead of all other encumbrances, and also unless we get a lien upon the grain to be produced from the seed. No private individual could insist upon harsher terms than those upon which the Government is insisting, so far as the settlers of the West are concerned. Such harsh terms cannot be squared with any expression of a desire to aid the people of the West in the crisis in -	which they now find themselves.

Minister of Finance says that he has known frequently of cases where property is in liquidation, and where receivers are appointed and receivers' certificates issued which come ahead of the interest of mortgagees. That is quite true in the case of proceedings which are taken by the mortgagees themselves. Where the mortgagees are the parties to the receivership, the receiver is practically their officer, although appointed by the court. In that case the court will issue receivers' certificates which will come ahead of the mortgages; but my right hon. friend has never known of a case where a second or a third mortgagee, who has instituted proceedings, can hiave receivers' certificates issued at his suit which will come ahead of the prior mortgages.

When the Wabash railway went into the hands of receivers, that was done at the instance of the creditors and subsequently at the instance of the bondholders. The receivers' certificates are prior to all claims against that road. The same is true of the Pere Marquette railway.
I can give my hon. friend the reference in the Wabash proceedings.
In what state?

Missouri. There were
several applications for a receivership, one

by the creditors and subsequently one by the bondholders.

My hon. friend, who is very familiar with eourt proceedings, has been obliged to go to the State of Missouri to get a precedent. Other gentlemen have gone to Missouri in the past, and they have secured information perhaps equally valuable.

I will give my hon. friend an instance in Canada. I once had to do with the liquidation of a very large company, and it became necessary for us to get funds with which to carry on the work. We got authority from the court for the Bank of Montreal to advance money. That money was considered as a prior claim against the assets of the company.
I have in mind another claim. My hon. friend reminds me that when I was a youth practising law, I learned a great deal from him. In the case of the Crown vs. Sieve-wright, I appeared at the instance of my hon. friend and on his behalf for the Crown. I was very pleased and proud to do so. The case went to the Supreme Court subsequently, and it was held that the Crown had a prior claim over the assets of Sievewright from the time he signed the bond until the receivership became effective. In the case of the Maritime Bank vs. the Queen, which arose in New Brunswick, and which went to the Privy Council, it was held that the money deposited by the province had a prior claim over the creditors of the bank.
Having come from New Brunswick, I understand that we have the same characteristic there as have the citizens of Missouri; we have to be shown. In that instance the people of New Brunswick were shown just as the people of Missouri have to be shown.

My hon. friend stopped short in the lessons which he learned from me. If he had remained longer, perhaps he would have known that the reason why the Crown obtained precedence in the cases to which he referred is that by common law the Crown has a prior right against the assets of the subject.
Exactly.

But that prior right must have reference to the debtor's property at the time when the Crown's claim first arose. You could not give a claim to the Crown to-day and take precedence over a mortgage which was executed yesternay.
Except it be for salary.

That, of course, raises another question. In that case it does not make any difference whether it is the Crown or not. I am quite familiar with all the cases to which my hon. friend has referred, and I am quite familiar with the fact that liquidators under the Winding-up Act can obtain money which would be a first claim; but my hon. friend knows just as well as I do that under that Act the interests of mortgagees are brought before the court and are dealt with by the court just the same as are all the rights of the other creditors. That is an entirely different principle from the issuing of receiver's certificates which will come ahead of a mortgage. I have never known of a case, in Canada at all events, where in proceedings to which the first mortgagee is not a party, a receiver's certificate can be issued which will take precedence over the first mortgage. I do not believe that any such case can be found.
I am very sorry to detain the committee by reason of any remarks I make. I did not expect to provoke such a spirited defence of this legislation as that which has been entered . upon by hon. gentlemen upon the Government benches.
I regret to be compelled to say that I have not been at all convinced by the argument that the hon. gentlemen have made. They refer to 1908. Conditions were entirely different then. The country was comparatively new and there were comparatively few patented lands. There were fewer mortgages and not so many loan companies engaged and not so much money was invested. The Solicitor General says that I am taking the side of the moneyed interests. If it gives him any pleasure to say that, he is quite at liberty to say it. I should have thought from the intelligence oif the Solicitor General that he would have realized that I am taking the side of simple justice. A loan company or mortgagee is just as much entitled to justice as any other portion of the community. While I believe that this seed grain should be advanced, and while this side of the House will cheerfully support the Government in advancing it, what I object to is that this Parliament should ask the legislatures of Alberta and Saskatchewan to violate every principle of justice and interfere with vested rights by placing those who are now first or second mortgagees so that their lien shall come only second or third, and this

without asking the consent of the people whose rights it is intended to take away.

I had not intended to speak on this subject, but inasmuch as I live within one of the provinces affected so injuriously by reason of the drouth to which the Minister of Finance referred, I rise to make one or two observations. I have found that, as a matter of fact, most of the loan companies are particularly desirous that this legislation should pass. In the law office in which I carry on business when I am at home, we have had to do in the last few years with the loaning of very large sums of money, and much of it has been loaned in the very district affected by the drouth. Foreclosure proceedings have been threatened and, unfortunately, in some instances, foreclosure actions have actually been brought. When these actions were brought it was represented to the large loan companies, the trust companies, that it was probable that the Government would come forward and loan money for the purpose of securing seed to the settlers. When that became apparent, the companies at once dropped their foreclosure actions, realizing that this action on the part of the Government would enable the lands to be planted and would add value which would enable them to get back their money. It was then pointed out that the Government would not make these advances unless they were given a prior claim. But, as the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) has said, the Crown has a prior claim under the common law. All that is done, then, under this legislation, is to assert in statutory form the common-law right of the Crown. We have regard to the fact that the money is advanced for one purpose only, namely, to save the farmer, and the principle that he who saves should have a first claim against that which he has saved. This is an ordinary case of salvage.

Did the mortgagees
object?	,

I was going on further- and I am giving concrete cases. When it was pointed out that the result would be that the Crown would have a prior claim over their mortgages by reason of the legislation to be passed by the provinces, most of these companies were content. Why? Because the added value of their security made it advisable that this should be done. Suppose that they had gone on to foreclose-
I have in mind several cases-the property [Mr. Pussley.7
would not have been bought; there is nobody to buy it; and they would have to take title. What would that mean? It would mean a piece of idle land. But when, last fall, it became evident that the Government would furnish the seed grain, the people banded themselves together and by cooperative effort in many instances they prepared a larger acreage for seed than has ever been prepared in Southern' Alberta, looking to the seed grain to enable them to plant. And the- loan companies that have a first mortgage were content to have it so, rather than have on their hands pieces of land taken by foreclosure. They said: Our security is more valuable by reason of the seed being planted this spring, even though the lien for that seed is made a first claim against the land.

The loan companies
being willing, why not get them to sign consent?

I am just coming to
that. I went West eighteen years ago. The seed grain bonds to which the hon. gentleman referred had not run out, and I well remember the difficulties connected with them. The man to whom the seed was advanced signed a bond, and two or three of his neighbours signed with him as guarantors. It was quite natural that in a country so sparsely populated as it then was, each man was both principal and guarantor. Some of the principals left the country. In the Land Titles Office many seed grain bonds were registered and many a man had to pay not only for his own seed grain but as endorser for the seed grain given to others. That is the reason why the province, in 1908, would have nothing more to do with this bond business.
The whole theory on which the legislation of the provinces proceeds is to make it as simple as possible, and to do by statute and inexpensively that which would require large expense to do in individual cases. This legislation is the legislation of the provinces, not of the Dominion. We have the Torrens system of land titles in Alberta. When a mortgage is given against a title it is entered upon the certificate of title in the Lands Title Office as a first charge. That stands. This seed grain lien is to be made, not by Act of Parliament but by Act of the provincial legislature which is composed of men in touch with local conditions. This Dominion did not insist on any specific lien, but pointed out what would be most simple, most direct.

best calculated to meet the difficulty at the least expense. We have a statutory declaration by the province of Alberta that the seed grain lien shall rank first against the crop produced from the grain and for the purposes of repaying the loan. Could anything be fairer?
I am afraid the hon. member for St. John city has what may be called a political sympathy with the settler rather than a business sympathy with the investor. For I know his ideas of business too well not to know that, with his great capacity for business, he would challenge this Government and criticise it severely if it did not take steps to provide that the money of the people of Canada-it is the money of all the people-should be secured by a claim against the crop which is produced by this investment even though the property upon which it is produced is already mortgaged. The principles to which he has referred make this clearer. We have had comparatively little experience of receiverships of railways in Canada. But everybody who has studied the matter knows that receivers' certificates, in the United States, in England and in every other country, take priority over the claims of other creditors, whether they be first mortgagees, second mortgagees or any other. And they will continue to do so. I trust my hon. friend will not endeavour to make any political capital out of what he calls " the harsh and unjust measures " the Government has taken. Consider the situation to the south of the line. The State of Montana has been stricken as the province of Alberta has been stricken; but no relief was given to the settlers of Montana by the Federal Government of the United States.
They have cried aloud and in vain for the same measure of relief that we have given the distressed people of Western Canada. The people of the United States have been very much impressed with the difference in treatment. I had a letter this morning in which it is stated that a gentleman recently had ten inquiries to take up land in southern Alberta because it is apparent that our settlers are so generously treated in times of trouble and stress and drouth that it is a good country to settle in. My hon. friend is not serious when he says that we are unjust to the people of the West when all we have done is to say that repayment of advances must be made. All we have done is to say that when the money of the people of Canada, east or west, north or south, has been kindly and generously voted by the
men of Ontario and Quebec to relieve 'distress in Alberta and Saskatchewan, we shall not be blind to our obligations and duties and to declare that this salvage money, which is going to make great added wealth for each quarter-section and each half-section of Alberta, shall be repaid out of the added wealth thus created. It will enhance the value of each quarter-section and each half-section to an extent that will leave an equity in favour of the original owner that would not exist but for the very relief that we are advancing. My hon. friend, I am glad to see, has a sympathetic consideration for those in the West. In 1908 he was not averse to taking a prior lien against the mortgagee-but he was then a member of the Government and he is now in Opposition. Of course, if you can create sympathy on the part of the settler, make him think he has been harshly treated, per-adventure-I say peradventure-he may vote for your party; but I think he has too fine a sense of justice, too high a realization of what the Government has done in advancing $10,000,000 to assist the settlers of the West, to be affected by such a cry. That action will not be forgotten. There could be no better advertisement for Canada as a whole than thus to show the sympathy of the men of the east, those who have the greatest amount of money, for those in less fortunate circumstances in the West. I trust we shall hear no more about the injustice of this matter.

Does my hon. friend
think the political consideration is uppermost in the minds of the Government when they are making the seed grain appropriation?

I am very pleased to
say that I know it is not, for the largest measure of relief has been afforded in the constituency of the 'hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan), who happens to sit beside the hon. gentleman, and who knows that a great deal of relief given has been given to men of the other political faith, those who came into Canada some time ago and who were led to believe that there was only one side to vote for. They are, however, seeing the error of their ways. I know that these men are able to go to the stores where they formerly purchased, Whether they are Liberal or Conservative, and get their goods just as in days gone by and the Government pays the accounts. I know that my hon. friend will at least give the Government credit for that.

I was led to believe that the hon. gentleman thought that the Government was thinking about the vote of the men from the West in the next election because he took credit to the Government for voting this money, and he hoped the settlers in the West would not forget the Government at the next election. He thought the men from the West had reason to feel gratitude towards the Government for what they are now doing.

My hon. friend is
entirely mistaken. What I said was that it was painfully apparent that hon. gentlemen opposite were endeavouring to show to the settlers that they had been treated badly by the Government, in order to induce them to vote with his side; but I said I thought they were men of larger intelligence and greater understanding than that, and would realize that the relief which had been accorded to them had been received from the whole people of Canada.

I think we are getting away from the real purpose of the resolution. In so far as liens and mortgages are concerned, as I am not a lawyer and do not know the merits of these particular arguments, I shall not discuss them. The assistance that has been rendered to this particular district in western Canada will save the mortgages of the loan companies within the next few years. That is my view of the situation.
There is also this fact to be considered- I want to be candid and fair-that if the Government of Canada had not come to the relief of that district last fall, there would unquestionably have been an exodus of people from that district back to the United States and back to eastern Canada; and the result would have been that many homesteads would have been left on the hands of the mortgage companies of Canada. The Government are assisting the settlers by providing relief to maintain them, and then they are providing them with seed so that they may hope to get a crop this fall. They are also providing feed for their stock. I say that this is a necessity. If we get a crop in southern Alberta this year it is going to maintain the population there, and I am not discouraged about the future.
In the year before last the state of Kansas, one of the greatest producing states in the American Union, had a complete crop failure. That state in its early days had a precarious history. People went in there and settled; they met with crop failures and many left the state; but to-day Kansas

is one of the most productive states of the Union, and its farmers, per capita, are amongst the wealthiest farmers of the United States.
Over 100,000,000 bushels of wheat.

They had a crop failure in 1913 but last year they had the biggest crop in their history-so I am not discouraged about the future in Alberta. We have had good crops there. In this particular district, east of Lethbridge, there have been crops of 40 bushels to the acre of wheat. If that was done in one year it can be done again, and I believe the Government of Canada will receive back all the money it is expending in this particular regard. I believe that the loan companies will eventually have their mortgages cleared off and that the country will be prosperous and successful. I have been told by men in my own district that they started in Manitoba in the early days. I remember a gentleman who settled around Carberry who said they had to overcome so many obstacles there the first two or three years he was in that district that the men who could afford to get out got out and the only people who remained there were the people who could not afford to get out; yet those men who remained are to-day amongst the wealthiest and most prosperous farmers in Canada. I believe that the same thing will be said of southern Alberta in the days to come. It is true that I come from that district and that I am an optimist about it even when the clouds are hanging heavy over that particular country; but a man who has lived there and has seen large crops raised cannot help believing in that country. If our farmers had been in the condition of the farmers of Kansas in 1913 the Government would not have needed to assist them; but the fact is that our country is new, the people have just gone in there, they have very little, if any capital, and have a great deal of expense to meet in the earlier period of their settlement. Consequently when they faced a severe crop failure they had to look to somebody, or some organization, or some Government for assistance. If they had been in that country for a number of years and had had a series of good crops so that they could have laid money aside, they would have been in the same position as the farmers O'f Kansas in 1913; they could have overcome that obstacle and not worried about the future.
I would like to impress upon the members

of the Government that the assistance they have given has been probably beyond the amount that was at first intended; there is no question about that; but they have undertaken a policy of assisting the settlers of that district and I would urge upon them to carry that assistance out as far as possible until the crop of this year is assured. There is every reason to believe, if present indications are any indication, that we shall have an exceptionally good crop in southern Alberta this year. But what I wish to point out is this. As I said, when the Minister of Finance had the amendment to the Bank Act before the Committee the other day, the farmers of southern Alberta were up against these obstacles; they had no crop, and they had no feed for their stock; and they could not get any assistance from the banks. That is the position the majority of them were in. The Government granted relief to the farmers and their families, and they are grantifig assistance now in the way of seed grain and feed for stock. But I find in the regulations regarding feed for stock, a limitation which is going to interfere with the development of the mixed farming idea in that -section, and that is, that very little, if -any assistance is being given to the farmers towards keeping milch cows on their farms. The result is they are being compelled to sacrifice that kind of stock. I am also advised that the feed which is being advanced for farm work-horses is not sufficient to enable farmers to carry out the farm work as it should be carried out at the present time.
I have a petition here from Foremost, which I will read in order to impress upon the Government the view of these farmers. Foremost is in the heart of the drouth district in Southern Alberta :
Whereas we, the undersigned petitioners, are agreed that the Government allowance of one-half bushel per acre of feed oats for spring work on the farm is far from being a sufficient quantity to properly conduct the spring farming operations, our horses having just come through a hard winter without grain, we believe that an allowance should be made of two (2) gallons of grain to the horse per day for two weeks before work on the land begins and one bushel per acre for all acreage for which each farmer has received seed grain.
Thai is the statement of the farmers themselves. I intend to forward this petition to the Minister of the Interior, in order that he may look into the matter and ascertain whether the statements are warranted.
There is another point to be considered. In our part of the country, if farming is to
be successful, summer fallowing has to be done, and done in the early summer months. If the farmers are not able to get feed at that time, either through the banks or through the Government-and I understand that the Government have not decided to continue their assistance any further than for spring work-the farmers will be up against the very serious problem of not being able to carry on summer fallowing, which is a prime necessity in that part of Alberta. I want to bring that to the attention of the Government, because it is a very serious matter. I repeat that, if the summer fallowing cannot be done this summer, it will interfere with the possibilities of a crop next year. It was established even last year that where summer fallowing was properly done there was a crop even in the drouth district, probably not very large, but a crop nevertheless. Summer fallowing is a necessity, and I wish to emphasize that point; also the point that assistance should be given in the way of feed for other farm stock. I do not say that assistance should be given to a man who is practically a rancher, but I mean the ordinary farmer with a few head of cattle, a few hogs and other stock. Feed should be given to these farmers so that they could carry the stock until they -are in a condition to provide feed themselves. The farmer will pay the money back, and if we have a good crop this year, and the prospects point that way, the Government will be repaid this fall for what they have advanced. I am strongly in support of the measure which is now before the House.

I
think we had better drop any objections we may have as to the mode of taking security. The procedure is not satisfactory in a great many ways, it is true, but T suppose there would be objections to whatever method was suggested. In some cases the mortgagees may be injured, but as a whole I do not think they will, although I cannot agree with the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) in his rather sweeping statement that the mortgagees will in no case be injured. The hon. member for Calgary intimated that if blame was to be attached to anybody it should be attached to the Provincial Government, but I say that if blame should be attached to any one it should be to the Dominion Government, for the Provincial Governments acted under compulsion. I am not finding fault with the legislation, in

its present stage at all events, but this question should not be made a political matter, although perhaps it was unwise of me to expect the hon. member from Calgary to treat it in any other way, if any political advantage was to be gained. My object in rising is this. I have been advised by certain people throughout the West that they are unable to obtain seed grain from this Government because their applications were not in early enough. Now, I do not think that should be made a fatal obstacle to their getting seed grain. I am sure the minister can easily understand why some of the applications were not in within the prescribed time. The matter was in such a state of . uncertainty that the farmers did not know where they were; first they were told that they could get seed grain, then they were told that they could not, and then that it was only for farmers on unpatented lands, and so on. I certainly think that the Minister of the Interior should not consider delay in getting in applications a fatal obstacle to the farmers getting seed grain. I think that every 'application which 'seems to be bona fide 'should be considered and help given, and I hope the minister will be able to assure us that the mere fact of being late in getting in their applications will not prevent these farmers from getting the seed grain which otherwise they would have been entitled to.

a less price and the farmers should have been getting their seed grain for less money than they are being required to pay to-day.
There is another matter which should be considered, and it is the fact that in the fall of 1914 there was coming out from time to time a demand for seed wheat in the restricted or drouth-stricken area. The Government knew on the 10th or 11th of January that in the province of Saskatchewan alone there were 6,000 applications for seed wheat outside of the drouth-stricken area. The Government took no measures then to buy the seed at a relatively low market price, as they could have done. In October, November and December there was not a tremendous break in the price of wheat, either upwards or downwards. I have the figures here, and they show that on the 1st of October No. 1 Northern hard sold at Fort William for $1.07J, and it ranged through the month at $1.04, $1.06, $1.14, the high point being $1.16. In November the price ranged from $1.17, the high point being $1.20, and on the last day of the month it was $1.15. In December it started at $1.16, running down as far as $1.15, and on the 31st of that month the price was $1.22. In January, the market opened at $1.26, and-inside of ten days it was up to $1.32, the price on the 25th of January being $1.39, and on the 30th of January $1.45. The great rise in the price of wheat at Port Arthur and Winnipeg took place in the month of January. If the Government had exercised reasonable foresight it might have purchased all the seed wheat required in November and December and thus have saved from 20 cents to 25 cents a bushel to the farmers who ultimately have to pay for it. As the maximum amount to be allowed to any farmer is 400 bushels, a saving of 2o cents per bushel would have meant to him $100. Then again, what was the necessity for the Government employing a special agent to buy this wheat? The Government had its Grain Commission, thoroughly equipped with proper facilities for buying, cleaning and handling seed grain and supplying it direct to the farmers. When the government of New Zealand wrote to the Department of Trade and Commerce asking for a supply of oats, the Minister of Trade and Commerce properly handed the purchasing of the oats over to the Grain Commission, and it is a fair proposition to say that the Government should have asked their Grain Commission to provide for supplying the seed grain. We

have confidence in the Grain Commission, and no doubt the Government has also confidence in it. The Grain Commission is a body in regard to which the present Government take a tremendous amount of credit in western Canada for having it appointed, although the fact is that when this Government came to power they enacted practically the legislation that was prepared in 1911 under the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We have a good deal of confidence all throughout the West in the Grain Commission, and the farmers and business men of the West would consider, had the Grain Commission purchased that grain and handled it, that the work would have been done in an absolutely honest and economic manner. I have nothing to say against the man appointed by the Government to buy this seed grain, I know nothing about him, but it strikes me that he has not handled the situation in an economic manner, and for that the Government must assume responsibility. When we look at the market price of wheat for five months prior to the time this seed wheat was purchased, it becomes evident at once that more was paid for the wheat than can be justified. I am convinced that the Government have paid too much for the grain and in the long run the western farmer must pay for it, and this year, at all events, he will not be in a very good condition to do so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The chief complaint of
the hon. gentleman seems to be that the Government have paid the farmers too much for their grain, because, of course, the great bulk of this grain has been bought from the farmers direct. It is true that the gentleman who was appointed by the Acting Minister of the Interior as a special agent to purchase this grain has in most instances, in order to get first-class grain, paid a slight premium above the market price, but when the hon. gentleman compares the price at Fort William with the price paid to the farmers of Saskatchewan, of course it is an uniair comparison, and he recognizes that himself when the states he had not taken into consideration the cost of bagging and cleaning, which is very considerable. All this grain was pur-, chased from the farmers and taken to the Government elevators.

If I had taken
that into consideration, the price paid by the Government would be higher than the prices I have given, and, therefore, to the

disadvantage of the farmer, who is paying for the seed.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The gentleman appointed is Mr. Lindsay, who I understand is a practical grain man, and who has been in the business for many years. He has had a great deal of experience, and it was his view that it would be much better to have one uniform price that we could charge the farmers for their grain, rather than establish one price for those who had their applications in prior to Christmas, when the price of grain was not so high, and another price for those who put their applications in later when the market price had gone up. It was deemed advisable to strike an average which would be just sufficient to save the Government from loss and such average was estimated at $1.50 per bushel.
As to the Government getting the Grain Commissioners to act as our agents to purchase the grain, I may say that it would he entirely too large a contract for them in addition -to their regular duties. It has really the special attention and consideration of one man, and I have no doubt that the minister had that in view when the appointment was made.

Who was the
acting minister at that time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Hon. Mr. Rogers. He selected this gentleman, and I understand there have been no complaints whatever against him. I certainly have received no complaints in regard to the manner in which he has discharged his duties.
I understand the Minister of Public Works would like to get rid of him now.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
understands that he understands something I do not know about, because I have heard no such statement from the Minister of Public Works. It is true Mr. Lindsay has been rather unfortunate, because he met with an accident while travelling in the discharge of his duties, and he was in the hospital for some time. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Martin) states, and in that he is confirmed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson), that there should be no time limit within which applications have to be received, and that this Government should accept every application, no matter how late it comes in. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Martin) will see that the very argument he is using in regard to the prices charged the farmers would be 85
knocked on the head if we accept his suggestion at this late date when grain has reached so high a price. If you add to the present price the cost of cleaning, the cost of freight, and the cost of bagging, it would make a tremendous addition to the cost we are now charging the farmers. The longer we leave the time open for applications, the higher the price the farmers will have to pay.
It does not matter how high the price is, that would not prevent the Government purchasing at the market price.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
How on earth will the Government know how many bushels to purchase unless there was a time limit for application. There was a time limit set in 1908, and I heard no outcry on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite against it then. There was a time within which applications were received in 1908, and there was a maximum quantity of grain allowed each farmer. We have had some complaints that we are not allowing as a maximum a sufficient quantity of grain to the farmers. In 1908, when the other Government was in power, the maximum quantity was 250 bushels; it is now 400 bushels. We recognize the necessity of having a greater maximum to-day, in view of the larger acreage that is being prepared for crop, and therefore we are allowing 400 bushels as a maximum instead of 250 bushels. We had to have a time limit, otherwise our buyer would not know how much grain he should purchase. That time limit within the drouth-stricken area was the 31st of January. Those living in the drouth-stricken area have no excuse whatever if they did not have their applications in long prior to that date. If there are applications coming in now from that area, there is no excuse, because the whole West was circularized with regard to that time limit. As I explained the other day, in a portion of the country similarly situated, drouth-stricken but without the area set aside, the time limit for receiving grain was the 20th of February. In all other portions of the province the time limit was the 10th of March. I discussed this pcint with Mr. Bruce Walker, who has this matter in charge, and it was considered that that was the outside date at which the Government could have the grain purchased and have it go through all the processes which I have indicated, in order to reach the settler's hands in time for them to put the crop in. He stated to me that no person

n-m

who claims that the time limit should be extended beyond that date to any extent for receiving applications, purchasing the grain, cleaning it, shipping it out and so on, can fairly understand the condition of affairs that we would be up against if we extended the time limit beyond the 10th of March. I am not going to say that this is an absolute law like that of the Medes and Persians, which we cannot change. If the Government has a sufficient stock of grain on hand, and if the individual cases sent in beyond the time limit are found to be extremely necessitous and the grain is absolutely needed and there is no money to pay for it, I am not going to say that we shall not pass favourably upon such cases, because it is much better to allow the farmers to have the grain than to turn around and dispose of the grain afterwards. We had to set a time limit, and that time limit was a very reasonable one.
What will be the time limit for repayment?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The payments are due on or before the first day of January, 1916.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Having listened this morning to the discussion on the question of seed grain, I wish to say that I believe there are not many millers or grain dealers in Canada who will object to the standard of profit established by Government in the purchase and sale of this grain, The Finance Minister told us this morning that the Government was going to spend about $10,000,000 in the purchase of seed grain. And the Minister of the Interior said that the price they were selling the grain at was $1.50 a bushel. At this price $10,000,000 would represent about 6,500,000 bushels of grain. In answer to a question asked in this House, which question and answers will be found in Hansard, the minister gave the average price paid for wheat for this purpose as follows: October, $1.10 a bushel; November, $1.13; December, $1.14 and January, $1.49, an average of $1.21i a bushe'l. The Minister of the Interior told us that the Government were only entertaining applications received prior to the 31st of January. So, we have reason to say that the grain they are selling at $1.50 a bushel they purchased during the months I have mentioned at an average price of $1.21i a bushel. Now, this price was about 10 cents a bushel highei 
than the market price at Fort William. When one buys wheat at ten cents above the market price, we have reason to suppose thatx what he is getting is first-class seed wheat ready to put into the ground. But we will allow them 8i cents a bushel for cleaning and bagging this grain. The difference in freight between Saskatchewan and Fort William will pay the freight to the point where the seed grain is required. This makes the price to the Government $1.30 a bushel, which means that the Government is working on a margin of profit of at least 20 cents a bushel, which, on this deal will represent $1,300,000 as the amount which the Government have to come and go upon in the purchase and sale of this seed wheat. That is all I have to say in that connection. It is a matter which the Government can settle with their borrowers and the people from whom they are buying the grain.
It has been suggested by people in the West that the Government buying this seed grain ought to see to it that all who sow the grain shall be compelled to take out hail insurance; for I understand that the individual farmer loses his crop by hail probably three times for once he will lose it by drouth. I commend this to the consideration of the minister.

I wish to find out definitely if the agreement made with the Alberta government and the legislation passed by the Alberta legislature provides for a lien On the crop grown this year not only for seed grain but for feed advanced to those farmers in the drouth-stricken district?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Is there a similar agreement with the province of Saskatchewan? Has that government agreed to give a crop lien or chattel mortgage for the purchase price of the seed grain?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The agreements are the
same.
