That is, the lien will not only affect the land, but the Government may take security on the crop?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

It struck me there was
something in what was said by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Warnock) with respect to the proposed amendment to the Bank Act. So far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, outside the burned-

out area I do not think it will make any difference. That is, the Government will only get the seed grain mortgage on the crop if seed grain is advanced; and if not, the Government will not have a mortgage, and the bank may advance the money and get that seed grain mortgage. But in the burned-out area in Saskatchewan or Alberta, a man gives a lien on his crop of next year in order to get an advance of feed, fodder or hay for his stock. But if he does not also get seed grain from the Government, where is he going to get it? The hanks will not advance on his security. It seems to me that, so far as the burned-out are,a is concerned, the amendment to the Bank Act will not be of any advantage.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman assumes that a man's credit is gone when he has given a lien on his crop for the feed advanced to him.

The minister will admit
that if the Dominion Government has a lien or a chattel mortgage on the growing crop for the purpose of securing the advance made to him for feed, no bank will advance money for seed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That depends on the amount.

There is no question about it in my mind. As I have said, it may not affect the country outside the burned-out area. There is one other matter: It seems to me the minister has not given us any assurance yet that a man making application for seed grain will get seed grain.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I cannot give that assurance, because I do not know whether the grain can be purchased at this date or what would have to be paid for it. The hon. gentleman was finding fault with the high price we charge the farmer. But I do not think we should be justified in going on the market and buying to-day unless to meet cases that are very extreme. At this time I do not think there would be any excuse for us doing so. Not only that, but as pointed out to me by the commissioner who has looked into this matter very carefully, I do not think we should have time to go into the market and purchase that grain, ship it to elevators and have it cleaned and put in sacks and then shipped and distributed, in time for seeding. I have already said that if, after supplying the wants of the present applicants we have grain on hand, we will cater to the wants of those whose 85J
applications are yet to come in, or that came in after the time limit had expired.

It seems to me that the statements of the minister to-day are not exactly the same as the statements made by him on February 10. On that date he wound up his address by saying definitely that every application would receive proper consideration.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Within the time limit.

No, there was no time
limit fixed in his address of the 10th of February. He said that every application would receive proper consideration. I quite recognize that some time limit must be fixed by the Government, but on the 10th of February the minister did not fix any time limit. He said every application would receive proper consideration. From his statement on February 10 a representative of one of these constituencies in this House would have been justified in saying to any person who inquired about the matter: If you have lost your crop through some misfortune, drouth or something of that kind, your application will receive proper consideration at the hands of the Government. That is exactly what has taken place, and from the 10th of February applications were made out by people in western Canada for seed grain, but they were told definitely that the time had expired and, as I said before luncheon, great uncertainty has existed during the past three or four months in western Canada as to whether the Government were going to supply seed grain. I am not finding fault with the supplying of any amount of grain that may be necessary to care for the people of the West, but I am criticising the way in which the matter has been dealt with by the Government officials in western Canada. The minister and other members will remember that for a period of three or four months every individual in the West was in no doubt as to the supplying of seed grain. Everybody was led to believe by Government newspapers and officials that seed grain was going to be supplied beyond all doubt to every person, whether on patented or unpatented lands, and the letters sent out by the department and statements made in Government newspapers in western Canada did not even fix any limit of area; every man, whether a farmer or a business man, was misled by the circular letters sent out by the Department of Immigration, with headquarters at Winnipeg and by statements published in

the Government press throughout that country. To-day we ought to have some assurance from the minister that, even if a man makes application to-day, his application will receive some consideration. Of course, if the Government cannot get grain, they cannot supply seed, but there was a time within the last five or six months when grain could have been got and got at a much less price than to-day. Take the drouth-stricken area, where the Government knew, when every man in the West knew as early as August 14, when the crops were proven to be a failure, that a large quantity of seed grain would be required, did the Government buy any seed grain? I asked some questions in order to ascertain that', but they were changed to notices of motion for orders, and so I cannot get the information before the close of the session and therefore cannot intelligently discuss this phase of the question. The condition of the matter is simply that for three or four months last fall, when grain could have been purchased at a reasonable price, $1.05, $1.10 or $1.15, the Government purchased a very small quantity of seed grain. I shall not criticise the Government for not looking after people outside of the stricken area, but I do criticise them for not having provided seed grain at reasonable market prices for the burnt-out district. They are charging farmers there $1.50 for seed grain which could have been bought for very much less at an earlier period had they chosen to do so. In so far as my figures given this morning are concerned, I presume it is a fair statement that the Government have probably purchased about
5.000.	000 bushels of seed grain up to date. According to the figures I gave this morning, which are beyond dispute, there has been m one month a loss of 6 cents a bushel, in another of 10 cents a bushel, in another of 24 cents a bushel, by the delay in purchasing grain. It is a fair assumption that on the
4.000.	000 bushels there has been an average loss of 10 cents a bushel, perhaps not a loss but an over expenditure by the Government, so that the total amount that has been over-spent runs anywhere from $500,000 to $1,000,000. It is true that the Government do not lose the money as it will be extorted at a later date from people who cannot afford to pay it. The minister should certainly give us some assurance that every proper application for seed grain will receive consideration at the hands of the Government, even now.

I think if the hon. gentleman were as solicitous about the welfare of the settlers as he is to make capital against the Government on this question he would speak in a different tone. He is adopting a most unreasonable attitude. It has been a most difficult situation to grapple with. We have been doing our very best to meet it. The hon. member blames the Government because they could not foresee last August the amount of grain that would have to be purchased even for the drouth-stricken area. That is most unreasonable. Last January, from within the drouth-stricken area, there were received during four days when Mr. Bruce Walker was in Ottawa- and he estimated while here that there would be 600 applications awaiting him on his return to Winnipeg-9,000 applications.
These applications came to the knowledge of Government officials in western Canada long before January.

A small proportion may
have.
If that is the case the Government officials who have been running loose in Saskatchewan the last six months have not been of much use.

I think they tried to do their duty and have done it well under the circumstances. The hon. gentleman blames us for charging the farmers so much for grain, and in the next breath he urges us to go out in the market and buy at still higher prices. If he would consider a moment and try to deal with the situation as we have tried to do, in a fair manner, he would not be so keen in criticism. The provincial government of Saskatchewan estimated that it would take for relief within the drouth-stricken area one-half million dollars, but they found that in a short time they had expended $1,200,000. The provincial ministers told me that they had not the slightest idea of the extent of relief they would have to grant; and if the hon. gentleman's own friends, living on the ground, could not estimate the requirements of those in destitute circumstances more closely than that, how can he blame us for not having been able to tell, several months in advance, the amount of seed grain the farmers would require. Many applications that have come in have not been legitimate applications. It has come to my attention within the last week that

some farmers have been getting seed grain and selling it to the elevators, and some of them are to-day under arrest for doing so. A great many of those later applications, I have not the slightest doubt, have not been deserving cases; they have not been the kind of cases that we set out to assist in the first place. I have no doubt that the men who have put in their applications since the time limit, after the West had been circularized that there would be a time limit beyond which no applications would be received, could have got credit at the banks to purchase grain. Besides that, 1 understand that the provincial government took up the cases that we are not supposed to deal with and circularized the farmers of the West to meet their agents on a certain day in order to be dealt with; and now, because we do not deal with every application that comes in, no matter whether it was received before or since the time limit, no matter whether we have grain or not or at what price we would have to buy it, the hon-. gentleman is trying to bring the Government into contempt and saying that we 'have not been meeting the just requirements of the western people. I think his criticism is entirely unjustified. It has been a most difficult position, and Mr. Bruce Walker is deserving of praise, not of such censure as the hon. gentleman has passed on him, for the manner in which he has met the situation. The amount of grain that had been purchased up to the 2nd of March was between three and four million bushels of wheat and about the same of oats.
I think the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) made a miscalculation in his estimate of the profit which the Government would make, by assuming that all this was wheat. Now, we did not purchase that quantity of wheat. As a matter of fact, there was- very little difference between the quantity of wheat purchased and the quantity of oats. In addition to that, we purchased some hundred thousand or more bushels of barley.
In conclusion, if we have on hand any grain, after all the just demands that reached us within the time limit have been satisfied, we shall then consider those applications which reached us after the time limit, and shall supply the deserving cases so far as we can. Further than that I cannot go, and further than that it would not be reasonable to expect me to go.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and agreed to.
Mr. ROCHE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 85, respecting seed grain, fodder and other relief.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	*

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 78, to amend the Bank Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.
On section 1-loans for purchase of seed grain:

Does subsection 10 of this section relate to what is known as the secret lien? My hon. friend will remember that we have discussed this principle on several occasions. As I understand it, bankers have the right to secure what is known as a secret lien on any industry, and other creditors of the industry have no reasonable means of ascertaining this liability to the bank. For example, a firm may be supplying goods to some industry or institution apparently doing a good business, but if that industry or institution should get into financial difficulties and fail, the firm that supplied it with goods discovers that the bank has a lien prior to every other creditor, and may not be paid one cent of what is owing to them unless the industry or institution has enough assets to pay all its liabilities; and at the same time the bank gets paid in full. The principle has its advantages, but could not some method be devised by which the bank's lien, if not registered, might be filed in some place where other firms doing business with the institution that has given the secret lien could ascertain what security there was before giving that institution any great line of credit ? I know that one of the arguments in favour of the secret lien is that establishments might go to the wall if the banks were not allowed to help them in this way. But is the good accomplished greater than the evil that may be done to the firm that supplies this institution with goods ? Personally I have not made up my mind on that point. I have discussed it with some manufacturers, who, of course, think it a very good thing when they are giving the secret lien themselves, but a very bad thing when they happen to be the creditor'. Is there not a middle course that could be adopted to overcome the difficul-

ties which have arisen in connection with this matter ?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
During the absence of my hon. friend the other day we had a general discussion of this very topic when the resolution preceding this Bill was under consideration; the matter has also been discussed upon every decennial revision of the Bank Act for a long time past; and the argument which has been suggested rather than put forward by my hon. friend has always been put forward on the occasion of such discussions. In a word, I may say that, so far, it has appeared to Parliament that the advantages in favour of empowering the banks to take secret liens upon merchandise in connection with the carrying on of the trade of the country have b^-en regarded as outweighing the disadvantages which my hon. friend has suggested. I was very much surprised myself to learn that liens are taken throughout the country by the hundreds, if not by the thousands, in the course of a single day. They are taken by branch banks all over Canada. It can be very conveniently done under section 88 of the Bank Act. * These liens may be paid off the next day or the day after. After twenty years' experience, if not more, I think the experience of the business community has been that no very serious disadvantage has resulted from these secret liens. On the other hand, the advantage has been great, enabling manufacturers to get their raw material and to manufacture their product, and then pay off the lien. My own view is that the range of transactions in which the secret lien might be taken should not be extended without the most careful consideration. It was discussed upon the occasion of the last revision of the Bank Act whether the banks should be permitted to take chattel mortgages upon farmers' grain or cattle and other live stock. I think, that while it was not the unanimous opinion, it was the general opinion of Parliament, that it would be unwise, for two reasons. In the first place, it would place the farmer at a disadvantage with the bank itself. A bank would obtain a chattel mortgage on all he possessed. Secondly, it would prejudice the right of creditors, such as storekeepers and others. On these grounds we did not favour allowing the bankers to take chattel mortgage securities. It would be extremely inconvenient, in the multitudinous transactions that take place between merchants, manufacturers and banks, to compel the
rMr. Graham.]
registration of every lien which is taken in respect to merchandise.
The question was raised the other day whether it would not be advisable that these liens which we are now permitting the banks to take under this legislation should be registered. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) took the view that merchants and others would be loth to extend credit to farmers if by chance they might be cut out through the operation of the secret lien. It was pointed out to him that there was not the machinery in the different provinces to enable the Government to provide under legislation of this kind for the registration of liens. I pointed out that in the province of Quebec, for example, mortgages or liens upon personal property were illegal, and that there is no provision in the province of Quebec such as exists in Ontario for the registration of chattel mortgages. Therefore, if at this time we determined that these liens should be registered, as the legislation is general, we should be obliged to create machinery for registration in all the provinces. We might have to enact that they should register these liens with certain courts or officers and that certain fees should be paid. Altogether, if we were proposing to enact such legislation, it would be a matter that would require very careful consideration, which consideration would require a greater length of time than we have, at all events this session, still remaining at our disposal.
There was another feature that was not brought out in the discussion the other day, and that was that the charge for registering these liens would of course be borne by the farmer. In the present condition of the West, which it is designed that this legislation shall aid, it is not advisable that we should increase the charges which may' be imposed by the banks on the western farmers by requiring that these liens shall lie registered. This legislation covers only advances made for a specific purpose-seed grain. Seed grain is vital to the West in order that the crop may be sown. If the crop is a good one, as we all expect, the amount realized from the crop will be many times in excess of the advances made for the purpose of securing seed grain. I think the western provinces have recognized that advances made for seed grain are exceptional and they have special legislation-"dealing with seed-grain mortgages.
There is one other feature that I pointed out the other day, my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) being absent, that is, that this

legislation is temporary. This is not a permanent amendment of the Bank Act.
Not like the tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: War taxation can hardly be described as permanent taxation. This legislation is temporary in character. The legislation will have effect from March 15, 1915, and in order that the banks may not have to await the final passage of the Act, I caused them all to be notified of the terms of the Bill and the form of security which they might take. They, of course, will rely on the Bill being passed in substantially the form in which it now is before tjhe House, and I have no doubt that some of them are acting upon it now. I pointed out also that I had made inquiries from all the chartered banks in Canada as to whether this legislation would be helpful. They all said that the determining, the controlling factor in their extending of credit would be the general standing of the 'borrower. I think that is a sound banking principle, hut it appeared to me also from their replies that it would be of some material assistance to the farmers of the West if the bankers were put in the position of obtaining this additional security. I think that any farmer who is in good standing will be able to obtain an advance for seed grain probably without this legislation, but this legislation may help even his case, and there are some cases no doubt in which the ability to obtain the security may be decisive with the banker in considering the question of whether or not an advance shall be made. I explained the other day that this legislation had not been asked for by the bankers, but that it had been asked for by others-by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. W. H. Sharpe) and by others who are interested in the West and who know the conditions prevailing there.
The minister speaks of this legislation as having a limited duration. What limit does he intend to put to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For the present year. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated the other day that personally he could see no reason why this legislation should not be made permanent, but that inasmuch as it was an experiment we would be better able to judge of its results after we had seen how it worked out. I think there is much to be said for that view. If it turns out that this legislation is useful and not likely to
prejudice the interests of creditors I should be prepared to take into consideration very carefully-because this is a matter that would require very careful consideration- the question of whether it should be permanently embodied in the Bank Act. At present we only go so far as to bring in legislation which will assist the present situation existing in the West.

I am sorry that I was not here the other day when the argument in favour of this legislation was presented. I want to assure the Minister of Finance that I did not have special reference to this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know.

I was considering the larger view as to how what is known as the secret lien of the banks affects industries generally. I have as much confidence as any one in the West that the situation is just temporary and possibly the little difficulties that the West is experiencing now may not be such a bad thing for the country in the long run. I earnestly agree with any attempts that are being made to enable the farmers to get money from the banks. Possibly I would not go so far as to say that this legislation enables banks to give them money, but it enables farmers to get money from the banks. That is the way I prefer to put it. There has been some criticism as to whether the banks are doing their full duty to our great industries in the country in the present time of stress. I will not discuss that question, as I discussed it the other day. It always did strike me as a little anomalous that a bank should have the privilege of getting a prior security over all other creditors without the other creditors knowing it. That is a point that strikes the public as being very peculiar. But that is apart from this question, as the Minister of Finance has explained. I only rose to point out to the minister that I had no reference at all to this legislation because it is extremely necessary, and I would not throw the least straw in the way of having it made clear that the farmers will be able to get money from the banks on the best terms possible in order to tide them over the difficulties that now face them in the West. I have every confidence thait these difficulties will be tided over and that western Canada will continue to be a great and important part of this Dominion.

The minister pointed
out that in some of the western provinces special provision is made for security being taken on growing crops. In the province of Saskatchewan, and I believe in the province of Alberta, the Chattel Mortgage Act forbids the giving of any security on the growing crop other than security which may be given for seed grain. In the chattel mortgage itself the particulars of the grain supplied must be given as to quantities and prices, and an affidavit as to the bona fideness of the transaction is provided for. Consequently, under our provincial law, security on growing crops can be made use of for only the one purpose of purchasing seed grain. As the operation of these provisions in the Bill is confined to advances made only for the purpose of purchasing seed grain, I see no objection whatever to the conditions being made permanent. I understand the minister to say that he only wants this legislation for this year. I think the Bill might very well go through in a permanent form, because it looks like good legislation. If the provisions were that security could be taken by the bank for any other purpose than seed grain, I would object to it, but as it is limited to that one purpose, I think that it is not only good, but that it should be made permanent.

Does not the minister
think there should be some affidavit attached to this schedule in which the borrower could be made to declare that this money is to be used for the purpose of purchasing seed grain? I think the schedule as it now stands may leave an opening for fraud, although I do not think, of courser that the iarmers would be guilty of such a thing.

I am with the hon. member for Saskatoon as to the wisdom of some such legislation as this, and I also agree with what appears to be in his mind that probably there will be permanent legislation on this subject by and by. I do not know if other provinces have the same legislation as to the giving of securities on growing crops as the province of Saskatchewan has. I do not agree with the minister's reasons for not requiring registration; I do not think they are good reasons, with all due respect to the hon. gentleman. There may be some provinces in which there is no provision for registration of any chattel mortgages, but why should that be any objection to having a

provision in this Bill that in any province in which there is provision for registration, these liens must be registered in accordance with the law's of that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the law of the province of Quebec there is no provision for registration, because a chattel mortgage is absolutely prohibited.

That does not prevent you from having a provision in this Bill whereby the lien should be registered in any province where there is provision for registering such a lien, in accordance with the law' of that province. I see no objection to that, but I do see every objection to allowing the banks to take liens without registration. I am satisfied it would work very badly in Saskatchewan, and I can see where a great deal of difficulty would arise. I do not know what the provisions of the law in Alberta and Manitoba are in this respect, but I fancy they are very much the same as in our province. The cost of registering is only 25 cents in Saskatchewan, and	I	think it is	about
the same in other provinces. The fact that there is not such a provision in this legislation will cause the farmers a great deal more loss than the paying of a small fee for registration. There is no doubt it will injure the credit of the farmers generally not to have registration. I have seen quite a number of these seed grain chattel mortgages, and sometimes they are made by mortgagees who have never seen the grain at all, and I have no doubt that in practically every case where the bank advances the money it will not be a delivery of the seed grain at all. If I want to borrow money from the bank I can sell my seed to the bank and then I can re-buy and give my mortgage, and that is the way it will be done. In that way we will find that a very large proportion of the farmers of the West will have their crops mortgaged. There is no objection at all to that in my mind, so long as the liens are registered that everybody can ascertain in the registry office whether or not such a farmer has given security on his crop. I certainly think the minister should never dream of passing this legislation without having a provision for registration in any province where registration is allowed, according to the laws of that province.

I am not at all surprised that a law'yer like my hon. friend (Mr. Thomson) should be in favour of registration, but being a farmer myself I am

very much opposed to it in this case at the present time. My idea was to let the legislation go through as it is, because if you require registration the farmer will have to have a regular chattel mortgage form and that would mean five dollars for a lawyer to draw it up and seventy-five cents for registration. It is in order to do away with these hardships on the farmer that I am in favour of passing this Bill as it is.
I think my hon. friend is a long way off in reference to the charges of the lawyers.

I have paid those fees
before now.
If this legislation requires registration I do not think there is one lawyer out of a thousand who will ever draw a single chattel mortgage.

They would not need to
if the Bill passes in its present form.
They would not need to under the provision I ask for.
If registration is required, you would need to have a regular chattel mortgage.

No. The hon. member
for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) has told us what is required in Saskatchewan, and 1 think the same applies to the other provinces. The instrument will show bona fide for what reason the mortgage is given, and the affidavit of the mortgagee must show the same thing. I think the laws in the different provinces in reference to this matter are much the same. This Act might provide that such a form need not be used, and you do not need to go to a lawyer.
They would go to a lawyer.
My hon. friend need not worry about the lawyers. The farmers are just ias liable to go to a lawyer under the Bill as it is at present than if registration were required.

The remarks of
the Minister of Finance to the effect that he regards this legislation as experimental and that it may be followed later by permanent legislation, brings up the question of the banking facilities in this country. I am not now going to make any long criticism of the situation, but there is a very strong belief	in	the country to-day thitthere is not sufficient banking accommodation	for	the farmers. An excellent example has been set to Canada by other countries which have passed special banking legislation for the benefit and the relief of farmers. I see no outcome of the the present war except the widest kind of revision of our banking legislation with a view to giving greater banking facilities to the farmers. The chairman of the Conservation Commission, Sir Clifford Sifton, a short time ago delivered an address in Montreal in which he pointed out that the great need of the western farmer to-day was banking accommodation and that he could not , get it from the ordinary large banks which had their headquarters in the East and their western branches administered by local managers. I think that criticism was sound. He said further that there was a necessity in the West-and I believe throughout this country-not only for large banks but for smaller banks, very much after the style of the local banks in tho United States, which have proved of great assistance to the farmers in the West. I do not see why a farmer should not be able to borrow money from a bank on his real estate. Progressive banking legislation always makes provision of that kind. The minister says that he will have to reconsider the whole question. I know that he will have to reconsider it after the war is over or before it is over. Having the farmer always in view and that puts me in order-we shall have to have a banking system based on a national currency and a great national bank, the Bank of Canada, made up of all the banks of the country, in the same way as the National Reserve banks of the United States have been created. The latter were created by compelling all the banks in the United States to join in taking stock in those National Reserve banks. The national currency of the United States is the best currency in the world,	and our national	currency is the best currency that we have in	this country. We	are
going to validate certain action taken by the Minister of Finance for a larger use of the national currency. I am not going to blame him for it. Therefore, when we come to deal with banking relief for the farmer, it must be based upon two things, namely, a great national bank to which all the banks will be subscribers, and the emission of national notes in place of bank notes for the use of all the banks comprising the national bank of Canada. That national bank will have another function, namely, to be a bank of rediscount. The country is in need of that great relief. We

I was one of those from the West who took up this matter with the Minister of Finance two or three weeks ago, and he told me that a Bill would *be introduced along the line suggested by myself and others. I was induced to speak to the Minister -of Finance on the subject by correspondence I had with bankers in the city in which I reside. There has been a feeling that legislation of this kind would be of assistance in enabling the banks to advance money to farmers for the purchase of seed grain. The object was if possible to give the banks an opportunity to loosen up a little money for the purchase of seed grain for farmers who were not in the class designated by the Minister of the Interior in the legislation we have just been considering. It seemed to me it would be wise legislation if it relieved the bank of anything that now hampered it in advancing money in such cases. As to registration, I do not think it can make much difference in the present case. In Saskatchewan, in Alberta, and also in Manitoba, we have provision for what we call seed grain mortgages. The only thing for which a chattel mortgage can be given on a growing crop or a prospective crop is for the purchase of seed grain. The present Bill does not change the circumstances, but gives the banks the power to take a lien on a growing crop, and whether it is registered or not, it seems to me, it does not make much difference. As a matter of fact, the lawyers will not profit by this, as has been suggested. Seed grain mortgages in our country are usually drawn, by lawyers, because the document is less simple than a chattel mortgage. But this measure provides a simple form which will be in the hands of the bank, and will be filed in the bank. As the measure is for the purpose of assisting the farmer, it is just as well not to bother about registration. It is provided in schedule G of this Bill:
Inasmuch as the said advance was made on the representation that seed grain would be purchased.
The man represents to the bank that the money he seeks to borrow is required for the purchase of seed grain, and even though he does not buy seed grain, the bank still has a mortgage on his crop. I would not criticise that. For the sake of our financial
institutions and the stability of business, our banks must be protected.
As to what has been said by the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), I have not his theoretical knowledge of our banking system; but I have one criticism to offer. I believe that, so far as the West is concerned, the banks have handled a very difficult situation there for the past eighteen months very well. And, by the way, the Minister of Finance will admit that, so far as the West is concerned, we had a financial stringency long before the war was ever thought of. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) made a speech in this House on agricultural credits in April, 1913, shortly after the Naval debate, in which he spoke of a financial stringency as existing. That was two years ago; and we have had that financial stringency ever since.
In Saskatchewan we have very few manufacturing institutions, and our province is better off since the war than it was before. The war has not benefited the, wildcatter and the real estate subdivider, but it has benefited the average business man and farmer by improving the prices of our commodities. So, financial stringency has not been caused by the war so far as Saskatchewan is concerned. But what I was going to say is that our banks are large chartered banks, not local institutions. They are all controlled in eastern Canada, and the men at the head of them have not the knowledge of western Canada that they ought to have. My only criticism of the Canadian banking system is that vast sums of money are gathered in the cities of Eastern Canada and loaned to great manufacturing institutions in huge sums, and the little fellow in the West has no chance to get any money. That is a criticism that will be agreed upon by men from western Canada sitting upon opposite sides of this House. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance can do anything to rectify that system. It is pointed out that the American banking system is better for local needs than our own. I do not think their banks are as strong as ours, but the advantage of them is that the money is gathered at local points and administered by local men who know and understand local conditions and the needs of the people of the locality. In the West we do not reap the benefit of the money gathered in; it goes to the East, and we do not see it again.

This is a subject that has been discussed a great deal, and I

would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. M. Martin) a question about it. If I understand him, he intimates that money deposited by western people is not used in western Canada, but is sent to be used by eastern people. Now, I understand differently, and I have tried to ascertain the facts. I understand that there is less money deposited, in the West than is used in the West, and that instead of western money coming east, eastern money is all the time going west, But that is the point I raise, and if any one can give me information on it I shall be glad to have it.
I think there can be no doubt about eastern money coming West, but I have been led to understand that there is a large movement the other way. I have no figures to give the 'hon. gentleman.

The matter discussed has engaged my attention during a good many weeks of the last year. There have been many attempts in western Canada to solve the difficulty in connection with the lack of money to carry on not only farming operations but many other operations.
The banking system of Canada, it seems to me, may be considered under several heads. First of all, you have the capital of, the banks. The capital is the property of the shareholders of the banks absolutely. Over that, it seems to me, Parliament should have no power. Parliament has no reason to interfere with what men do with their own money which they subscribe for a corporation called a bank. With that capital they may buy offices, lands, premises-do anything they like. Then, secondly, we have the deposits made by the depositors throughout Canada. The duty of Parliament is twofold: first, to preserve by adequate legislation the rights of the depositor, and, secondly, to insure by reasonable legislation that these deposits are used by the banks for the public interest as well as for the making of profit. Then there arises the third position, that is, the franchise or privilege which is conferred upon the banks by Parliament. By the acts of this Dominion we have conferred upon banks the right to issue paper money to the extent of their paid-up capital. In other words, when three or four men band themselves together as a corporation and call themselves a bank, they have a right to issue paper money to the extent of the paid-
up capital of the institution. That is an extraordinary franchise, an extraordinary privilege, an extraordinary power given to individuals who, by an accident, are able to call themselves a bank instead of some other kind of a corporation. For that franchise this Parliament has a right to hold a bank to the strictest account, and in the exercise of those powers this Parliament must stipulate that they shall be exercised for the public interest and not for the benefit purely of the private individuals. That is the paramount duty of Parliament, and that duty Parliament has always endeavoured to discharge in times gone by by the passing of what are called Bank Acts. But with the development of society, which, after all, is very complex in these days, the question as to what powers and privileges should be given to banks is becoming of immense importance, and the real question we have to consider in this Parliament is to what extent the granting of so large a franchise as the right to create paper money to the extent of paid-up capital of the bank
More than that now.

Yes, more than
that now, but I am speaking generally-to-the extent of its paid-up capital, and the extent to which the banks shall be com pelled to exercise these powers purely in the public interest as distinct from the right to exercise them for their own profit. I think that Parliament has been fairly reasonable in restricting the powers of banks and preserving the rights of the people. I devoted a great deal of time to the matter last fall, and I was confronted with this condition, and it is a very difficult one: the difficulty in the Dominion of Canada lies in the fact that we have too few deposits and that the volume of our wealth is too small. That is the real difficulty; we might as well face it frankly. I took the trouble to-analyse the situation in western Canada. I started out to criticise, and I was somewhat censorious, because I thought the banks had to some extent failed in the discharge of the duties which devolved upon them by reason of the powers conferred upon them by Parliament. What did I find? That west of the Great Lakes the deposits bore no proportion whatever to the loans; there is more money loaned in western Canada by 100 per cent than the aggregate deposits of the people there. When confronted with that difficulty what could I do? The hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin)

says there are no western banks. On the contrary, the Union bank changed its headquarters to Winnipeg, the Northern Crown bank has its headquarters in Winnipeg, and the Vancouver bank has its headquarters in Vancouver. The Weyburn Security Bank has its headquarters at Weyburn, Saskatchewan. The Union Bank of Canada has in western Canada, with but one exception, the largest number of branches, and I once heard a rather distinguished gentleman, a director, I think, of one of the other banks, say that next to the Canadian Pacific railway western Canada owed more to the Union bank than to any other corporation for establishing branches in the West. But the volume of deposits in western Canada is insignificant compared with the loans. Let me give an illustration. The city of Calgary borrowed at one time $4,000,000 from one of the banks in Canada. The aggregate deposits in all the banks in Calgary, outside of commercial loans is, I believe, less than $4,000,000; so that that one corporation, the city of Calgary, had borrowed from one bank as much money as the aggregate deposits of all the citizens of Calgary ! There are two or three corporations in Calgary with loans running from $500,000 to $1,000,000.
I took up the question because many financial institutions in western Canada had come to the conclusion that the only way in which there could be any permanent addition to western Canada's wealth was by a policy of production. I do believe that the future of Western Canada rests entirely upon the development of a settlement plan upon a large and comprehensive scale. I do not believe that any good will be done to western Canada by merely inviting settlers into that country and sending them here, there and everywhere. I believe that in the future, after the period of readjustment and reconstruction comes in Canada, after the war and after peace, the hope of Canada lies in our being able to define, lay down and carry out a carefully prepared and well considered scheme for settlement. That scheme must involve many things which this is not the time nor the place to discuss, but to wrhich I have given some consideration; but in so far as the banking system is concerned, while I started out last fall with the idea that the banks had not treated the West fairly, after a very great deal of attention and consideration, 1 came to the conclusion that we were being loaned about twice as much as we had on deposit, and I felt that my strictures upon the banks
had been somewhat unfair. But to this extent only the banks are to blame for some of the extravagant ideas that have prevailed in western Canada. The first great impetus given to the sale of real estate in Calgary was given by a bank; in Edmonton and other places the same thing may be said. Banks have been buying lands at very exorbitant prices; they have always selected the best corners in communities, and they gave the first fictitious value to land in many western cities. I say that frankly, but the answer given to me is this-

The remarks of the hon. gentleman are very interesting, but it is my duty to draw his attention to rule 13, which states that in Committee of the Whole discussion must be strictly relevant to the question under consideration.

I very much regret that my remarks are so wide of the subject under consideration. I shall defer to the ruling and make no further observations along the lines on which I started out. The whole business of banking in Canada at the present moment, owing to our limited capital, consists in being able to lend the savings of nine persons to the tenth, and the duty of the bank is unfortunately to determine who that tenth person shall be. Until our deposits have multiplied and increased we shall not be able to do more than make the savings of the nine persons suffice for the needs of the tenth. But presently, as our savings and deposits increase, we may be able to lend the savings of four persons to the fifth, and later the savings of two persons to the third, and possibly eventually do even better than that. But I say, in all fairness, after very careful consideration of the circumstances of the situation feeling just as the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) has done, engaging sometimes in somewhat violent criticism, and assuming a somewhat censorious attitude towards the banks, that I am . convinced, first of all, that it was none of my business what they did with their paid-up capital; And, secondly, that having the deposits of various people throughout Canada they should be circumscribed and hedged round by legislation that is sound and based on proper principles, and that for the franchise they enjoy they should be held to the strictest account.
I should say this further. The Minister of Finance has shown a more intelligent desire to meet the demands of the farmers

of the West than any official that I have known for many years, and when faced with the very difficult situation that arose by reason of the shortage of funds on the part of industrial concerns, he went out of his way to endeavour so far as he possibly could to ensure that industrial development should not stop, and that the farmers in all cases where it was possible should receive small loans-because they have only asked for small loans. While his modesty may prevent him from stating it, I should like to say that the circular letter he sent to the general managers of all the~chartered banks last fall, directing their attention to the necessity of doing everything they could to extend credit to the agricultural classes in western Canada, has been fraught with good results, and has done something to alleviate the burden which the farmers have had to bear in days gone by, and has done something to make it possible for them to carry forward their operations, looking forward with a spirit of optimism to the crop that will come this fall. That is my only excuse for tresspassing on the time of this committee, and I very much regret if I have somewhat wandered from the question under consideration and spoken rather more widely than I should hav,e done.

speechtext: Sin no more.

When I suggested to
the Minister of Finance that a declaration or affidavit should be annexed to Schedule G, I did not have in mind the matter of registration at all, but the protection of other creditors. Under the Act as it stands there is nothing to prevent a man from borrowing two, three, or five hundred dollars from a bank and using the money for other than the purposes intended. It is true that Schedule G says that representation must be made that the seed grain will be purchased with the money advanced, but as the hon. member for Regina has pointed out that is protection to the bank. The ordinary creditor with whom the farmer deals should also have some protection, and I am sincere when I suggest to the Minister of Finance that there should be some sort of declaration or affidavit affixed to the schedule, in order to make either the bank or the borrower prove that the money will be used to purchase seed grain. I notice that by section 17 of the Bills of Sale Act for the province of Saskatchewan, in conveying future crops by a bill of sale,

The date of the purchase of seed grain, the number of bushels purchased and the price thereof per bushel must be stated in the mortgage as well as in the affidavit of bona fides.
I believe that if the declaration or affidavit were made out it would close up the loopholes or fraud, and give protection all round. The affidavit could estate the number of bushels purchased, the price per bushel, and declare that the money would be used for the proper purpose.

There was a request I was going to make of some member of the Government, and perhaps as the Postmaster General is new in the Cabinet he will listen to me more kindly than some of the older hardshells. Every session we have employed in the buildings a very competent staff of stenographers to look after the correspondence of the members, and while this staff is fairly well paid during the session, yet there is a long recess, and it has occurred to me that it would be advisable for the Government to employ them as temporary clerks throughout the year when the House is not sitting. I want to call the attention of the minister to the mail service between the city of Sydney and the town of New Waterford. The city of Sydney is the terminus of the Intercolonial, and the town of New Waterford is about seventeen miles distant. New Waterford has a population of 7,500 or 8,000, and the mail is carried

from the city of Sydney to New Waterford by stage coach along the shore, arriving at New Waterford at twelve o'clock and leaving New Waterford again at one o'clock or half-past one. It has been suggested to me that I should bring to the attention of the department the fact that it would be more convenient for the business public of New Waterford if the mail came over the Sydney Louisburg railway in the morning, when it would reach the town of New Waterford at nine o'clock. The outgoing mail might go over the same route, the train leaving about four o'clock in the afternoon, and thus the business 'community of New Waterford would have an opportunity of replying to the letters on the same day, I commend this strongly to the minister. I want to point out that the mails between Glace Bay and the other mining districts are taken in the evening or morning over the electric tramway, and it would meet the wishes of the large community living in New Waterford if the mail could be carried across the steam railway known as the Sydney and Louisburg railway-.
I wish also to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General the fact that the post office facilities in New Waterford are not what they should be. It is a town which has sprung up in ia very short time so that perhaps the matter has not been brought to the attention of the department before, hut the post office there is absolutely too small and too cramped to accommodate that growing community. This perhaps is a matter for the Department of Public Works, and I brought it to the attention of the minister last year. There certainly should be a commodious public building in New Waterford to enable the people there to transact their postal business.
What is the population of New Waterford?

Eight thousand, I think. In the last census it does not appear at all, because it is a mining town that has sprung up since 1910. [DOT] The postmaster, against whom I have nothing to say, whom I do not know at all, runs a grocery and general store, and the post office is in the store. It is perhaps the best building he can get and it is not his fault; but I do wish that the Postmaster General would ask his inspector to visit that locality and make a report.
He certainly will see for himself that it is not a suitable place for a post office. I am not urging this for any political reason whatever. The gentleman who wrote me 86
concerning this matter will not vote for me if I happen to be put up again for election. The same is true with reference to the mayor. I hope the Postmaster General will take into consideration the matters which I have brought to his attention.

The two matters which have been brought to my attention by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) are certainly important from the point of view of the two towns of which he has spoken. The first question to which he alluded was the service between North Sydney and New Waterford. I shall have that matter looked into. If we can accommodate the people of those two places, especially New Waterford, we will do so.

I was sorry to hear the Postmaster General say, in answer to my hon. friend the member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), that he would have an inspection made of the post office facilities at New Waterford, and that if they were not what they ought to be, he would at once place the matter before the Department of Public Works. I do not for a moment want it understood that I am opposed to giving further postal facilities to the town to which my hon. friend has referred; but the course indicated by my hon. friend the Postmaster General is one which has led to great evils which have occurred during the last three years especially, and also which occurred while I was Minister of Public Works. There is too strong a disposition on the part of the post office authorities to unload all those matters of increased postal accommodation upon the Department of Public Works. In some few cases while I was minister, I succeeded in making an arrangement under which better postal accommodation could be given to important towns without the necessity of erecting new buildings. In a case where a postmaster could not give sufficient accommodation, we allowed him a reasonable amount for renting a building, say a large flat in a building, which could easily be obtained

in most of the small towns of Canada, and by means of which ample accommodation could be given for years to come. The difficulty is that the Post Office Department will not allow anything at all to the postmasters that will enable them to give reasonable accommodation to the public. The only alternative is to go to the Public Works Department and to have a new and expensive building erected, which involves heating and a caretaker, and depreciation and an enormous expenditure, as compared with the small expense which would be necessary if the Postmaster General were to arrange with the different postmasters throughout the country to give them some small additional rent so as to enable them to provide additional accommodation.
This is what the result has been in the last three years. I want to call the attention of this Government to it, because I think it is deplorable. I do not wonder that hon. members laugh, because this is the first time I have had to discuss a dismissal in this House. But this was so serious, so glaring, so completely without any reason whatever, that I believe it should be brought to the attention of this committee. Since I was elected to represent the constituency of Medicine Hat and during the time the patronage was handled by my opponent and by another gentleman in whose hands he

placed it, I had no reason to complain of dismissals until this moment. There were practically none until six or eight months ago, when the patronage passed into the hands of some gentlemen who were bound to get rid of every Liberal office holder in the city of Lethbridge, and they have practically succeeded. I do not place the responsibility on the present Postmaster General; he was not the occupant of the office when this dismissal took place. From 1885 until last October, Mr. E. N. Higinbotham was in the postal service in Lethbridge. He became connected with it when the office was first established in that city. He was appointed postmaster in 1906, and had filled that position to the satisfaction of all classes of the community. On the 13th of October, he received this curt notice from the post office inspector at Calgary.
I am directed to inform you that Mr. Alvin Ripley has been appointed to succeed you in the postmastership at Lethbridge and that it is proposed to transfer the office to his charge as soon as the necessary preliminaries can be arranged.
This was the only notice that Mr. Higinbotham received. No reasons were given for the change. There was indignation throughout the city of Lethbridge when the an-nouncment was made. That feeling was not confined to Liberals but was just as strong among the Conservatives of that city apart from the patronage committee. A petition was circulated, not among the people generally, but among the Conservatives in the city of Lethbridge. It was addressed to the Postmaster General. Every person who signed that petition was a supporter of the Conservative party in 1911, and so far as I know is still a supporter of that party. They addressed to the Government the following petition, which I wish to read to show you that Mr. Higinbotham held the esteem and respect of the Conservatives of Lethbridge, that his services as postmaster were satisfactory to the people, and that there were no charges that could be preferred against him as a partisan or as an inefficient official. The petition reads as follows:
Lethbridge, Alta., Oct. 19, 1914.
The undersigned, who have no hesitancy in declaring that they are supporters of the Government at Ottawa, desire to bring to your attention the proposed removal of Mr. B. N. Higinbotham from the position of postmaster at Lethbridge.
We believe that there should be no change in the postmaster. Mr. Higinbotham has given satisfactory service, and we can learn of no complaint whatever from the public. As a matter of fact, no charge has been made against Mr .Higinbotham, who has simply been noti-

fled a successor has been appointed. During the time , he has been postmaster, we do not know of any offensive political conduct on his part. He has been a courteous, painstaking official, giving the duties of postmaster his undivided attention. We feel that it is a grave mistake to remove him from the posititon under these circumstances. We are only too willing to suggest that an investigation should be held, because we feel that an inquiry would establish there was no warrant whatever for the action which it is proposed to take in the case of Mr. Higinbotham.
We are bringing this matter to your attention, as we feel that in cases of this kind it has been your policy to refrain from removing from office men who .have conducted themselves properly.
This petition was signed by about sixty supporters of the Conservative party and was taken to Ottawa by two Conservatives. They made the trip from Lethbridge to Ottawa to present the case to the Government, and came back with some hope that Mr. Higinbotham would retain his position. But after a month of the first notice the office was transferred to the new postmaster. You will observe that in the petition a request was made for an investigation, and I think it had been announced as the policy of this Government that investigations would be granted in cases of this kind. But no investigation was granted in this case. No opportunity was given to Mr. Higinbotham to establish that he. had given efficient service and that he had not been a partisan in any way. Let me say that the only other two dismissals of postmasters that I know of in the constituency of Medicine Hat were the dismissal of the postmaster at Grassy Lake, a small place of probably 100 or 200 inhabitants, and the dismissal at Magrath, a place of 900 or 1,000. In these instances the postmasters were given an investigation, and were removed only after an investigation had been held. But in the city of Lethbridge, where a gentleman held a position in the service from 1885 until 1914, no investigation was granted; no charges were preferred against him and the Conservatives of the city of Lethbridge protested against the Change and sent a deputation to Ottawa to register their protest. I say that there is no excuse for this dismissal. I asked the Postmaster General for the reasons of the removal of Mr. Higinbotham and my question was answered in the House on March 8. I asked:
1.	What was the reason for the dismissal ot Edward N. Higinbotham, as postmaster at Lethbridge, Alberta?
2. Was an investigation asked for?
3. Was an investigation held?
4.	If so, what was the result of the investigation?

To this the Postmaster General (Mr. Cas-grain) replied:
1.	On the 23rd September, 1914, the departmental officers were instructed by the Postmaster General that as soon as the Lethbridge public building was ready for occupation it was the intention to appoint a new postmaster, and the superintendent was requested to keep in touch with the progress made, and as soon as it was ready for the department to take possession to inform the Postmaster General so that the change could be made without delay. This was done in accordance with instructions, and the Post Office Inspector, on the 9th October, was instructed to make the change.
2.	In a petition in favour of the late postmaster, which was received at the department in November last, it was suggested that an investigation should be made, but the appointment to the postmastership and the transfer of the post office to the new incumbent had already been made.
3.	No.
4.	See answer to No. 3.
The argument here is that when the Government build a new post office the new post office must be equipped with a new postmaster, provided that the old postmaster is of Liberal politics. I am sure the present Postmaster General is not going to carry out a policy of that kind. Mr. Hig-inbotham was an able official, a man who had been commended by his superiors; and he was succeeded, not by a gentleman who had had experience in the postal service, but by a gentleman who was managing a retail business in the city of Lethbridge, who knew no more about directing a post office than a child. Another statement made in reply to my question was that an investigation was not granted because the appointment to the postmastership and the transfer of the post office to the new incumbent had already been made. I say that that is not the case, and the facts do not bear that statement out. The transfer had not been made when the request came from the Conservatives of Lethbridge that this removal should not take place. The transfer did not take place until November 23. The new post office was unoccupied and Mr. Ripley did not become postmaster until November 23; and this deputation came to Ottawa during October and asked that Mr. Higinbotham should be retained in office. I understand that the deputation received some encouragement when at Ottawa, that some members of this Government were very much shocked to know that action of this kind had been taken when there was no warrant for it. I understand that very strong expressions were used by some members of the Government. There was a
delay in the transfer of the office from the old postmaster to the new postmaster and the new post office was not occupied for over a month from the time the notice come to Mr. Higinbotham that Mr. Ripley was to succeed him as postmaster. I am dealing with this case at some length because in my particular section of the country it has aroused a good deal of feeling and resentment, not amongst Liberals alone, but amongst all classes of people except those who think the spoils system should be generally adopted. I have here a resolution passed by the Presbytery of Macleod, a church organization which is interested simply in the welfare of the country and of our public service. I read it to you to establish that this particular dismissal aroused a great deal of feeling amongst the people of southern Alberta. Their petition reads:
Tlie Presbytery of Macleod beg respectfully to call the attention of the Right Honourable, the Premier of Canada, to the following:
1.	That there are clear evidences in certain governmental quarters of an attempt to perpetuate the system of distributing political offices among party supporters, which is antiquated, discredited, and hurtful alike to national loyalty and national effeiency.
2.	That on the occasion of his last visit to Lethbridge, Sir Robert L. Borden laid down in public the principle that no civil servant should be dismissed unless on good grounds and after fair investigation.
3.	That in spite of this declaration, Mr. E. N. Higinbotham, of Lethbridge, has received notice of his summary dismissal from the postmastership of that city, without reason or excuse being given.
4.	That Mr. Higinbotham is one of the best known and most highly respected citizens in southern Alberta, being one of the pioneers of Lethbridge.
Further that he has been in the service of the Post Office Department almost continuously since the year 1885, Ailing the position of postmaster for the past eight years.
Further that during all that time he has given most efficient and satisfactory service and commands the confidence of the entire public as well as the loyalty and devotion of his staff.
And further that he has not participated in politics since his appointment to office.
5.	Further that in view of these things this Presbytery do emphatically protest in the name of justice and of good government against this flagrant procedure, and request that the Premier give some explanation of this action and will take such steps as will rectify this wrong.
In so protesting the Presbytery assures the Premier that they are voicing a sentiment which prevails very widely throughput the Lethbridge district.
I have read that resolution merely to show that there was a strong feeling throughout the district over this dismissal, which it

was felt was not warranted. I have tried to establish here to-day, that Mr. Higin-botham was removed without any reason being given, that an investigation was asked for by sixty-five or more petitioners who felt that he should be allowed to retain the office, that this investigation was refused, and that the transfer did not take place for nearly a month after that investigation was asked for, so that there was plenty of time to have held an investigation. Mr. Higin-botham is a type of official that any government should be proud to have in its service. He gives full attention to his office,' and has, during the whole period he has been in the postal service at Lethbridge, had the reputation of giving the public an excellent service, and courteous treatment. I do not think that the department had one complaint to make between 1885 to 1914 about the administration of the post office at Lethbridge. I consider this dismissal as one of the most cold-blooded that has taken place since this Government came into power in 1911. There was abso'-itfiy no warrant for it whatever, and when the simple request for an investigation was made by their own friends, this Government refused to grant an investigation. The statements made in that petition and in the resolution are all non-partisan; they are not made by Liberals protesting against the dismissal of of a Liberal, but by Conservatives or by a representative body like the Presbyterian organization for southern Alberta. I claim that no defence can be offered for this dismissal; and it certainly is no encouragement to the men who enter the postal service to feel that, after they have served the public for as many years as Mr. Higinbot-ham did, and have given good service and kept out of party politics, they will be bound to lose their positions in the end because a few Conservatives want the offices for friends of their own.

I just wish to say a sentence or two in reply to the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), and while I am on my feet I should like to say that I know Mr. Higinbotham, and I can say that everything that my hon. friend (Mr. Buchanan) has said of him as a gentleman well worthy of filling any office is absolutely true according to my own knowledge. I want to point out to my hon. friend from Frontenac that perhaps it is not well to be too severe on the former Postmaster General because he followed what is the method pretty generally followed by ministers of departments in regard to this iniquitous system of patronage, of which many of us on both sides of the

House are tired. We should not be too severe on the former Postmaster General in this case, because he failed to detect that Sir Clifford Sifton was properly a very bad case, largely because he was gravitating towards a camp where that sort of thing has evidently been done up to the present time.

I should like to say a few words in answer to the remarks of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in regard to post offices and post office accommodation. Of course, the committee knows that there are two kinds of postmasters: in some parts of the country postmasters have to furnish their own premises; and in others post office buildings are furnished by the Government. When a member of this House says from his seat in Parliament that the accommodation in his city or town is inadequate, or that inefficient service is being given, I think it is my duty to have the matter investigated, and to send down an inspector of the department to see whether or not there is room for improvement; and if the city or town in which the post office is situated is one in which the Government has built or should build a post office, under the rules which have been followed for a long while by both parties, it seems to me that if the necessity for it is shown to exist, I shall be justified in trying to impress on my colleague the Minister of Public Works the necessity of erecting a suitable building there for a post office.-On the other hand, if this is a town in which the accommodation is furnished by the postmaster himself, the inspector of post offices will be able to inform me whether the premises are sufficient, or whether I should call upon the postmaster to furnish better accommodation.
