I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. McCrea) if it would be fair that-I should treat this old employee harshly by dismissal rather than allow him to go along for the present, without perhaps doing as much work as the other employees, so that he might recover his health and go back to the duties of his office. I leave that to the good heart and good feeling of my hon. friend. If Mr. Genest is an insurance agent and has been carrying on business as such, that would seem to be evidence that his illness was not as we were told, and of course such a state of things would have to be put an end to.

I have not asked for Mr. Genest's dismissal and neither have I said that I have positive proof that he was acting as an insurance agent. I said that was my information, and I am asking the Postmaster General to investigate the matter.
I certainly shall.

My information is that Mr. Genest's health has been so recovered for some'time that'he has been able to act as an insurance agent and is receiving a revenue from that source. I am not asking for his dismissal, but I do say that if he is capable of acting as an insurance agent and derives revenue therefrom, he should confine himself to the work for which this Government is paying him.
I think you are perfectly right.

I wish to cite an
instance which has occurred in my constituency and which is somewhat similar to that mentioned by my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan), but very much worse I believe. Of course, the tu quoque argument is an old argument, and I do not say it is a good argument, nor do I say it is a bad argument, but it has the merit at all events of being often used. My hon. friend from Frontenac (j.u.r. Edwards) referred to a case which occurred in the town of Souris, which is not in my constituency, and he attributed it to the influence of Sir Clifford Sifton. At one time my constituency was part of Sir Clifford Sifton's constituency, and when the Liberals came into power he simply turned out all the postmasters in tnat district. I have about sixty-five postmasters in the constituency, and I can say that only five out of the sixty-five have been changed since 1911.
The case to which I wish to draw the attention of the House is this:	Mr. Alexander McKnight was postmaster in tne town of ooissevain since the very day of iis inception. He was not only postmaster, but he built at his own expense on the main street of the town and in the centre of that streeit a splendid stone building, the lower flat of which was entirely given up to the post office, and he fitted it up with the very best furniture for that purpose. We then had a post office that certainly was a credn to any town of the size of Boissevain. Mr. McKnight was absolutely non-partisan. I could challenge any man in the town or in tne constituency to state that they ever even heard Mr. MeKnignt men,.on politics. In fact, he used to annoy me considerably, on account of the trouble I had with him, because he would not even vote for a school trustee or in the municipal election. He absolutely kept his hanus clean-perhaps I should use the word clear-of all polices in every sense of the term. He was a man in whom the people of the town had the utmost confidence; no more highly-respected citizen ever lived. Well, what occurred? In 1908 or previous to that Mr. McKnight received one afternoon notice that he would have two days to get out of the office and make room for his successor. Then occurred, somewhat similar to w^hat occurred at Lethbridge. The leading Liberal citizens, including among them the man who represented Turtle Mountain constituency and two defeated Liberal candidates, protested against the removal of Mr. McKnight from that post office. They went so far as to do exactly what my hon. friend said they did in the case of Lethbridge, and they sent a deputation to Ottawa, but it was of no avail. I remember a statement made by my partner particularly, who is a good Liberal and none the worse for that, and he said: there is no danger of Mr. McKnight being turned out; the Liberal party does not do things that way. In due time Mr. McKnight was turned out, and the Liberals held a meeting and raised money and made Mr. McKnight a splendid presentation, and every leading Liberal in that district, or so many as could get into my house where the presentation was made, made the statement that it was the last time they would ever vote for Sifton. Most of the hon. gentlemen present are old enough politicians to know that this is a promise that is very quickly forgotten. However, I want to put the facts of his case on record. I do not

know that anything so lhars'h as the treatment of Mr. McKnight ever before occurred in Canada. In view of what occurred then, I will go so far as to say that my experience up to the present in my own constituency in connection with this Government is that they are entirely too sensitive about ohanging postmasters or any other Liberal officials.

I think the Postmaster General has elaborated somewhat and explained what was rather deficient in his previous statement. I understood him to say he would not take any steps to have the post office accommodation improved under the administration of the Post Office Department, but that he would rather look to the Department of Public Works for that. His last remarks on the subject seem rather to indicate that if in the town referred to he found, after consultation with the Deputy Postmaster General, that increased accommodation should be given, he would see that that increased accommodation is afforded. That is where the difficulty is as between the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works, and it is that difficulty which causes large expense in the Department of Public Works. When I was Minister of Public Works it was the same as I suppose it is now: the Post Office Department wants to have as large a net revenue as possible, and it refuses to make any sufficient allowances to postmasters to enable them to give increased accommodation, and so it gets the Public Works Department to erect buildings. The salaries paid the postmasters are small, and so the postmasters only go to as little expense for rental as they can manage to get along with. My point is, that instead of encouraging or insisting upon the Department of Public Works erecting new buildings, which entail all the expense of caretaking and heating and depreciation, if the Post Office Department would allow one hundred dollars, or a hundred and fifty dollars, or two hundred dollars a year, or a little more in special cases, there would be secured that increased accommodation which for a good many years would be entirely satisfactory to the people of the community.
That is what I want to impress upon my hon. friend the Postmaster General. Let him not look entirely to having a surplus revenue in the Post Office Department, but let him look to the accommodation of the public. I hope my hon. friend will be more successful than J was at times in 
urging the Postmaster General to do this very thing. I thought that in many cases if he would allow the postmasters a small additional amount so as to enable them to secure additional accommodation, the public would be thoroughly satisfied, and the country in the aggregate, because the country is large, and there are so many thousands of post offices, would save millions of dollars.

I am very much obliged to my hon. friend for his advice. I will try to follow it; and if my hon. friend comes back to the Treasury benches, if he is not very old then, I hope he will put into practice what he is preaching now.
Mr. PUGSLEY': It is very good advice.

Will the minister make a statement as to the continuation of the franking privilege to the Aberdeen Association? Some years ago, under the auspices of Lady Aberdeen, an association was formed in the city of Ottawa, with branches throughout the West, to distribute literature amongst the settlers in the remote parts of Canada. The franking privilege was given to that association. Volumes of literature were donated to the association, and the ladies at the different centres in the West attended to the distribution of it. From my knowledge of the association, its work in distributing that literature is a very worthy one. At the end of last year the ladies in Saskatoon were informed that the franking privilege would be withdrawn; and as they had a great quantity of literature on hand, they asked me about the matter. I wired to the Post Office Department asking if this were the case and for all information. From that day to this I have not had any response to my wire except an acknowledgment of its receipt. I am told that later the ladies had word from one of their branches in Canada that the franking privilege would be done away with on the first of February of this year.
I understand that is not the case. At any rate, as the matter is so uncertain and as the Post Office Department has given no information, the ladies of Saskatoon have disbanded their association because they cannot undertake the distribution of the quantity of literature that they have on hand and pay the postage on it.

I have heard of this
association before, and I know that it is a most excellent one and one which does very good work. The work done by this associa-

tion consists in this, that the members of the association collect literature from all parts of the country and distribute it in the remote parts of Canada, where libraries do not exist and where it is difficult to obtain literature. For some time this literature has been distributed through the mails gratis. This was easier to do and not so -expensive before the change came as to the -carrying of the mails by railway. Before I get through with my Estimates, I will explain to the House how it is that now we pay much more for carrying the mails by rail than we used to do. The mail matter has increased enormously; and if we were to give the franking privilege of the mails to all the deserving institutions, not only would our revenue decrease very rapidly, but we would have such an enormous mail to carry that it ^vould cost us tremendous sums of money to carry it. I received the communication to which my hon. friend alluded, and I received some deputations of ladies and gentlemen who impressed upon me the desirability of renewing the franking privilege. On the one hand I must say that, after hearing the gentleman, and especially the ladies who addressed me, I would have wished to be able to assure them that I would continue giving them the franking privilege; but, on the other hand, the committee will understand that I have a duty to perform, and that, whatever may be my feelings upon the subject and whatever may be the very good aims that those charitable associations may have in view, I have to protect the revenues of the post office, and I am not able to say yet whether or not it will be possible for me to continue giving the Aberdeen Association, however deserving it may be, the franking privilege. A certain period has been fixed by agreement between me and certain persons who have interviewed me upon the subject.
The minister said that some time he would be able to make some definite announcement. The work of the ' association has been paralyzed by the indefiniteness of the matter.
A very important deputation from Toronto waited upon me upon this subject, and I gave it the answer that my hon. friend is asking for now, and I will communicate to him later.

Will the minister be
good enough to give us a statement of what persons enjoy the franking privilege now?

I will have a statement made and will lay it on the table.

speechtext:
['I have a statement
upon this question which I will read:
The lock for closing mail bags now and for the past twenty years in use in the service having outlived its usefulness, the Ontario Equipment Company In 1912 submitted to the department a lock for which they had obtained patent rights from the inventors, and the firm manufactured 10,000 of these locks for the de partment, it being the intention to have this number of locks tried out in certain portions of the Dominion before giving any further orders.
When this lot of locks was delivered, however, they were found from a post office standpoint defective and unsuitable for the service, and could therefore not be entertained, the department refusing to pay for the same, and the whole lot (10,000) was rejected and returned to the Ontario Equipment Company.
The company then submitted a similar lock, but greatly improved and overcoming all the objections found to the former one, besides being somewhat less costly than the first lock submitted; but, profiting by past experience, before placing an order for this improved lock the department submitted a certain number to practical post office men, as well as to expert locksmiths, in various cities throughout the Dominion. The unanimous report from all these officers was so much in favour of this', '

lock that the department placed an order for 10,000 of them with the contractor, and is now engaged in the organization of a system for the introduction of this lock into the service gradually, it being the intention to thereby spread the necessarily heavy expenditure in connection with the introduction of the new lock through the whole service, over a period of several years.
This lock is repaired free of charge, under a guarantee, for a period of two years, hut owing to the simplicity of the construction, the repairing of this lock after that period is hoped to be virtually nil. The average cost of obtaining new locks and repairing old ones has been between $8,000 and $10,000 annually, and this sum will be quite sufficient for the gradual introduction of the new lock, without increasing the average annual expenditure whatever.
The lock costs 75 cents and the key 18 cents, making a total of 93 cents. The lock formerly used cost 80 cents and the key 20, or $1 complete. We gained 7 cents on each lock, and we have a much better lock.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Casgrain, the House adjourned at 10.52 p.m.
Wednesday, March 24, 1915.']
Has the Postmaster General made any arrangements with the mail carriers for extra allowance on account of the parcel post they are obliged to convey?

No; the contract made between the mail carriers and the Post Office Department provides that nothing is allowed for extra mail matter which they carry, and until now we have not found any case in which we could grant an extra allowance. Some cases seem meritorious, and these we are investigating. The contract

provides that an allowance proportionate may be made to the mail carriers, if they are obliged, for instance, to use more horses or vehicles, or if they are put to some other extra expense. Up to the present time, there was only one case, I think, and that we are examining into it to see if we should grant any extra allowance.

It appears that the inauguration of the parcel post system has resulted in application by the railways to the department for an extra allowance, I think, of nearly a million dollars. I presume the railways are carrying the mails under contract, as the couriers are; and as the department has given this extra amount to the railway companies-at least so I understand, though I may be misinformed-I would suggest that whatever treatment is accorded the railway companies in this matter should be extended to the mail couriers. I know of several instances where mail couriers have to carry a much greater hulk of mail matter than before the inauguration of the parcel post system. I have several cases in mind of couriers Which would make out a good case for extra remuneration for their services. I discussed the matter with the former Postmaster General a year ago, and he said the post office inspectors would be asked to report on each case. Mail couriers in my county have asked for an extra allowance, but no investigation has yet taken place. It might be that the extra allowance in such cases would not be very great; but the fact that the couriers are under contract and technically obliged to do this extra work is no reason why their application should not receive consideration. Even if a courier is not obliged to buy an extra horse, yet he has an extra load to carry and the service is much more difficult to perform. At certain seasons the roads are bad and travelling difficult and the extra weight of mail matter carried by the couriers should be a ground for extra remuneration. The greater the amount of work the greater should he the extra compensation. I think there is scarcely a courier in the province of Nova Scotia who could not make out a case that he is performing extra work by reason of the parcel post system and that extra compensation should be given.

The question raised by the hon. gentleman is an important and interesting one. It has already occupied the attention of the department. The hon. gentleman will remember that a year and a half ago the rates to the railways were changed, and the railways obtain now a

much larger allowance for hauling the mail than they did before. That is not altogether due to the parcel post system but to the fact that the mail matter generally has increased considerably. Before the time to which I have referred the railways were paid $132 per car per track mile; now, they receive 16 cents per mile for a postal car; 9 cents for cars half postal and half express, and 4 cents for a baggage car. This means a great increase in the expenditure of the department-about a million dollars. The railways have applied for additional remuneration because the weight of mail matter is increasing all the time, but they have not yet received it. The department has had several interviews with the railway officials, but we have come to no conclusion. If the mail matter becomes so voluminous that we have to increase the amount already given to the railway corrfyanies it will be only fair that any cases in which the mail couriers can justify their claims, these claims should be entertained by the department; and the hon. member and the committee may rest assured that every case will receive the most favourable consideration and that, consistent with the duty which I owe to the public, I shall see whether ea-ffi case is one in which the allowance should be increased.

I can point out a case in which the Postmaster General would be justified in granting an extra allowance to a mail courier, that is, the contract between Grandigue Ferry and West Arichat in my county. A steamship subsidized by the Federal and Provincial Governments plies between Mulgrave, the terminus of the Intercolonial railway at the strait of Canso, and the towns of West Arichat and Arichat. During the summer the mail is carried by the steamboat to these points, but in the fall, when the steamer does not make daily connections with the trains, the mails have to be carried by the courier from Grandigue Ferry to Arichat. Owing to the inauguration of the parcel post system the volume and weight of mail has increased very considerably. Some months ago the old contract lapsed and new tenders were called for. I asked a question which was answered a few days ago, the question and answer being as follows:	-
Mr. Kyte:
1.	When did the contract expire for carrying the mails between Grandigue Ferry, Arichat and West Arichat, recently held by Joseph Parker?
2.	Were tenders asked for in respect of this service during the year 1914?
3.	If so, when were notices calling for tenders

posted, and what was the last date for receiving such tenders?
4.	Prom whom were tenders received, and what is the amount of each?
5.	(a) Who performed the service since the expiration of Parker's contract, (b) and what is the amount paid for same?
6.	Why was not the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer?
7.	What was the amount of Parker's contract ?
8.	When will the new contract be awarded?
Mr. Casgrain:
1.	31st December, 1914.
2 and 3. Tenders were invited twice. The first notices were dated 20th August, 1914, and tenders were due at the department on 2nd October, 1914. The second notices were dated 3rd November, 1914, and the tenders were due on 18th December, 1914.
4.	The tenders in both cases were considered excessive, and the department has been endeavouring to obtain more reasonable offers. It is not considered advisable to give the names and amounts of the tenders until the new contract has been awarded and executed.
5.	(a) Casie Parker, executrix of the late
Joseph Parker, who was responsible for the service, under the former contract, from 1st April, 1913, to 31st December, 1914.	(b) $3
per day.
S. Answered by No. 4.
7.	$495 per annum.
8.	As soon as a reasonable offer has been received.
After the notices calling for tenders had been posted, I understand some five or six tenders were sent into the Department. It is quite true that the lowest tender was considerably higher than the amount of the old contract, and I understand that is the ground upon which the Department refused to award the contract. The old contract was for $495, and had been running for a great many years. The parcel post system was inaugurated something over a year ago, and the courier complained to me several times that the bulk of mail had increased very considerably owing to the parcel post. He felt that he was, in all fairness, entitled to some additional remuneration. It is obvious that the service could not be properly performed now at the old rate, and, in view of the parcel post, the additional amount asked does not seem excessive; so there is no reasonable excuse for the department not executing the contract without further delay. The department are to-day having the service performed at a daily rate of $3, which would be in the neighbourhood of $1,000 a year; and I do not See how they can defend that rate of payment when they refuse to make a four-year contract for the carrying of this mail at a rate that would be a little less than $2 a day. I fear that the venom of party politics has not been completely
eradicated from the Post Office Department, notwithstanding that it is in charge of a very estimable and amiable Postmaster General. I received assurance from him a couple of weeks ago when I discussed postal matters in this House that he would not allow political considerations to interfere with the efficient performance of public duty by officials of his department. With regard to the tenders received for this contract, I believe that of the six tenderers five happened to be Liberals and one a Conservative. The lowest tenderer is a Liberal. His tender was considered excessive, and he wrote to tlie department making a very substantial reduction in the lowest tender, stating that if the other persons tendering reduced the amount of their tenders he wuuld make a further reduction to keep his tender^ still the lowest. This matter has been pending for many months and the tenderers are awaiting a decision by the department. Meantime some of them have prepared themselves for carrying out the contract by purchasing horses and carriages, thinking that in due course this contract would be awarded. The lowest tenderer particularly had reason to believe that his tender would be accepted. We hear from time to time justification by the Government of their conduct in increasing the salaries of some officials, that it is due to the high cost of living. This would apply with equal force to this mail contract, as the cost of living, the cost of horses, vehicles, feed and wages has increased. We know that in Nova Scotia, as in other provinces, a horse that' could be purchased four or five years ago for $100 cannot be had to-day for less than $150. We know that the cost of feed has gone up enormously. Hay that could be purchased a few years ago for $12 a ton now costs	$20 a ton,
and the same with regard to oats, and as regards the wages of the men required to assist in performing this work, men who could be got a few years ago for ten dollars a month and board have now to be paid $15 to $25 a month and board. All these things should be taken into account when the- department is about to execute new contracts for the conveying of the mail. I submit that the fact that persons do not tender for the^carrying of mails to the same extent to-day as they did some few years ago is no justification for this department's refusing to accept the lowest tender. I am bound to say that in years gone by there- was no class of public servant so

poorly paid as the mail courier. There was always competition among neighbours living in the country communities, which resulted in the mails being carried at a very low price indeed. But circumstances have changed in the last fifteen years in the province of Nova Scotia, and men who were then willing to perform this service for the Government at a very low price have found more profitable employment; and the competition is therefore not so keen as in the past. But I know of no case where the lowest tender for the carrying of mails ought not to be accepted. When tenders are called for in the ordinary course and several tenders are received by the department, the lowest tenderer ought to indicate the lowest figure for which the department should expect this service to be performed. Where there is proof of fraud or collusion between tenderers that is a different matter, and the department would be justified m looking into it; but where there is no evidence of fraud or collusion, and where a fair degree of competition exists between the tenderers, there is no justification whatever for the department insisting upon mail couriers performing this service at a starvation price, especially when it is recognized that all other servants connected with the Government are entitled to extra remuneration on account of the high cost of living. And in the case of the mail carriers there is not only the high cost of living to be taken into account, but the high cost of all the material and plant * which is necessary for the contractor to have in carrying on the service.

Is it the intention of the department to increase the remuneration of the mail carriers in proportion to the increased work, and on account of the increased risk there is in carrying parcel post matter in bad weather. If not, I know for a positive fact that in our part of Ontario there will be a complete smash-up of the service, and it will be no use for the Department to appeal to some of the members to try and have tne tenders lowered. If the pay is not increased .t will be simply impossible to get them to tender.
Mr. CASGRaIN :	I am glaa to have
this expression of opinion from both sides of the committee. I can assure the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) that I do not know the political colour of the gentlemen who have tendered for the mail service to which he has alluded. I was told by the experts in my department that

the demands were excessive. These men have been in the service for a very long while and have great experience, and of course I am bound to take my information, from them, and draw my conclusions to a great extent from what they tell me; for I have no personal knowledge of the service myself. But I do not mean to put any extra responsibility on their shoulders: I have to shoulder this responsibility myself. I think there is a great deal of force in what the hon. gentleman has said, and before I became a member of this House I felt somewhat that way myself on a great many occasions. But on the other hand, and especially in these times, I have to keep down the expenditure of the department, which is increasing all the time. But, consistent with my duty and consistent, with the laudable ambition of keeping down the expenditures as much as possible, I am disposed to increase the allowance to mail couriers.
In reply to the hon. member for Peterborough I think I gave the information he asked for before he came in. I said t"hat the railway companies, on account of the vast increase in the amount of postal matter which they are handling just now, have applied for a larger allowance; and we are actually in negotiation with them, but no conclusion has yet been reached. If we feel that the railway companies are, on account of the increased postal matter, justified in asking for an extra allowance, and also the mail couriers, the matter will be taken into very serious consideration by the department. If it is made plain to the department that the claims put forward by these men are claims that will bear tne light of day, we shall in every meritorious case increase the allowance.

I can see a frightful future if the merit of each case has to be established, because we may rest assured that all the couriers will think they have a meritorious case. Unless some business principle is adopted, the future looks to me extremely gloomy.

Up to the present we have not had a great many complaints on that score, and therefore I do not look to the future with such terror as my hon. friend does. We have had some claims, but not many, on account of the increased postal matter which the couriers have to handle.	-

The couriers in my district have nearly all told me what they expect, and I have assured them that tbn

department will probably treat their oases reasonably; and they are waiting for that treatment.

The Postmaster General told us that he was guided entirely by the officials of his department as to the reasonableness of the cost of a particular service. That is quite proper. But I should like to know whether his officials are taking into account the extra remuneration that contractors ought to be entitled to, on account of the extra cost of living, and the increased cost of the plant and material required in performing the service; also the increased remuneration they are entitled to in respect to the parcels post service which they are performing.
Certainly.

With respect to the particular case I am discussing, that is, the contract for carrying the mails between Grandigue Ferry, Arichat and West Arichat, the minister in answer to a question a few days ago stated that he would execute the contract as soon as a reasonable offer had been received. If I am correctly informed as to the figure submitted to the department by the lowest tenderer, I submit that there is no reasonable excuse for refraining from executing that contract. The circumstance that the service was performed at a lower figure some years ago ought not, in view of the circumstances to which I have called the attention of the committee, to have any weight with the department at the present time. I think there ought to. be no further delay on the part of the department in executing that contract. I am informed that the lowest tender in this particular case was for $650. The contract for years has been let at $495, so the difference in the amount asked for at the present time and the amount that has been paid for the last 15 years, is only $155. In view of the circumstances I have disclosed to the committee, I say there is no justification for the department refusing to enter into this contract. This is the first time that the contract is sought for under the conditions imposed by the parcel post sytem, and it may be taken for granted that those tendering for this service took into account the extra work on account of the parcel post system; so when this contract is let the book will be closed so far as any extra remuneration will be asked for by this contractor during the term of his contract.

Are all the railways being paid for carrying the mails, or only some of them ? I am told that a railway in my constituency carries the mails for the first 80 miles undeT the old Railway Subsidy Act and is paid for that distance, but that for the remaining distance of 120 miles, from Matapedia to Gasp6, they are paid nothing. Is that the case ?
The reason for that is that the railway from Paspebiac got a special subsidy.
This railway is not paid at all.
The department pays 3 per cent of the subsidy to the Finance Department.
Does the minister consider it fair treatment of a railway which has been eking out an existence to compel this company to carry mails without paying them for it?
I am told that this is the law, and that it has been for some time.
Would the minister tell the committee with what railway companies he has readjusted the rate for carrying the mails?
All the railway companies in Canada, except a few which carry the mails for the subsidy I have just spoken of. I have not a list here, but if the hon. gentleman wants it I can give it to him.
The readjustment has been made with the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern, and those that have not received this more generous treatment are the smaller companies?

It is impossible for me to give the information this evening, but if the hon. gentleman wishes it I can give it to him at a later stage. It is with the larger companies that we have made this arrangement.
I would be very glad indeed if the minister could bring that information before the committee when we again take up the Estimates of his department.

Does the minister not think, having some knowledge of the conditions in the Gaspe peninsula, that this railway company should be paid for the service they perform? The manager of the railway was here the other day, and he

spoke to me about the matter. Has there been any change in the policy of the department in regard to mail contracts? What happens when a mail contract is about to expire?
Tenders are called for except in some cases where the contract is renewed because the price is considered satisfactory to the department.
Where there is any change in the price are tenders called for?
Yes.

I do not want to resurrect old issues, but the predecessor of the hon. gentleman cancelled a number of mail contracts in my county without giving the old contractors a chance to tender. I do not want the minister to follow that practice. We were fresh from the fray then, and I suppose that was the reason.

I wish to say a word or two to the minister in connection with the present postal arrangements in the city of Strathcona. Strathcona has been amalgamated with Edmonton, and forms a part of the city. We have a post office in the old city of Strathcona, and, as I understand, the department still recognizes the old city for postal purposes. The new stamp tax is going to inflict a hardship on the people of Edmonton in sending mail from one portion of the city to the other. The department, I understand,, was to change the system or name of the post office as soon as the city of Edmonton agreed upon a proper street numbering system. That system has been in existence now for something like one year, and yet I understand the department has made no move to change the name of the post office and put the office on a city basis, the same as the main office in the old city of Edmonton. I would like to know if the minister has done anything further along this line.
We have not received notice that this change has been made, but as soon as we receive notice we will make the change. We will take notice now from the hon. gentleman.

I give you notice now, because this is a grievance we have been suffering under for a long time. At present a letter from one portion of Edmonton to another is only allowed to go through on a one-cent stamp basis by the courtesy of the postmaster on one side of the river or the other. But in many instances an inexperienced clerk will return a letter for lack of

postage, and great inconvenience is thereby caused to those who are sending letters. I wish to say a word in regard to the question of mail contracts. On the 18th of this month I put the following question on the Order Paper in regard to tenders for carrying the mails between the post offices at Calmar and Telfordville:
1.	How many tenders were received in connection with the contract for carrying mails between Calmar and Telfordville?
2.	What are the names of the tenderers, and the amount of each tender?
3.	Who received the contract?
4.	Who is carrying out this contract, and to whom is payment being made?
To which the following answer was given:
1.	Three.
2.	J. H. Vanalstyne, $400; F. M. Grant, $468 ; I. J. McKinney, $700.
3.	I. J. McKinney offered to reduce his tender to $398, and the contract was awarded to him. The post office inspector reported that McKinney refused to sign a contract and submitted the name of W. J. Dent as a suitable person willing to accept $398. Mr. Dent's offer was accepted.
4.	W. J. Dent.
As a matter of fact these tenders were asked for and the local patronage committee, I regret to say, allowed politics to enter into this case. The tenderer who had put in the highest tender, Mr. McKinney, was recommended by the local patronage committee as being a proper person to receive this contract. Fortunately for the service, Mr. McKinney was a man of high character, and he refused to be a party to any such business as is shown in this answer. Mr. McKinney's tender was $700, and yet according to this return he agreed to bring down his price to $398, two dollars less than the price of the lowest tenderer, who unfortunately had been a liberal and who had been carrying the mail prior to this. When it is suggested that Mr. McKinney had agreed to reduce his tender from	$700 to $398 and had
then refused to sign .the contract it is evident on the face of it that he never made any such agreement. The agreement was made for him by the local patronage committee, who desired Mr. McKinney to do the work. The lowest tenderer was Mr. Vanalstyne, who apparently was completely ignored in the matter. The strange part of this is that Mr. Dent, who had not tendered at all, was awarded the contract at the price of $398. My information is that Mr. Dent is not carrying this mail at all, but that the lowest tenderer, Mr. Vanalstyne, is carrying the mail under a subcontract or verbal arrangement with the

contractor. I submit that this is a most unbusinesslike method of carrying on the business of the department. I do not think the Postmaster General knows anything about it, but these answers, on their face, would indicate that the return is absolutely incorrect. I wish the Postmaster General would see that everything is quite right in connection with this contract.

I will look into that
case.

1 wish to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the condition of the post office service in a part of Montreal which has come under my notice. Westmount and Notre Dame de Grace are two parts of Montreal which have progressed most rapidly during recent years. On Victoria avenue, Westmount, close to the limits of Notre Dame de Grace, the post office there is kept by a gentleman named Fry, with his wife, and his brother. No allowance is given for that post office, and it is probably the post office in which most business is done in Westmount. The post office returns show the gross receipts from it to be $13,000 with 7,604 money orders issued to the value of $65,000. With the exception of St. Catherine Street West post office and St. Henri it is I think the largest sub-post office in Montreal. The building is a small shanty of about 25 feet wide and 40 feet deep, and in addition to it being a post office it is a book-store and news-room. At certain hours of the day, men, women, and children who go there have actually to stand out on the sidewalk to wait their turn before they get into the building. That post office building is nothing less than a disgrace.

Is that a post office
where mail is received only, or is the mail distributed from it?

I think it is only a mailreceiving station. The distributing post office for Westmount is at the corner of Greene avenue and St. Catherine street and this office is on Victoria avenue, which is a transfer point for the urban and the city f street cars. The gentleman in charge of this post office is a very competent man and one who has given general satisfaction to the public. I asked him why he did not have better premises and he replied that he had asked the department lately for an allowance of some kind and he had been waiting to rent a very nice building on the 87
corner of Victoria avenue and Sherbrooke street, but the department would give him no allowance. If in a case like this the department had granted an allowance to this postmaster to rent a new building which at the time was unoccupied, a great service would have been rendered to the locality, and it would not have been necessary to go to the expense of putting up a large and costly public building in that immediate vicinity. The nearest post office to that on Victoria avenue is the new Yvestmount post office at the corner of Greene avenue and Western avenue, which has not yet been occupied. The old post office, at the corner of Greene avenue and St. Catherine street is a small brick building. I have no doubt that the minister wants to put his postal service on a proper footing and I think he should look into these matters.
The new post office in Westmount will be occupied in a few days.

The new post office will serve the people going down Greene avenue, but it will be of no use to people using Victoria avenue which is quite a distance away. There is another matter to which I would draw the attention of the Postmaster General, and it is that Sherbrooke street, from Victoria avenue, Westmount, through Notre Dame de Grace to Montreal West, is the only avenue towards the West from Sherbrooke street to Montreal West, and is the most frequented boulevard in the western part of the cilty, and there are no post office facilities from Victoria avenue to Montreal West, a distance of three miles. There is an old gentleman named Baker, whom the minister may know, a retired school-master and military man, and he tells me that within the last year he has worn out a pair of shoes walking down to Montreal post office.

What kind of shoes had he on?
Mr. CARV1LL: Was he a military officer?

He tells me he wore out his shoes walking down to the Montreal post office trying to impress on the postmaster and his assistant the importance of having a sub-office in this locality. A number of new stores have been erected all along that street, and I believe that whether the Postmaster General has an embarras des riches or not, he should give a post., office to that locality between Westmount and Montreal West. The post office in Notre



Dame de Grace at present is an old building near the church of Notre Dame de Grace, which was established in the old days when Notre Dame de Grace was a rural municipality, when to-day it is part of the city of Montreal, and the main traffic through it is now on Sherbrooke street where there are no post office facilities. A sub-post office should be erected halfway between Victoria avenue and Montreal West. I hope the Postmaster General will look into these two glaring cases which I have brought to his attention.

The postmaster at Victoria avenue, referred to by my hon. friend, gets an allowance of $200 a year for rental and besides he gets a commission on all stamps, postal notes, and money orders that he sells, so that, it seems to me, he should have suitable premises for the business done there. I understand that this is a suboffice where stamps, postal notes and money orders are sold, and that it is a receiving office only for mail. This gentleman has an allowance and perhaps he ought to accommodate the public better than he does. As to the other stretch of street, where my hon. friend says there are no post office facilities, surely there must be postal boxes?
Yes

My hon. friend says that a great many stores have been erected there recently, and it would seem strange if some of the owners have not applied to the department for permission to sfell stamps. I shall very carefully read over the remarks that are made in the House on this matter, and we shall try to give as much satisfaction as we can.

The public do not know
whether the postmaster at Victoria avenue receives an allowance or not, but they do know that the accommodation is not sufficient. The minister knows the character of the people who reside in Westmount and that they are among the very best class of people in the city of Montreal.
I know.

And when people come to that tumble-down old shanty and have to wait together in crowds to get in as best they can for parcel post and everything else, they rightly think it is not a credit to the Post Office Department. Neither is it a credit to the post office administration to have a stretch of three miles on Sherbrooke

street, from Victoria avenue to Montreal West, without a single sub-post office.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, who, I think, is attempting to give a proper service in the Post Office Department, a condition that exists in my province that requires to be looked into. The service is becoming demoralized.
Oh, oh.

I will point out to the minister and to those hon. gentlemen who say "Oh, oh," why I feel justified in my remarks. Last year, during the session of the House, I found that most of the letters I wrote never reached their destination. Several letters written to me did not arrive. When I returned home I found that a number of people had a similar complaint, and 'a little later on a young man in the post office service, a railway mail clerk, fell under suspicion. The post office inspector put letters into the post office with marked money in them. Those letters disappeared. The young man was arrested, and the money was found on him. He was taken before a magistrate, and for some reason or other the inspector could not find time for several days to appear at the trial. Finally, when the inspector came to the trial, he could not remember the marks on the money; in fact, he could not remember anything, and the case was dismissed, because there was no evidence. Leniency may be a good thing to exercise in some instances; but that is carrying it to an extreme, and it will have a very bad effect on the whole service, because the circumstances are well known. That is the worst case that I have to relate. The whole service, from the top to the bottom, is going wrong. No care is being exercised. The rural mail system prevails very largely in my province. For some reason or another the mail couriers are illiterate men or careless, and the carelessness is extending to every one, so that, when a letter is mailed now, there is no certainty at all that it will reach its destination. The service in all parts of the province is very poor; there is a great deal of insubordination and inefficiency; there is demoralization and worse. I believe the minister is honestly trying to give to the people of Canada a good service, an improvement on that of his predecessor. I ask the minister to look into these matters.

I am very sorry to hear that the service in Prince Edward Island is

as bad as my hon. friend says it is. Did my hon. friend ever report this state of affairs to the department?

I reported it first to the postmaster in my town, because I thought he was the guilty party. I found out subsequently that he was not. I feel satisfied that, if the Postmaster General makes an inquiry, he will make an improvement in the service. It is just as well to be plain. There is a great deal of drinking going on in the department.
That does not apply to the department here.
I hope not.

I promise my hon.
friend to send a teetotaller to that province to make an investigation.

I am informed that a number of post offices have been closed in the neighbourhood of Red Point, and that the post office at Red Point still remains open. If the other offices have been closed, why is the posit office at Red Point left open?
Has the rural mail service been established in Prince Edward Island?

The rural mail service
has been established in nearly all parts of the province.

That is the reason, I
suppose, why the post offices have been closed.
What is the salary of the postmaster at Red Point, King's county?
We will get that information.

In the spring of 1914,
tenders were called for carrying the mail between Cardigan bridge, Cardigan, and An-nandale. Who tendered for that
9 p.m. service and to whom was the contract awarded?

Did the hon. member
ask a question about that?
No.
I am not able to furnish the information this evening, but I will give it to the hon. member.
On the subject of the rural mail system, will the minister tell the committee how the system is working in the lower parts of Quebec?

There were some parts of Quebec where the minister had difficulty in introducing the system, were there not? I understand that in my own constituency tenders were called for, but the department refused to let the contracts because the tenders were too high.
I believe so.

Has anything been done
since then?
We hope that something will be done in a short time.
Are there any rural mail routes in Bonaventure?
No.
Or in Gaspe?
Not yet.
In Rimouski?

I have not before me
the figures as to the different constituencies.
Is the rural mail delivery system paying its way?
I am told that it does not pay, and it never will.
What is the average loss in a year?
I have not the figures before me, but I shall be able to give them.

I understand the system
is not paying in the United States.
No.

What is
the saving from the closing of post offices?
I will look that up.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the rural mail delivery in the county of Lapraire-Napierville. At Saint Constant, in my home parish, complaints are often made to me concerning the Saturday delivery. I will give the facts: When the general scheme was planned, a gentleman was sent from Montreal for the purpose of laying out the route; but instead of taking into account the boundaries of each parish, he took in for example part of I,a Fortune de Saint Philippe, thence through the parish of Saint Constant and up again into the " Petite Cote " of Saint Constant and stopped at a point in the parish of Saint Michel. So that the inhabitants of the Petite C6te of Saint Constant who, before the starting of the new system, used to get their mail at the village of Saint Constant now get it from La Fortune de Saint Philippe, which is at a distance of six miles from the village of Saint Constant.
Everything runs smoothly until Saturday. Then there is no delivery until the next Monday with the result that these people are deprived of the Sunday mail; and it is on Sunday that they most require it. If the boundaries of the parishes had been taken into account in the laying out of these routes, the mail would still be delivered at the village of Saint Constant and the people

could get their mail as usual on Sunday after mass. The minister is quite aware that the farmers who work every day from five o'clock in the morning to eight o'clock in the evening will not find time to read the newspapers on Monday morning.
Will the hon. member kindly tell me why the mail is not delivered on Saturday evening?

I presume that in many cases the mail comes in too late from Montreal; but where I reside, the mail for La Fortune de Saint Philippe, gets in at 5 o'clock in the afternoon. The case of La Fortune de Saint Philippe is repeated all over the county. I should suggest to the minister to have the mail delivered on Saturday evening or else to return to parish boundaries in establishing rural routes.

I am afraid that there is a little too much truth in what the bon. member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. J. J. Hughes), alleges with respect to the Post Office Department. There is a general belief, whether rightly or wrongly, that the postmasters in the country sections are not as careful as they should be and that the secrecy that should be maintained is not observed in these offices. In fact, there is a suspicion that it is not safe to send mail matter through some of these offices. 1 grant that a good deal of that may be due to suspicion. The wholesale dismissals that took place under the late Postmaster General as compared with the almost inappreciable number that took place under the Liberal Administration-
Oh, oh.

-to which I will refer later on, may be responsible for these suspicions. Hon. gentlemen opposite laugh, but it is a fact that, under the late Administration, in the rural districts there were very few dismissals, and these only for cause. The reason for the difference may be that whereas formerly, postmasters were paid only $12.50 a year, and it was hard to get anybody to take the office, while there was no inducement for anybody to seek it, now the salary is $50. You can understand how the party friends will seek the job. The result is that wholesale dismissals of postmasters in country places have taken place under this Government That is a fact that cannot be disputed. I am not saying that the Liberal party are any better than the Gonservative party, I am not saying that they are not just as

human as the Conservative party. I am pointing out the fact and not discussing what may be the answer. Perhaps because of the fact that these wholesale dismissals have taken place under the present Administration, there is a suspicion, that may in many cases be ill-founded, on the part of a certain section of the country, that justice will not be done through these offices; but, nevertheless, there is this fact that some of these postmasters who have been appointed as a reward for political services, think they can do just about as they like.
They cannot.

And it is a notorious fact that under the late Postmaster General, the Iago who presided over the department since 1911, a condition of demoralization has arisen, the service to-day is looked upon with disrespect, it has been brought into disrepute by the ihanner in which the late Postmaster General administered his department. The spirit of the law, so far as the postal regulations are concerned, was practically disregarded by him, the system of awarding contracts after calling for tenders became a veritable farce. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) pointed to a case in his county under the present Postmaster General. I do not wish to say anything in the way of flattery of the present Postmaster General, but the country at large regard his appointment to the high office which he fills as a very much needed and decided improvement, and they feel that under him the postal service will be improved, that there will be a decided uplift in the administration of the department. As far as the service is concerned, I am sure that the country will read to-morrow with interest and with a great deal of satisfaction the assurance which the present Postmaster General gave that he would follow a straighter course and would aim at higher ideals than his predecessor.
I did not say that, I could not say that.

You could not say that ? I am not saying that you did make a statement of that kind in so many words, it would not be. courteous to your predecessor to do so; but we heard from the hon. gentleman an assurance of the course which he intends to pursue, and if he will pursue that course it will be a deviation from the course pursued by his predecessor. I had occasion to point out last year several cases I knew of in my own constituency where the system of tenders was absolutely disregarded, where the late Postmaster General undertook to award contracts to men who were not the lowest tenderers, and did so in violation of the spirit, if not of the letter of the law; cases where, after having awarded contracts, he undertook to wantonly break those contracts without any regard to the fact that a contract is sacred, and that a contract to which the King's name is put should be regarded with a great deal more seriousness than an ordinary contract.
Could the hon. member name any of the contracts given out in that way ?

I named them last
session, I quoted the evidence, I cited the pages of Hansard and the documents brought down from the department, and proved the cases so conclusively that the minister did not attempt to reply, for there was no reply possible to the cases to which I referred. I have in mind one or two of those cases. Let me take the case of the service between Antigonish and Livingstone's Cove. Tenders were called for that service; the lowest tenderer was Mr. John R. McAdam, who happened to be a Liberal. There were five or six tenders, but instead of awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer, McAdam, the department began to look around for excuses to give the contract to one McPherson, who was recommended by the man who had charge of the patronage of the county. McPherson was recommended as a reliable man and iu was alleged that McAdam did not have property in his name. So they searched the records and found there was nothing standing in his name. He was a young man living with his father on a property worth from $2,500 to $3,500. He was the man to whom the property was to go on the old man's death. I think, as a matter of fact, he had a deed although it was not on record. Coming back to his tender, he had two sureties proposed as bondsmen for the due performance of his contract. Some doubt was thrown on one of his sureties, but Mr. McAdam wrote and offered to provide * a guarantee bond from one of the guarantee companies and he also offered two private individuals, each of whom was worth anywhere from $10,000 to $25,000. So there was no possible escape so far as the question of security for the performance of a contract was concerned and, as he said, he did not know that it was

necessary for him to be a millionaire in order to run a mail service. They juggled that contract back and forth. Then the man McPherson, recommended by the man in charge of the patronage and alleged to be a highly responsible person, turned out to be an imaginary man and he disappeared. It developed that his tender had been put in by another person for this man McPherson, who did not want the contract; and the late Postmaster General stated in a letter to the man in charge of the patronage that it put him in an awfully humiliating position. That was the effect of the letter which I read last session. The tenders, as I said, were juggled with and they had to call for tenders again, McPherson having left the country. While they were juggling with the tenders ten months had elapsed. During that time they had to make a special arrangement at $125 a month for which they paid out $1,250. Had they accepted McAdam's figure, the lowest tender, and there was no possible excuse for refusing it, it would have cost only $786, so there was a loss of $464 in ten months, a net loss of 60 per cent. Perhaps the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) thinks that that is good business or is justifiable.
Take another case in my own constituency, and when I can find such glaring cases in my little county with a population of 12,000 what must it be all over Canada? Take the case of the contract between Guysborough and Heatherton. The lowest tenderer there was Mr. Anselm Rogers.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

He had in competition with him a good Conservative, so the forces were brought to bear to see that Rogers did not get the contract. Objection was raised to his sureties and he wrote to the department-the file was brought down last year- and offered two sureties, one the local member, Mr. Trotter, a man supposed to be wonth from $40,000 to $50,o00, and Ithe other Mr. James Tory of Montreal, the local member of Provincial Parliament for Guysborough, estimated to be worth between $75,000 and $100,000. Yet in some way or other they managed to find that Mr. Rogers could not put up satisfactory security and they got him out and gave the contract to Mr. O'Connor. There was a loss to the country in the meantime, owing to their temporary arrangement with Mr. O'Connor, the previous contractor, who was paid tempor-

arily, of $650 in seven months. That was the loss as compared with what they would have had to pay if the contract had been awarded in a proper and businesslike way to the lowest tenderer.
That kind of thing has been going on in other sections of the county, and it has come to this now: No Liberal will put in a tender unless he does it for the purpose of bothering his Tory neighbour and making him submit a lower figure than he otherwise would; but they do not do that. The result is that the Liberals never put in a tender at all now, and there is no competition from that source. The Postmaster General stated a while ago that it was necessary to exercise economy in these strenuous times. That was a very good proposition for him to announce in this House, and one that the ministers on both sides of him might well follow. It is true that it is well to economize, but the service need not be starved, and. the couriers need not be obliged to work for the miserable pittance they get to-day and in the unfair manner in which they are working. If the Postmaster General will cut out the dishonest work that went on under his predecessor and carry out the principles he has enunciated today, and I believe he will, and award the contracts to the lowest tenderers, unless there is some legitimate reason for not doing so-and there may be a few cases of that kind-he will save hundreds of thousands of dollars all over the country, and be able to give the couriers something like reasonable pay for the service they are supposed to perform. There is a suspicion in the country, perhaps not very well founded in all cases, that the postmasters have not that conception of their duty which they should have, and it would be a good thing if the Postmaster General, now that he is new in the office, would inaugurate some system of discipline whereby their attention would be called to the fact that they are the servants of the public; and I am sure they would appreciate that themselves.
Some hon. gentlemen have referred to dismissals under the late Administration. I want to say that during the nine years I have sat in this House I have not recommended a single man for dismissal on account of political partisanship. Not a man in my district has been dismissed on account of his politics, or dismissed at all so far as I know, during the nine years I

have sat in Parliament; and my predecessor did not dismiss a single man in the county of Antigonish during the time he sat in this House from 1896 onwards. I have made some recommendations, and six new postmasters have been appointed. All of these were Tories, hut it was not because they were Tories that I recommended them, but because they happened to be situated in the most convenient part of the section. The late Postmaster General was not governed by any consideration of that kind, for in two places particularly, which I pointed out last year, he placed the post office at the extreme end of the district; and when the matter was brought to his attention he promised to look into it, but I do not think lie ever did. I refer to the post office at Doctor's Brook and the post office at Middleton, both in Antigonish county. Both post offices are at the extreme end of the district where they are not a convenience to the people at all. As I was saying, I have recommended six new postmasters during the time I have been in this House, and they were all Conservatives. I made no distinction between Liberals and Conservatives. Of course, other things being equal, I will be frank and say that I would recommend a Liberal. But the first consideration was the convenience and accommodation of the public, and that being so, I did not hesitate to recommend Conservatives when these vacancies occurred. There are 95 postmasters in the county of Antigonish and 19 of these have been dismissed under the present Administration, and more would have been dismissed but for the fact that the rest of them are nearly all Conservatives. In our time we made no distinction and, as far as my county is concerned, the majority of our postmasters were Conservatives; but I am bound to say there was not a single man against whom there was the slightest suspicion of improper conduct. I am bound to say that the postmasters in Antigonish county with scarcely an exception, Liberal and Conservative alike, are all straight and honest and can be depended on; they will do nothing crooked, which cannot be said of the postmasters in some other parts of the country. That is the record. I did not intend to say as much as I have, and I should now like to inquire of the minister why the contract for the service system between Antigonish and Sherbrooke was not awarded to the lowest tenderer? The tenders were received at the office of the Postmaster General on the 11th of December last. I think. The details
are given on page 51 of Hansard. Nine tenders were received, but seven of these were withdrawn, and I want to know why the Postmaster General did not award the contract to the lowest- of the two that were left. In this connection I may say that it sometimes occurs that persons put in tenders with the expectation of being bought up afterwards, and I have the suspicion that some of those seven put in tenders with that expectation, and had no intention of running the service when they put in their tenders. I can understand a case of that kind, and particularly with.this service. A few years ago there was a man on that route who ran a store halfway between Antigonish and Sherbrooke and did a large business, and he could afford to run the mail very much cheaper than anybody else. In fact, it was necessary for him to have a coach on that route in connection with his own business. It was currently reported at that time that certain persons tendered on that service who tried to hold up this man, also a tenderer, for a consideration to induce them to withdraw their tenders. As I was saying, I should not be surprised if some of these seven put in their tenders with the expectation of being bought off, and when they found there was nobody to do business with them withdrew their tenders. Perhaps they had put up no surety at all. But why was the contract not awarded to the lowest tenderer, and why did the department last December or January decide to call for new tenders?
When these tenderers withdrew their offers we had a suspicion that there was collusion between them.
Between whom?
Between the different tenderers, and that is why we called for new tenders. We received new tenders, which are much more favourable to the Government, and we have accepted one.
Has the contract been awarded?
If it has not been already let, it is being completed.
Did the minister receive any reports that there was collusion?
I do not think so, but it looked very suspicious, and that was our honest belief.

And when you arrived at that conclusion you decided to call for

new tenders? That was your sole reason for calling for new tenders?
Absolutely.

The hon. member for
Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) has re-[DOT]presented to the minister that, in the laying out of a certain rural mail route, an inspector from Montreal laid out the route in a way that did not give the best service to the parish. We have a similar case in the neighbouring county of Huntingdon in connection with the rural mail route between Hallerton, Barrington and Hemming-ford. An inspector from Montreal looked over the rural mail route and, I understand against the advice of the people to be served by that route put in the mail service to Hallerton from Barrington instead of from Hemmingford. I have a complaint from a merchant of Hallerton who is, I suppose, the largest user of the mail service, that owing to this route coming in from Barrington the service is delayed by from twenty-four to thirty-six hours. It has been represented to me that a much better and more satisfactory service could be had coming in from Hemmingford. Will the minister take this up with his department and have it looked into. In this connection I would like to know what the policy of the department is in regard to rural mail delivery routes where a majority of the patrons along the route refused to sign for the rural mail delivery? Does the department insist upon putting in a rural mail delivery against the wishes of the people?

To the first question
I would answer that the matter is actually being studied by the department and we will certainly take into consideration what my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) has said this evening. As to the second question, we do not grant a rural mail delivery on any route except where fifty per cent of the patrons have signed.

Would the minister make a short statement as to the progress of the parcel post system, and say whether he has in view an improvement of the system so as not only to widen its use but to cheapen its cost?

We are now studying this important question of parcel post in Canada. We have some special officers who are making a study of it. This is a question which I have not been able to master yet. It is a complicated question, it is a difficult

question, it is a question in connection with which one has to see what has happened in other countries so as to be able to lay down rules which will apply to this country. We are extending the system as much as we can. The parcel post service has been greatly extended in the city of Toronto, where, I believe, there are more parcels sent by post than in any other part of The country. In the province of Quebec we are also trying to extend it as much as possible. We are sending men around to introduce the system and show the people and merchants especially that there are considerable advantages to be derived from the use of this system.

If the minister will cut the price in half and put the cost below that of the express companies he will not have any difficulty in getting people to use it. As long as the public know that they can send an article just as cheaply by express as by parcel post and have the express company call around for it and deliver it at the other end, you can rest assured that the parcel post will not do a very flourishing business.

I am informed that
our charges are in many cases below those of the express companies.

There has been a great development of the parcel post system in the United States and all other countries where it has been adopted, and a courageous policy, looking to the development of the parcel post system, will make the Post Office Department the greatest public service department we have in this country. The more liberal the policy is in that direction the better the service will be and the more prosperous and useful the department will become.

The deficit in the
United States due to the parcel post system is $17,000,000.
And the saving to the people is enormous.

I want to say a word in regard to the parcel post. There is a feature of it, I know, that has received the attention of the hon. gentleman's predecessor, but I do not know how far he had succeeded in working out the difficulty. It is a matter of very great importance in the rural sections. We have hundreds of mail stage routes in various parts of the country. A considerable part of the revenue of the people who operate these routes was derived from the carrying ol parcels. The inauguration of the parcel post system has

very seriously affected the income of the men engaged in this occupation. There is no question that on many mail routes in the province of Ontario, and I dare say in the other provinces, the contract for carrying the mail was awarded at a low rate because of the passenger and small freight business that the owners of these stages did. I understand that the railway companies made certain representations to the Government and that some consideration has been given to them on account of the introduction of the parcel post system. That seems to be right and reasonable, but it also seems to me that persons who are engaged in the carrying of the mails on the various stage lines throughout the country have just as good a ground for demanding consideration because of the undoubted doss which they have been subjected to on account of the inauguration of the parcel post. I spoke about this to the Hon. Mr. Pelletier when he was Postmaster General, and he said that he was giving it very serious consideration. I do not know how far he got in his consideration of the subject or whether he reached any conclusion or not. It would not be reasonable to expect that the present hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain) in the short time that he has been in office has been able to work this out, but I do ask him to give it his very earnest consideration. I have many letters from different couriers who complain that their revenue has been cut down because of the parcel post, and I have told them that I had no doubt that in time the Government would give the matter its consideration and that they would get redress.
