Mr. Chairman, in 1907 and 1908, Justice Dugas, then member for Montcalm, had succeeded in obtaining the promise of a post office for St. Jacques de l'Achigan in the county of Montcalm. When I was elected in his place, Mr. Dugas said to me:	Mr. COMMONS
Lafortune, it is only after much trouble and hard work that I succeeded in obtaining this post office; I hope, sir, that you will carry on what I have begun. I pledged my word of honour that I would do all in my power to continue his work. In 1909, when I became a member of this House, the late Government at my request voted $15,000 for this post office. The land was bought, the plans were prepared and I was delighted to be able to spread the news that the post office was to be built at last. In 1910, all was about ready, with the exception of a survey which remained to be made and which occasioned .some delay in. starting work on the building. Then the unfortunate year, 1911, came upon us and the fate of the post office fell in the hands of my hon. friends.
Did a strike take place?

And the $15,000 which had been placed in the Estimates at my request were no more to be seen in the Estimates of the second session of 1911-12. At that session, I applied for it, and nothing was granted; in 1912-13, I renewed my application, but was again refused. Before prorogation in 1913, I grumbled a little; I told the ex-Postmaster General that it was unfair to have left out this item; I insisted so much and I grumbled so much that I secured the promise that at the next session this item would be put back in the Estimates. In the Estimates of 1914, I did, to my delight, find those $15,000 in the Estimates. I was glad that at last justice should prevail. But now I find that nothing has been done. The $15,000 were there right enough, but figures on paper do not build post offices. This year that amount again show's up in the Estimates, but if nothing be done towards construction, I am no better off. Do you call that justice? Is not the newr Administration bound by the obligations entered into by its predecessors? I take it that when a Government has decided upon the construction of a post office, it must be in earnest and convinced that such a building is required for the public welfare and I say it is of especial necessity in that parish. I know the spirit of justice and sense of fair play of the Postmaster General and I put the question to him whether that project will long be left in abeyance. I therefore ask the Postmaster General-and I take this occasion of congratulating him on the trust that has been placed in him by the Prime Minister, on the confidence he has been shown by his electors, and on his elevation to a post of 
honour; he is one of the most brilliant advocates of this Dominion-to him then as minister and lawyer, I plead for fair play and ask him to give instructions for the construction of that post office. Otherwise he would fall a good deal in my esteem; not that further negligence would do me any harm; on the contrary, the more inefficient an Administration proves, the greater advantage can an opponent derive from exposing it; and I should make the most of it. But I personally am not in question here; I only seek to obtain justice for my constituency, because I say that once he is elected, a member represents not Liberals or Conservatives but all the electors of his county. The same holds good for ministers of the Crown; they have to adfninister the affairs of the country not for the advantage of Conservatives or Liberals only, but for the public weal; all must receive at their hands the same measure of justice. Will the hon. minister delay any longer the building of this post office? The candidate I had the good fortune of defeating at the last election is the one to oppose the proposal, intending thereby to get even with me. But so far as I am personally concerned, I do not require this building; I have my residence at Saint Laurent, in the county of Jacques Cartier; but the electors of Montcalm are anxious for it. We can see the $15,000 item in the Estimates, but we cannot see the foundations of the building. The ex-Postmaster General has been raised to the Bench, so much the better for him. He was a good friend of mine, although now and then we had our little wranglings. He had seriously considered the request of the electors of Montcalm, but the post office is still where it was. I insist once more that the minister see to it that the people of Montcalm receive fair treatment. Let him take Government supporters as architects, favour Conservative contractors and engage Tory workmen, if he would, but let him give us the post office. Otherwise it will be said that justice is denied those electors, and surely the minister would not have that said of him.
There is another small post office I wish to speak about. I had the misfortune of having it christened " Lafortune." An investigation "was made into charges against the postmaster, a poor man who had one arm severed by a threshing machine. His dismissal v'as asked but nothing improper could be brought home to him. But as he had to go, a scheme was devised: the post office was closed; then later it' was reestablished under the name of " Marion," my opponent, and another postmaster was

appointed. From what I know of the Postmaster General's sense of fairness, he will not countenance those petty devices; he is above any meanness of that kind and had he been in office at the time, he would not have allowed such a thing to pass. I am confident that he will take into his special consideration what I have said in favour of the electors whom I represent _and, I trust, will represent for a long time to come.
I heard what was said by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Hughes). How could you expect that a court would without hesitation condemn an unfortunate employee of the Post Office Department who has taken 25 cents from a letter when the minimum penalty is three years. I have suggested and I insist again that the law should be amended so as to require the registration of every money letter. . If that were done, we would be spared the sight of good young men, belonging to respectable families, sentenced for the theft of 25 or 50 cents to three years in the penitentiary. There can be no surprise if the courts do all they can to save these young men from such a fate. The public, of course, must be protected; but I think it would receive more protection if the registration of all money letters was made compulsory. Registered letters, being easily traced, are not stolen; unregistered money letters are those that excite temptation. The minister knows that these thefts are committed by sons of respectable families, who have been recommended for their position by judges, senators or members. Not a week passes but application is made to me for the arrest of some of these unfortunate young men. It is a painful part of my duty. We should take away from these employees the opportunity of theft. If I thought the Government would favour a Bill to that effect I would introduce it immediately, but of what use would it be if it does not receive Government support. Some people steal $50,000 and $100,000 and they are sentenced to a few years only.
Will the minister please tell me if the post office which has been built in St. Laurent's parish will soon be open for business?
Yes.

I
seconded Mr. Monk when ,he asked for this po-st office, because in my opinion it was necessary. Although I am not member for that county, I have my residence in that parish, and I say that the post
office should be opened soon. I therefore make a special request for it.
Mr. Chairman, as I have said, I hope that the minister will give instructions to have the work on the post office at St. Jacques de l'Achigan started without delay, so that at the next session, if I have again the honour to sit in this House, I shall not have to scold the minister, with whom I -wish to stand well, provided he treats me with fairness.

Just a few words in reply to my hon. friend. And first, let me thank him for his compliments. Apparently he wanted to please me particularly so as to induce me to build the post office at St. Jacques. Unfortunately I am not Minister of Public Works, and the building of post offices does not pertain in any way to my department. I would suggest that my hon. friend repeat his speech rvhen the Minister of Public Works is present, and I fain would believe that lie will grant his request.

He
will so long as you recommend it.

The hon. member may rest assumed that I shall recommend this post office. But he has no idea how hard-hearted the Minister of Public Works is. I have asked him for a number of post offices in my own county, but I have not yet been able to obtain them.

In that
case, 1 shall help you.

Another question has been raised by my hon. friend; that is the punishment that should be meted out to those who steal letters My hon. friend, who has much experience with the Criminal Code, knows the seriousness of this crime and the consequence's it entails. The post office employee is a trustee, a servant of His Majesty, an agent of the people. If he fails in the performance of his duties, the punishment must be proportionate to the offence. Perhaps the penalty which is now provided is somewhat excessive-I am not prepared to discuss this point', but, in any case, it is a question which deserves the consideration of the Postmaster General and the Minister of Justice.
The interesting suggestion of the hon. member, that the public be compelled to register money letters, has been given out

again and again, and several times it was attempted to enact such a law. The attempt was made to introduce legislation to that effect such as exists in France- and I 'believe it is the only country where it is in force-but could never be adopted, because it could never find favour with public opinion. The Postmasters General who have sought to place this enactment in the statute 'books, have always met with opposition from the business community.

the impression that a new post office has been opened on St. Catherine

Mr. BOULAY' (Translation):	Yes. A
number of the settlers on that line come from the county of Rimouski, and that is why I am particularly interested in their welfare. Those good people ask for a daily service. I am
very thankful to the hon. member for having called my attention to the state of things that exist in that locality, and I can assure him that the question he has raised will have the immediate attention of the department.
Post office, outside service, mail service, $8,144,805.50.

What are the names
of the supervisors of Ithe parcel posit system? Where is the division between the eastern division and the western division?

Mr. GRAHAM.; What is Mr. Ross's position?
Superintendent of the city post offices for the western division. He is a most efficient officer.

A few weeks ago I addressed a letter to the department in regard to the mail service between River Bourgeois and Cannes and the railway station at Sporting mountain. That service has been a source of great dissatisfaction and complaint to- the people served by those two post offices. The Cape Breton railway runs from Point Tupper, the terminus of the Intercolonial, to St. Peters, and carries the mail for the post offices along the route. River Bourgeois and Cannes are two post offices that serve a community about two and a half miles from the station. At the present time the mail courier carries the mail from those post offices, to the railway station in the evening, and the mail is taken aboard the train and carried to St. Peters, where it remains overnight. The consequence is that all letters for Halifax, St. John, Montreal and all post offices west of River Bourgeois must be mailed in the afternoon about three o'clock. They are then carried to the railway station at Sporting mountain, put aboard the train and carried down to St. Peters, where they lie over night, and the next day they are carried west. The result is that those people have not the advantage of a daily mail service. What they ask for is a connection between those two post offices and the railway station morning and evening, so that letters that are written overnight or early in the morning may be taken Ito the railway station and despatched to their destination by that day's train. I had this matter up when Mr. Lemieux w'as Postmaster General in the late Government. He submitted it to his officials, and I believe the reason why they refused at that time to give this additional accommodation was on account of the cost. It would probably be double the amount which the department is paying at present for carrying the mail between those two points. Those two post offices serve about 1,200 people. There are six or seven merchants in the village. There is a church and a telegraph office; and the inspector
of schools for the district of Richmond and Inverness resides in the village, and he receives a large quantity of mail from day to day. A petition was forwarded to the department -some years ago, but it was refused on the ground of the increased cost. When the department is spending so much money for rural mail delivery throughout the Dominion, from which it does not expect, according to a statement made by the Postmaster General to-night, that the expenses will ever be paid; and inasmuch as t$ie people receive no advantage from a rural mail delivery in the county of Richmond, or as a matter of fact in any portion of the Island of Cape Breton, I do not think it too much to ask that an actual daily service at least ought to be given to this large district. Even though the revenue to be derived from the post offices to be served by this contract should not be sufficient to pay the cost of giving the people the service requested, I think under all the circumstances that that ought not to be an insuperable hindrance to the carrying out of the improvement which is so much desired. As I have said, we have no rural mail delivery. We do not expect it; there is no demand for it, at present at all events. I wish the Postmaster General would take this matter up and show his determination to advance the postal accommodation in all parts of the country by acceding to the request of the people of that part of the constituency I have the honour to represent, and not permit the consideration of one or two hundred dollars additional cost to stand in the way of this improvement in the public service. The Postmaster General was good enough to state, in reply to my letter of a few weeks ago, that the matter khould be given further consideration. I realize, however, that the case will be submitted to the same officials who had it under consideration a few years ago. No doubt the same objections will be raised by these officials against the improvements I suggest, such objections as were urged against the carrying out of the improvements in the mail service between Grandi-que Ferry and West Arichat to which I referred a few hours, ago. I do hope the officials will take a broader view of this matter than they have taken in the past and will give to this important community the accommodation which very much less important communities have in all parts of Canada, a real bona fide daily mail service between the post office mentioned and the railway station.

I had the matter up with my officials a short time ago. They are not so hard-hearted as the hon. gentleman thinks they are. The only reason why I have not come to a conclusion on the question is that during the session, as the hon. gentleman will understand, it is extremely difficult to settle these matters. I am constantly interrupted by hon. gentlemen coming to see me, and whom, of course, I am very glad to see. But it is difficult under such conditions to reach a conclusion in matters of this kind. We hope that the session will not last long, and then we will take the matter up again. I hope to convince the officials, if they are not of my opinion and the hon. gentleman's, that we ought to have the service that he asks for.
I should be glad to communicate the expression of good will on the part of the Postmaster General to the people who are so anxious for the improvements which I suggest.

I wish to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that the rural districts in my portion of the country, and I believe throughout Canada generally, are not given as good postal facilities as they deserve. In my constituency there are a number of places where they get a mail only weekly or twice a week. For years the " back to the land " .movement has been agitated. I do not believe there is a community in the Dominion-I am confident there is not in the province of New Brunswick-that ought not to have at least a daily mail. I would not give anything for the young man who wished to remain on the farm unless he could get his daily paper. Those of us living in other communities where we get our mail five or six times a day-and feel much put out if the mail is delayed by an hour-ought to be able to realize that people in a country district who receive a mail only once a week are not given proper mail facilities. I know the answer will be given that has been given on former occasions-that there is no revenue from these post offices. I remember coming to Ottawa a few years almost purposely to try to secure better mail accommodation and postal facilities for a certain community of forty or fifty farmers within four miles of the incorporated town of Sackville. I was met with the objection that there was no revenue from this post office. I answered that if a man got his mail there on a Monday he was not going to wait until next Monday to mail the reply. The post office 
at Sackville was given credit for the business of this smaller community. I speak on behalf of the country districts, especially those in my own constituency, but I believe I am voicing the opinions of the Maritime Provinces and of the Dominion generally. I believe we can do more to keep the young man on the farm, and to promote the " back to the land " movement by giving the people postal facilities than in any other way. We spend millions of dollars to get people to come from foreign countries to occupy the, very land from which we are driving our young men because we will not give them proper mail accommodation. I am a new member of this House, and do not know what the late Postmaster General did or did not do. But I have every confidence that the present Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain) is anxious to improve the service of which he is the head. I believe there is no department of Government that deserves more or better attention than the Post Office Department. If there is one department more than another that the people expect to get good service from it is the Post Office Department. I am not speaking on behalf of the large centres because they have very good accommodation now; but I do speak for the rural districts and ask the Postmaster General to take this matter into consideration and see if something can be done.
I am not finding fault; the Post Office Department has done very well. But I believe that more can be done, and in a way that will bring satisfaction to people in rural places. I strongly contend that they have not been given fair consideration in the past. Nor am I finding fault with this Government more than with the other.
I came here more often when the other Government was in power and received very poor treatment as to securing proper mail facilities for the constituency I now represent. I would ask the Postmaster General to give attention and see what can be done to improve the mail service in the country districts.

Since the Postmaster
General is disposed to do something for the improvement of the mail service, I would call his attention to the service on the International railway. I believe this matter has been brought to his attention already. This railway communicates between St. Leonard and Campbellton, a distance of 116 miles, and makes a connection between the Canadian Pacific railway, the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial railway. They

have no mail service on the train. It has been asked for on several occasions within the last two years, but nothing has been done. There are many settlements along this railway line, and they have no mail accommodation of any kind.
Does my hon. friend say there is no mail service on the railway?

No good service anyway; for it takes three days for a letter to reach Campbellton from Edmundston, a distance of 150 miles. While I am on my feet, I wish to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that the revenues of Canada are not well distributed so far as public buildings are concerned. I am ready to give some figures with reference to revenues from post office and from customs. And, as this money goes to the treasury of Canada, 'I think that these places are entitled to receive consideration.
In the town of Edmundston, with a population of 2,000, we have a very poor post office and the service is sometimes not good on account of the lack of proper accommodation. There is a postal revenue at Edmundston of $2,800 yearly, and during the last five years Edmundston has given to the treasury of Canada $150,000. Yet we have no public building. I notice that from Claire, during the past five years, the Customs Department has received $91,000. At St. Leonard $58,000 has been paid. We have not even one public building throughout the county of Madawaska. I bring this fact to the attention of the Postmaster General in the hope that he will make an effort to have a public building erected at Edmundston. The revenues are there, as I have shown, and we are surely entitled to one public building.

As I told the hon.
member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune), the erection of post offices and public buildings is not in my department, unfortunately for me; but I will make representations to my friend the Minister of Public Works and see whether I cannot bring him to build some more post offices, especially in my own constituency.
I see an item for drivers of automobiles, etc., for the post offices, $8,000. Does that include some of the cities where they collect letters by motor?
In Toronto we have a great many motor trucks collecting mail, and the system is a very good one. We have motor cars in other cities.
In Montreal?
No, the transfer of mail there is done by contract with the Montreal Transfer Company.	.
How many of these other motor cars are there? I mean the ones that do not carry mails but the other kind of males?
One in Ottawa, one in Montreal, one in Toronto, one in Sherbrooke and one in Quebec.

Yes.

This one must have been going about fifty miles an hour, violating all speed laws; it was too late for post office hours, and it seemed to me that every official in the city must have had one that night. Yes.

In offices which are called revenue offices, where the postmaster is paid simply by the revenue, we do not appoint; but in the offices which are called semi-staff offices, where the postmaster is also paid by a proportion of the revenue, we appoint the employees ourselves and establish the salary. In some post offices in my own county, Sackville, Shediac, etc., are the employees engaged by the Government or by the postmaster?
By the postmaster.
I understand that the Post Office Department have supervision over the employees. .
To this extent, that if complaints were made we would tell the postmaster that he had to get other help.

I do not wish to make any charge against any pai'ticular postmaster, but maxxy complaints have come to me by letter, supplementing my own personal knowledge, that the young men and girls employed in these post offices are inefficient and do not attend to their duties properly; for instance, letters are all mixed up and placed in the wrong boxes. It is unpleasant for a citizen to have to makeaconx-plaint about these matters. I know that the mistakes are not committed wilfully, but some more stringent regulations should be made and enforced by the department, so that people would not be under the necessity of either putting up with that class of service or else making formal complaints. People do not like to do that sort of thing, which would perhaps lead to the dismissal of a neighbour. . In case of a charge being laid an investigation is held, and it is not pleasant for a citizen or a man in business to appear as complainant. Proper supervision is not made of the post

offices where the postmasters employ help. I see by the Postmaster General's report that in some places the postmasters rent buildings. Is there any possibility of them renting buildings of a certain price and receiving a higher allowance for rental from the Post Office Department?
The Post Office Department pays them an allowance based on the revenue, and the postmaster is bound to provide suitable pi'emises from his allowance.
The department might allow a postmaster $400, who is only paying $200 rental. Could that happen?
He must give adequate accommodation.

Adequate is a very elastic
word which can be interpreted in a great many ways. Take Sackville, for instance. I am not finding fault because there is not a better post office there, but I should like the Postmaster General to urge his colleague to put up the building for which a lot costing $8,000 has already been bought. I think this discussion
would not oe complete if we did not ask the present minister whether the famous padlocks have proved satisfactory and the number that were purchased during the past year.

I have a statement
upon this question which I will read:
The lock for closing mail bags now and for the past twenty years in use in the service having outlived its usefulness, the Ontario Equipment Company In 1912 submitted to the department a lock for which they had obtained patent rights from the inventors, and the firm manufactured 10,000 of these locks for the de partment, it being the intention to have this number of locks tried out in certain portions of the Dominion before giving any further orders.
When this lot of locks was delivered, however, they were found from a post office standpoint defective and unsuitable for the service, and could therefore not be entertained, the department refusing to pay for the same, and the whole lot (10,000) was rejected and returned to the Ontario Equipment Company.
The company then submitted a similar lock, but greatly improved and overcoming all the objections found to the former one, besides being somewhat less costly than the first lock submitted; but, profiting by past experience, before placing an order for this improved lock the department submitted a certain number to practical post office men, as well as to expert locksmiths, in various cities throughout the Dominion. The unanimous report from all these officers was so much in favour of this



lock that the department placed an order for 10,000 of them with the contractor, and is now engaged in the organization of a system for the introduction of this lock into the service gradually, it being the intention to thereby spread the necessarily heavy expenditure in connection with the introduction of the new lock through the whole service, over a period of several years.
This lock is repaired free of charge, under a guarantee, for a period of two years, hut owing to the simplicity of the construction, the repairing of this lock after that period is hoped to be virtually nil. The average cost of obtaining new locks and repairing old ones has been between $8,000 and $10,000 annually, and this sum will be quite sufficient for the gradual introduction of the new lock, without increasing the average annual expenditure whatever.
The lock costs 75 cents and the key 18 cents, making a total of 93 cents. The lock formerly used cost 80 cents and the key 20, or $1 complete. We gained 7 cents on each lock, and we have a much better lock.
